title: The Seeds of State Capture: Merit and Patrimonialism in the Colonial Bureaucracy
authors: SARAH BRIERLEY, NOAH NATHAN, GEORGE KWAKU OFOSU, TINGXUAN ZHU
abstract: Bureaucracies vary in the extent to which hiring is meritocratic versus patrimonial. Such outcomes are typically seen as the result of politicians’ behavior. However, politicians often delegate hiring to existing bureaucrats. When political leaders are socially distant from communities they seek to govern and these areas are peripheral to politicians’ core interests, bureaucrats’ private preferences can dominate hiring decisions instead. Colonial and other forms of external state-building typify cases where patrimonialism created by bureaucrats, not politicians, can emerge. Digitizing individual-level records across six decades of British rule in Ghana, we find evidence of patrimonialism rather than meritocracy in the hiring of African staff, with large inequities across ethnic groups. Our results demonstrate the underexplored agency of local bureaucrats in state-building and highlight conditions under which bureaucrats’ preferences, rather than only political principals’, shape state institutions. They also challenge conventional wisdom about why, and when, newly-independent African states became “neopatrimonial.”

title: The Influence of Police Unions in Local Elections: Evidence from U.S. Cities’ Spending and Performance
authors: MARIA CARRERI, EDOARDO TESO, RUI YU
abstract: Despite growing attention to local policies governing public safety issues, and mounting reports of police union spending to local candidates, the role of police unions in local politics remains understudied. We address this gap by assembling a novel, large-scale dataset on campaign finance in U.S. mayoral elections, covering 2,303 races across 1,073 cities from 2001 to 2019. We document that police unions frequently donate to mayoral candidates—especially in mid-sized and large cities—targeting likely winners and incumbents, and without displaying clear partisan bias. Using a within-city design that accounts for heterogeneous treatment effects in the presence of staggered treatment timing, we find that the election of a police-union-backed mayor leads to an expansion in police department size. However, we do not find improvements in police performance in these cities, suggesting that unions’ political involvement, while providing additional resources, might also be associated with reduced incentives for effort.

title: Who’s Asking Whom? Gendering in Parliamentary Interactions
authors: Denisa Kostovicova, Tolga Sinmazdemir, Lanabi La Lova, Vesna Popovski
abstract: Male domination is asserted and reproduced through speaking behavior in parliaments. We address the enduring challenge of women’s marginalization by examining the interactive nature of speech. People adjust their speaking behavior based on the gender and status of those with whom they interact. Analyzing over 2,500 question-and-answer sequences in the Croatian Parliament (2004–20), we identify interactional asymmetry: male MPs ask fewer and shorter questions of female ministers than of male ministers, and engage in shorter exchanges with women than with men. Notably, female MPs partially replicate this pattern, posing shorter questions to female ministers. Female ministers, however, use their executive status to assert authority and respond with longer answers than men, despite their marginalization as women. We reveal how non-cooperation through withholding speech and limiting engagement with women operates as a form of power in interactions, reproducing parliaments as masculine institutions whilst affecting the quality of government oversight.

title: Energy Burden and Satisfaction With Democracy: The Political Consequences of Market Risk in Germany
abstract: Recent years have seen steep increases in energy costs for households. To date, research on the political consequences of this emergent risk is limited. To explore this relationship for the context of Germany, we leverage an instrumental variable design, drawing on zipcode level data on energy prices, household expenditures, and individual political attitudes. We present causal evidence that rising energy costs contribute to decreased satisfaction with democracy (SWD). We argue theoretically and show empirically that the effect is driven by a pocketbook mechanism. By centering the consequences of household energy cost, we contribute to existing lines of research investigating the relationship between perceptions of economic well-being and SWD for the specific context of energy markets. The political implications of rising energy prices will likely become increasingly salient in the future, as governments tackle the challenge of designing socially just energy transition policies.

title: Unforging Autonomy: The Political Subordination of Brazil’s Itamaraty
authors: Katherine Bersch, Gabriela Lotta, Mariana Costa Silveira, Izabela Correa, Kutsal Yesilkagit
abstract: Understanding how bureaucratic autonomy is undone is as important as understanding how it is built. We develop the concept of unforging autonomy to describe the unraveling of supports that sustain bureaucratic independence. Autonomy rests on two pillars: internal institutional arrangements and external constituencies that sustain legitimacy. Drawing on thirty-one interviews and documentary evidence, we examine Brazil’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Itamaraty), long considered a paradigmatic case of bureaucratic autonomy. We show how former President Jair Bolsonaro exploited vulnerabilities in the diplomatic career system by politicizing promotions and postings, weakening professional norms while turning diplomats’ external alliances into political liabilities. The case reveals how interventions targeting seemingly narrow institutional weaknesses can undermine deeply entrenched bureaucratic autonomy, with broader implications for the resilience of established institutions.

title: Tilting at Windmills: Evidence on Momentum and Hot Hands
abstract: Successes and failures often appear to propagate. According to one common belief, the experience of winning or losing can alter the cognitive and emotional state of performers, generating a psychological momentum that helps or harms subsequent performance. This belief is often used to rationalize the so-called hot-hand phenomenon, and has been applied to contexts ranging from horseshoe pitching to stock market trading. However, the existence of a causal effect of winning on subsequent performance remains debated. I test whether wins cause more wins (and losses more losses) using a large natural experiment involving almost a quarter billion online chess games. I find that performance is serially correlated, consistent with the existence of hot hands. Surprisingly, however, I find no evidence of causal effects. Players that were given a small random advantage in one game have no advantage in the next. The null effect is precisely estimated, providing credible evidence against the hypothesis that success breeds success in online chess.

title: Happy Pills? The Health Consequences of the Dramatic Increase in Antidepressant Use
authors: Giuliano Masiero, Fabrizio Mazzonna, Sandro Steinbach
abstract: This paper examines the health consequences of the rapid increase in antidepressant consumption in Switzerland (2002–2014). Using a shift-share instrumental variable approach, we exploit regional variation in sales driven by product innovation (the shift) and the market power of pharmaceutical firms (the share). Our findings reveal that a one defined daily dose per 1,000 inhabitants increase in antidepressant sales raises hospital admissions for adverse drug reactions by 18% and for depression by 6%. Financial incentives for self-dispensing doctors and reduced access to psychotherapy emerge as key drivers, highlighting concerns about overtreatment and suboptimal prescribing practices.

title: Opposition Strategies and Democratic Transition Failure: Affective Polarisation and Institutional Fragmentation in Post-Gaddafi Libya
abstract: An extensive literature has investigated the importance of governing political elites in the transition from authoritarianism. However, we still know very little about the role of opposition forces, especially in conflict zones within the Global South. This article addresses this research gap by analysing how parliamentary opposition strategies contributed to Libya’s transition outcome. It examines the opposition strategies directed against the Islamic majority within the General National Congress, the country’s first elected parliament after Gaddafi’s fall in 2011. It uses primary data drawn from semi-structured interviews conducted in 2023 with former politicians, academics, political journalists and non-governmental organisation (NGO) activists. The findings illustrate how, although opposition strategies were aimed at countering Islamic influence, they resulted in the destabilising consequences of affective polarisation and institutional fragmentation.

title: The Winning Formula of the Populist Radical Right: Insider Narratives and the Making of a Representative Claim
abstract: The literature has explained the success of the populist radical right (PRR) through demand-side and supply-side factors, but it has typically adopted an ‘external’ perspective, leaving unexplored how PRR parties themselves interpret their success. This article investigates the winning formula of this party family from an ‘insider’ perspective, drawing on 21 in-depth interviews with representatives of a clear case of PRR success: Brothers of Italy (Fratelli d’Italia, FdI). Rather than testing the causal claims of the literature, we theorise these insider accounts as strategic narratives of success: they show how FdI representatives draw on ideological, organisational and leadership repertoires, selectively appropriate elements of the external environment, and, most distinctively, mobilise valence-inspired self-descriptions (especially coherence) to construct a claim of distinction within the party system. In this context, coherence operates as a strategic device that signals the party’s unity and political consistency – anchored in FdI’s refusal to join broad coalitions – performing discursive work of self-legitimation in PRR normalisation.

title: Ideology and Utopia in the Governance of Migration: The Case of the 2024 Pact on Migration and Asylum and the Common European System for Returns
abstract: This article interrogates the 2024 Pact on Migration and Asylum and Migration and the 2025 proposal for a Common European System for Returns (CESR) through the dialectical relationship between ideology and utopia. Drawing on Ricoeur's complementarity of utopia and ideology, Levitas' Utopia as Method and critical discourse analysis, we examine how these instruments construct an idealised narrative of orderly, efficient, rights‐based governance while consolidating intensive control infrastructures. Findings show that (1) a discourse of urgency and novelty pre‐legitimises restrictive measures, (2) promises of operability and efficiency materialise in expanded data exchange and externalisation mechanisms, and (3) procedural clarity and fundamental rights are mobilised as markers of EU moral authority. We argue that the Pact and the CESR exemplify the complementarity of utopia and ideology, revealing how utopian imaginaries of good governance and ideological border control are not opposites but rather mutually reinforcing dimensions of the European border regime.

title: Emotion and Moral Framing in Migration Aspirations: A Natural Language Processing Study of a U.S. Emigration Reddit Community
authors: Nari Yoo, Jeong Taek Lim, Doohyun Park, Peixuan He, Sou Hyun Jang
abstract: Research on the United States and migration has concentrated on arrival, and much less is known about why people in a wealthy democracy come to want to leave. This study examines 7855 posts written between November 2021 and April 2026 in r/Amerexit, an online community for people in the United States who are considering emigration. Natural language processing identified the themes, destinations, emotions and moral vocabulary of that discourse. Of the 15 themes, four describe conditions in the United States that users give as reasons for leaving, among them healthcare costs, racism and gun violence, and distress about the future; five describe what users expect to find elsewhere; and five concern pathways such as citizenship by descent, remote work and visas. Spain, Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany and France were named most often. The moral language overwhelmingly concerned care and fairness and rarely loyalty or authority, so the grievance is stated as harm done to people. Emotion moved with political events, and differently at each: the month after the US Supreme Court's June 2022 Dobbs v. Jackson decision brought more talk of pathways and more hopeful anticipation, while the month after Donald J. Trump's January 2025 presidential inauguration brought higher anxiety and more care‐based moral language. These posts share a judgement that the United States no longer supplies conditions the writer values, in a domain that differs from writer to writer. Where fear about the country's direction turns that judgement into an intention to leave, we call the orientation political‐affective displacement.

title: Running in Context: Marginalization, Political Ambition, and Candidate Emergence
The decision to stop “counting” explains numerical underproduction in primates
authors: Laura E. Seidler, Lena L. Jannasch, Stephanie Westendorff, Andreas Nieder
abstract: Sequential numerical production requires generating a target number of actions, but the mechanisms governing the termination of counting sequences are unclear. We trained two rhesus macaques to produce instructed numerosities by generating the corresponding number of actions in response to sign numerals or dot arrays. Although action sequences were controlled for temporal parameters, both monkeys performed accurately across both stimulus formats. However, their performance accuracy showed a systematic asymmetry: underproduction occurred more often than overproduction, contrary to predictions from perceptual numerosity judgments governed by Weber–Fechner scaling. This asymmetry was mirrored in reaction times, with longer latencies for underproduced sequences and shorter latencies for overproduced ones. A stochastic accumulation-to-bound model in which a decision variable evolves across counting steps and triggers termination when a threshold is reached can account for both accuracy and reaction-time patterns. These results provide evidence for a sequential stopping process that contributes to numerical production, relating counting behavior to general principles of decision formation.

title: Belonging to a group with shared ideology leads preschool children to resist revising their beliefs despite disconfirming evidence
abstract: Shared beliefs can bring people together but may motivate prioritizing group affiliation over facts supported by evidence. Indeed, affiliation with a group whose membership is tied to shared beliefs (i.e., ideology-based groups) has led adults to endorse and maintain false beliefs. We demonstrate that this resistance to revise beliefs that form the basis of group membership has its origins in childhood. In three studies, 4- to 5-y-old children ( N = 192 ) endorse a claim about a novel causal system and subsequently join a group that shares their endorsement. Children randomly assigned to a focal Belief-contingent condition learn that their membership in the group is based on this claim, framed as a shared belief. We contrast this with conditions where group members hold the same shared belief, but this belief is not a condition for group membership (Experiments 1, 2, and 3), and where group members hold to the same claim framed as a “guess” (Experiment 2). After joining a group, children see evidence that their initial endorsement was incorrect and then have an opportunity to revise based on the new information. Only when group membership was contingent on the shared belief did children hold on to (and act on—Experiment 3) their initial incorrect endorsement. These findings suggest that the affiliative power of ideology has developmental roots; even in our earliest years, affiliative motives override truth-seeking and rationality. Thus, our early-emerging motive to identify with groups may underlie later cases of evidence denial and polarization.

title: Modest loss of sleep increases susceptibility to cybersecurity threats
abstract: Sleep restriction leads to impaired cognitive processing across domains. I examined whether the transition to daylight saving time (DST), typically accompanied by compromised sleep, would lead to an increase in the probability of falling prey to a simulated phishing attack using a fully naturalistic experiment with random assignment and blinding. A predatory email was sent to employees at the University of California, Irvine (N = 11,218) either on the morning of Monday following the transition to DST or one week earlier. The transition led to a ~13% increase in the probability of clicking a suspicious link, without affecting the probability of opening the email or reporting it as spam. These results demonstrate that even modest, mundane, and acute loss of sleep has real-life, potentially hazardous, implications for cognitive function.

title: When Insurers Exit: Climate Losses, Fragile Insurers, and Mortgage Markets
authors: Parinitha Sastry, Ishita Sen, Ana-Maria Tenekedjieva
abstract: This paper uses a range of natural experiments to show how mispricing of climate risk in mortgages and property insurance creates large taxpayer exposures and leads to excess credit flows to risky areas. Our central finding is that the government-sponsored enterprises’ (GSEs) policies for evaluating property insurers are a crucial source of this mispricing. We assemble a comprehensive new dataset on both mortgages and insurance to analyze these dynamics in Florida from 2009-2018. We begin by documenting a breakdown in the quality of insurance provision, with new under-capitalized and under-diversified insurers dominating insurance markets. These fragile insurers have high rates of insolvency, which we show causally increases mortgage defaults after natural disasters. We find that the GSEs’ reliance on third-party ratings of insurers leads them to accept insurance from companies at high risk of insolvency without pricing for it. This creates large taxpayer exposures, with an estimated 25% of the GSEs’ expected losses in Florida coming from insurance fragility. Most starkly, we show that private lenders strategically respond to the GSE mispricing. Mortgage denial rates are sensitive to insurance quality in the jumbo segment where loans are retained, but not in the conforming segment where loans are offloaded to the GSEs. This suggests that, all else equal, fewer conforming mortgages would have been originated if lenders screened insurance fragility as they do in jumbos.

title: Channeled Attention and Stable Errors
authors: Tristan Gagnon-Bartsch, Matthew Rabin, Joshua Schwartzstein
abstract: People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant will, in the long run, fail to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn’t matter or that a distinction doesn’t exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the models. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely to be stable. Whether an error is discovered depends on the structure of the decision problem but is not tightly linked to its level of harm; arbitrarily costly errors can persist while trivially inexpensive ones may be detected. Nevertheless, no error is robust both to changes in the decision environment and to shocks that expand attention: every channeled-attention error is vulnerable to some perturbation that would reveal it. We use the framework to analyze the stability of psychological biases and empirical misconceptions, as well as to explain why fresh eyes catch mistakes, why people use overly coarse rather than overly fine categorizations, and why people recognize errors in others that they miss in themselves.

title: Labor Market Tightness and the Reversal of Inequality Trends in Germany
authors: Christian Dustmann, Martin Friedrich, Carl Gergs, Uta Schönberg
abstract: Germany experienced a sharp rise in wage inequality over the two decades leading up to the Great Recession. However, a remarkable trend reversal occurred in 2010—well before the introduction of the minimum wage in 2015—when wages at the bottom of the distribution began to grow more rapidly than those higher up. This paper attributes the reversal to an increasingly tight labor market after the Great Recession, supported by strong domestic demand, and operating through several interrelated and mutually reinforcing channels. Consistent with this hypothesis, job-to-job transition rates and between-job wage growth rose markedly after the recession, especially for workers at the lower rungs of the job ladder. Concurrently, workers increasingly moved from low-paying to higher-paying firms, compressing the worker-weighted distribution of firm wage premia. Tighter labor markets also reduced assortative matching between workers and firms, lowered the skill premium, and weakened firms’ monopsony power.

title: Competition in Markups: A Theory of the Lerner Index in Networks and General Equilibrium
abstract: What determines demand elasticities and markups in production networks, where firms' demand and pricing are interdependent? I propose competition in markups, an equilibrium concept in which firms choose markups, taking other firms' markups as given. In partial equilibrium with vertical structures, it links upstream demand elasticities to downstream characteristics without backward induction and ties pass-through to the curvature of final demand. In general equilibrium with arbitrary industry networks, it microfounds firms' demand elasticities and markups through their within-industry market shares and four industry-level network statistics---cycle, substitution in production, substitution in consumption, and consumer-price impact. Empirical analysis of Compustat firms from 1997 to 2019 confirms the predicted variation of industry demand elasticities and firm markups. Relative to an exogenous-markup benchmark, endogenous markups dampen the aggregate TFP impact of a productivity shock to an industry's largest firm by 6% for the median industry, and by up to 48% across industries.

title: Optimal Policy Rules in HANK
abstract: We characterize optimal policy rules in a business-cycle model with nominal rigidities and heterogeneous households. The policymaker has access to two instruments: the short-term nominal rate, and lump-sum transfer payments. A policymaker with a traditional dual mandate that targets aggregates uses the same policy rule as is optimal in the textbook New Keynesian model. We then consider a policymaker with a distributional objective. The optimal policy rule now contains an additional term, reflecting the effects of the policymaker’s instruments on consumption inequality. Since, in our model, monetary policy only has very limited distributional effects, this additional term does not materially change optimal monetary policy. Fiscal stimulus payments, on the other hand, have strongly progressive effects and are thus well-suited to cushion the distributional effects of cyclical fluctuations.

title: Fertility and Family Leave Policies in Germany: Optimal Policy Design in a Dynamic Framework
abstract: I develop and estimate a life-cycle discrete-choice model of fertility and female labour supply to study the optimal design of a range of child-related policies. First, I examine two German reforms that introduced wage-contingent parental leave payments and expanded access to low-cost public childcare. I find that both reforms raised completed fertility, with the parental leave reform having a particularly strong impact on highly educated women. Second, I solve for a budget-neutral optimal policy portfolio that maximizes either aggregate welfare or fertility, while ensuring that welfare and fertility do not decline for any education group. I consider four prominent child subsidies as well as the degree of tax jointness. My results show that optimal policy has the potential to increase welfare by 0.5% or fertility by 5.7%. While the solutions are qualitatively similar, they prioritize different policy instruments depending on the specific objective being targeted.

title: Tax evasion at the top of the income distribution
authors: John Guyton, Patrick Langetieg, Daniel Reck, Max Risch, Gabriel Zucman

title: The Choiceworthlessness of Transformative Heroism
abstract: History abounds with transformative moral heroes—agents devoting their lives to uprooting entrenched unjust structures. Though philosophy has said much about heroes generally, this distinctive class remains undertheorized. This matters because they are among our most celebrated moral exemplars, and much of our sense of moral progress rests on them. Yet they characteristically act against familiar constraints on responsible deliberation, pursuing apparently infeasible and inefficacious projects while foreclosing tractable alternatives that would secure demonstrable goods. We establish this tension and argue that the most promising attempts to dissolve it fail. At best, this shows that moral theory is structurally conservative, as its standards of responsible deliberation systematically favor mitigation over transformation. At worst, it reveals a deeper instability in moral theory, as it seems to depend for its progress on agents it cannot vindicate.

title: A Defense of Affirmative Action for Conservatives
abstract: The suggestion that academia should promote political diversity, implying as it does that the status quo is severely deficient, is commonly rejected on the grounds that to do so would require “affirmative action for conservatives.” That conclusion is typically treated as a reductio ad absurdum even by those who support conventional race‐ and sex‐based affirmative action. Nevertheless, this paper defends affirmative action for conservatives on both negative and positive grounds. It argues that since conservatives are discriminated against throughout academia, policies that benefit them in admissions and hiring would not be unjust to those who bear its burden. And it argues that the advantages of increased political diversity would accrue not just to those with heterodox opinions but would improve the intellectual atmosphere of academia at large. Hence, conservative affirmative action promotes the traditional academic mission and its norms of meritocracy, academic freedom, and the pursuit of knowledge; and it is not unjust to those with orthodox political views.

title: Net Migration By Age: The Flow-Difference Approach for Estimation and Forecasting
authors: Hana Ševčíková, James Raymer, Adrian E. Raftery
abstract: Highlights We present the flow-difference method to disaggregate total net migration by age. It models the age-specific flows of in-migration and out-migration to derive age-specific net migration, even in the absence of data on such flows. We show that the resulting net migration predictions are greatly improved over existing methods that model only the net migration totals.

title: The Early Origins of Biological Aging: Maternal Income, Education, and DNA Methylation Patterns at Ages 9–15
abstract: Highlights Maternal income at birth predicts children's epigenetic aging more strongly than later income. Children of college-educated mothers show lower epigenetic age acceleration at ages 9 and 15. Socioeconomic gaps differ by epigenetic clock: PhenoAge attenuates, Dunedin-PACE holds, and GrimAge grows by 15. Girls with faster epigenetic aging at age 9 experience menarche earlier. Higher GrimAge at age 9 predicts slower height growth between 9 and 15.

title: When It Rains: The Dual Impact of Rainfall on Child Survival in Rural Senegal
abstract: Highlights We analyze how rainfall anomalies affect child survival in semiarid rural Senegal. The study uses 50,000 child records over four decades from the Niakhar HDSS, the oldest in Africa. Past rain shortfalls raise child mortality while current rainfall shocks matter less. Rainfall seasonality shapes children’s vulnerability to rainfall anomalies. Food scarcity and disease exposure jointly drive these mortality effects.

title: Racial Inequalities in Health and Social Policy: Examining the Relationship Between Medicaid Spending and Self-assessed Health Among Poor Single Mothers
abstract: Highlights Greater average state Medicaid spending is associated with better self-rated health for poor single mothers. This relationship is stronger for poor, Black single mothers than poor, White or Latina single mothers. Spending variation by state generates substantial spatial inequalities in health. States with larger Black populations spend less, creating a mismatch between effectiveness and implementation.

title: Racial Disparities in Infant Drug Testing: A Research Note
authors: Mallory Dreyer, Cydney M. McGuire, Jennifer M. Silva, Kosali Simon, Coady Wing, Engy Ziedan
abstract: Highlights Black infants were tested for drug exposure at more than twice the rate of White infants. Among those tested, both groups had similar positive rates—approximately 20%. Clinical risk factors explain only 38% of the racial disparity in testing rates. The remaining 61% may reflect differential treatment or unmeasured clinician observations. These findings raise concerns about fairness and trust in clinical decision-making.

title: Citizenship and Immigrant Longevity: Evidence From U.S. Census–Linked Social Security Administration Death Records
abstract: Highlights We link full-count 1920–1940 U.S. censuses to death records to study citizenship and longevity. Immigrant men who were citizens by 1930 lived 7.6 months longer than those without first papers. Sons whose fathers were citizens by 1920 lived 4.1 months longer than sons of noncitizens. Earlier naturalization is associated with greater longevity gains in both generations. Adjusting for fathers’ SES and sons’ early-adult SES reduces the fathers’ citizenship effect.

title: New Materialism, Harm, and Hierarchies in Nature
abstract: This article is about an internal contradiction within the ascendant philosophy of new materialism, namely that its ethical opposition to harm clashes with its ontology. In the first part, I summarize new materialists’ attention to material entanglements and rejection of hierarchies in nature. In the second section, I argue that diagnosing and addressing harm to ecosystems and individuals (almost) always depend upon a hierarchy of beings within that ecosystem and a set of pre-determined potentials/preferences of how individual entities should be, two principles that new materialists explicitly reject. In the conclusion, I suggest that new materialists’ contradictions surrounding harms mean that they can either maintain a concern over ongoing damage to ecosystems and beings or their opposition to immaterial potentials and a hierarchy among beings—but not both. My preferred option is to retain the former and to accept that we must have some hierarchy among and within beings to address ongoing ecological deterioration around us. I close by outlining how new materialism’s key insights might be put in dialogue with other voices on the relation between humans and the rest of the world.

title: America's most “far‐reaching institution”: The work and legacies of the Freedmen's Bureau
abstract: Reconstruction was the American state's first sustained peacetime intervention into local communities, and the Freedmen's Bureau was its most important component. What was the social impact of this program? Using an original data set on Freedmen's Bureau operations, we link the distribution and duration of Bureau offices to local socioeconomic outcomes. We find that the Bureau had positive effects for both Black and White residents of counties that hosted offices. Moreover, these effects were accompanied by the development of local administrative capacity and moderated by office longevity. The effects persisted for decades, though the magnitude attenuated for Blacks and increased for Whites as Jim Crow deepened and local government increasingly oriented policy benefits toward Whites. The findings indicate the importance of bureaucratic organization for policy implementation and suggest the 19th‐century federal government played a larger and more successful—albeit unequal—role in citizens’ lives than commonly believed.

title: Too Much, Too Little, or Just Right? Identity Processes and Motivations Explain Everyday Evaluations of Time Spent on Social Media
authors: Serena Soh, Zhenchao Hu, Sanaz Talaifar, Alan Meca, Noah Vinoya, Rui Pei, Samantha J. Grayson, Sumer S. Vaid, Nilam Ram, Jamil Zaki, Gabriella M. Harari
abstract: Emerging adults use social media—and evaluate their use—while navigating the critical task of identity development. We investigate how evaluations of time spent on social media are associated with (a) individual differences in identity development and (b) situational fluctuations in identity-relevant social media motivations. In our longitudinal field study ( N = 2,251; 87,283 observations), emerging adults forming their identity tended to evaluate their social media time as balanced (i.e., the right amount), whereas those evaluating their identity tended to perceive imbalance (i.e., too much or too little time spent). Using social media to connect with others was associated with momentary perceptions of balanced use, whereas doing so to explore personal and professional goals was associated with imbalance. These findings suggest that emerging adults’ evaluations of their time spent on social media may depend on how well use aligns with identity-relevant needs. We discuss implications for psychological and digital well-being.

title: Seeing and Hearing YouTube: Linking Media Design to Children’s Attention Span and Viewing Control
authors: Minjung Kim, Drew P. Cingel, Allyson L. Snyder
abstract: To examine how audiovisual characteristics of YouTube content are associated with children’s attention span and viewing control, we conducted a two-wave longitudinal survey in 2023 and 2024. The final analytical sample consisted of 195 Korean parents of children aged 4 to 6 whose children reported the same most frequently viewed YouTube channel across both waves. Videos from children’s most frequently viewed YouTube channels were coded for visual (scene changes and special effects) and audio (dialogues and sound effects) features. Structural equation modeling (SEM) results indicated that greater exposure to visual and auditory features in Year 1 content was associated with lower levels of children’s attention span and viewing control one year later. Dialogues, an audio feature, demonstrated the strongest negative association with both children’s attention span and viewing control. These findings highlight the importance of considering the design features of children’s digital media when examining associations between media environments and children's attentional and self-regulatory behaviors.

title: Foreign Faces in the False: Immigrant-Targeting False Posts on Social Media and Their Impact on Immigrant Perceptions
abstract: This work investigates three interrelated questions around false information targeting immigrants as a broad social group on U.S. social media (thereafter referred to as immigrant-targeting false SNS claims). Study 1 examines content-level features that potentially attract readers’ attention: a quantitative analysis of PolitiFact data showed that relative to those not specifically about immigrants, immigrant-targeting false SNS claims exhibited a stronger negative tone and were more about race-related issues. Study 2 experimentally investigates the effects of immigrant-targeting SNS claims with distinctive media frames (defined as claims emphasizing either economic or health-related concerns) and that of corrective approach (with vs. without fact-checking flags): participants who viewed immigrant-targeting SNS claims flagged as false reported lower threat and anxiety perceptions and higher positive trait perceptions than those who viewed unflagged claims. Regarding the reference groups—specifically, “legal” versus “illegal” immigrants—participants associated with their perceived anxiety, the effect of fact-checking flags was conditional on the SNS claims’ media frames. Study 2 also uncovered that cognitive reflection and actively open-minded thinking play distinct roles in shaping how people respond to immigrant-targeting misinformation and fact-checking labels.

title: Cognitive and Emotional Processes Involved in Co-Viewing: A Naturalistic Comparison With Solo Viewers
abstract: Video co-viewing is a central part of everyday media use, yet little is known about the cognitive and emotional processes involved in co-viewing. To facilitate theoretical development in understanding message processing in social contexts, this study theorizes four interpersonal factors that shape co-viewers’ psychological processes. As a first step toward this broader theoretical goal, we focused on interaction-free moments (i.e., silent with eyes fixed on the television) during co-viewing and investigated co-viewers’ cognitive and emotional processes by comparing them with solo viewers, within a naturalistic context where conversation is allowed. Compared to solo viewers, co-viewers exhibited (1) more positive and less negative emotions, (2) heightened physiological arousal though not significantly so, and (3) higher levels of respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA). Co-viewers’ higher RSA support the proposed social vigilance effect where the presence of a viewing partner triggers self-regulation processes as co-viewers monitor and anticipate potential interactions during naturalistic co-viewing.

title: Joint Land Titling and the Marital Bond in Southwestern Uganda
abstract: When a randomized intervention in southwestern Uganda offered fully subsidized land titles to agricultural households, the majority of husbands chose to add their wives’ names to the title, a striking result given the persistent gender asymmetry in land ownership across Africa. This study investigates the social dynamics underlying that result, asking: What does a joint land title mean for couples in practice, and do women benefit as intended? We draw on fieldwork observations, conversational interviews with selected couples, and interviews with community leaders. Our findings indicate that women's marital bargaining power increases, consistent with household bargaining models. Critically, we identify an additional channel: a joint title symbolizes a husband's commitment to his spouse and marriage. This symbolic dimension is crucial, as women's property rights are threatened under marital insecurity. Joint titling thus shapes marital dynamics not only by strengthening women's bargaining power but also by encouraging what we term “cooperative power”—a fortified marital bond that inspires investment in the marriage. By applying ethnographic approaches to numerical outcomes, the study shows how qualitative inquiry complements survey research in examining the meanings, motivations, and social logics underlying observed demographic and economic behaviors, offering insight into family processes in contemporary Africa.

title: Parental Migration During Childhood and Later‐Life Major Depressive Disorder
abstract: The rise of migration in many communities across the Global South raises questions about its consequences for the children of migrants. Previous studies have primarily examined the immediate impact of parental migration on children's well‐being, while its cumulative effects across the life course remain largely unknown. Drawing on retrospective life histories, prospective monthly residency data, and novel diagnostic measures of mental disorders from the longitudinal Chitwan Valley Family Study in Nepal, this study examines the relationship between parental migration during childhood and later‐life onset of major depressive disorder (MDD). Results indicate that parental migration during childhood is associated with a reduced risk of developing MDD across the life course, although this benefit is exclusive to the younger cohort. These findings suggest that in a context where migration is prolific, parental migration may serve as a protective force against adverse mental health outcomes in later adolescence and adulthood, thus revealing a potential source of long‐term inequality in high out‐migration countries such as Nepal.

title: Assessing the Quality of the Family Interrelationship Variable in Classificatory Kinship Populations
abstract: The family interrelationship variable is widely used to study household structure, child fostering, and intergenerational support. Yet its measurement validity has not been assessed in populations with classificatory kinship systems—prevalent across most of sub‐Saharan Africa—where kinship terminology groups relatives by generation rather than by direct biological link. This study provides the first empirical assessment of this variable in a West African classificatory context. Using genealogical data from the SLAM (Suivi Longitudinal au Mali ‐ Longitudinal survey in Mali) survey in rural Mali, linked at the individual level to the 2009 national census, we compare census‐reported relationships to the household head with genealogically reconstructed ties among the Bwa, who follow a classificatory terminology. The results reveal systematic and directional discrepancies: nephews, nieces, and stepchildren are frequently reported as biological children of the household head. These findings highlight how the imposition of Western nuclear‐family categories in classificatory kinship settings produces nonrandom biases, leading to inflated counts of household head's children and underestimation of extended family ties.

title: Mind over Paradigm: Political Psychology in International Relations
abstract: Rose McDermott traces the rise of political psychology in international relations and argues that psychological concepts and methods have become central to the study of international security, even as their influence is often overlooked. For the fiftieth anniversary of International Security, McDermott analyzes how, unlike approaches centered primarily on systems, institutions, or states, political psychology emphasizes individual agency, including leaders’ perceptions, emotions, identities, biases, and decision-making. The article surveys how political psychology has reshaped debates over deterrence, signaling, the security dilemma, leadership, intelligence failure, status, reputation, credibility, emotion, and evolutionary behavior. Psychological research shows how misperception can destabilize deterrence, how leaders’ beliefs and personal characteristics influence intervention and escalation, and how status, pride, shame, fear, anger, and overconfidence can intensify conflict. McDermott also highlights newer work that uses experiments, neuroscience, genetics, and evolutionary theory. Political psychology remains theoretically fragmented and limited in predictive power because human behavior is complex, but its pluralism has generated valuable insights and questions for addressing war, cooperation, and global threats.

title: The Liberal Balance of Power and the Four Horsemen of Its Apocalypse
abstract: Jack Snyder argues that liberalism’s historical success rests on four competitive mechanisms: free markets, democratic elections, an open marketplace of ideas, and a distinctively liberal approach to the balance of power. These mechanisms’ effectiveness depends on a “visible hand” of laws, norms, expertise, institutions, and social practices that regulates competition and guards against instability. For the fiftieth anniversary of International Security, Snyder applies this framework to the contemporary crisis of the liberal order and the rise of illiberal nationalism that stems in part from deregulation, economic inequality, political polarization, media fragmentation, and attacks on democratic guardrails. He argues that the post-1945 liberal order worked better than previous illiberal and laissez-faire liberal alternatives because market competition was embedded within welfare states, Bretton Woods institutions, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and democratic accountability. In international politics, liberal powers have outperformed authoritarian challengers because liberal institutions enable more effective strategies, alliance cooperation, learning, and self-correction. By contrast, authoritarian “late developers” often respond to economic and security vulnerabilities through self-destructive strategies of militarized autarky and imperial overexpansion. Snyder nevertheless acknowledges liberal overreach, especially in peripheral “forever wars.” He recommends renewing democratic alliances, reforming the defense industrial base, steering clear of peripheral military interventions, rebuilding a constructive media environment, and developing socially embedded liberal institutions capable of addressing contemporary economic and technological problems.

title: Defending the Liberal International Order
abstract: Realists accounts of the U.S.-led postwar order cast skepticism on its liberal foundations or functions. G. John Ikenberry offers a different reading of the origins, logic, and character of this order. Theoretically and historically, there is more—not less—to this liberal international order than meets the eye, certainly the realist eye. While not emerging at a single order-building moment or from a unitary strategic vision, it evolved over the decades into arguably the most formidable and dynamic political formation in world history: a far-flung and complex system of economic, political, and security relations binding together the advanced industrial democracies; an order organized around bargains, institutions, and shared values and interests; and an order infused with principles of consent, reciprocity, and mutual gain. Theoretically, it deserves to be seen as a genuinely new type of international order. It is an order that established an array of commitments and restraints that, when combined, offered a sort of “third way” between two extremes: order based on anarchy and the balance of power, and order based on empire and domination.

title: Shore Thing?: Why the Stopping Power of Water Is Misconceived
abstract: Charles Miller challenges the conventional wisdom about amphibious landings, arguing that most amphibious landings succeed, and that they are no less likely to succeed than ground offensives. In fact, successful amphibious landings can provide more than a tactical advantage. An amphibious landing can be strategically successful if it ties into a broader plan that reduces the defender’s chances of prevailing in the war. The strategic utility of any military operation lies in its ability to undermine the adversary’s theory of victory, reducing its belief in the likelihood of a favorable outcome if the fighting continues. Amphibious landings can accomplish this in two ways— by gaining access to new land masses that are contiguous with the enemy’s core territory or sit astride key supply lines, or by outflanking the enemy in key theaters. The high-stakes Battle of Saipan during World War II, when the successful U.S. amphibious landings constituted a turning point in the thinking of many Japanese decision-makers about the outcome of the war, provides an example. Important policy issues hinge on this question. The difficulties of amphibious landings are one reason why some analysts argue that a Chinese invasion of Taiwan would be unlikely to succeed.

title: The Malacca Myth: Why the United States Should Be Wary of a Distant Blockade Against China
abstract: Hugo Bromley and Eyck Freymann argue that the United States should be cautious about threatening or imposing a distant naval blockade against China through the Strait of Malacca. Although such a blockade might restrict China’s oil imports and create short-term economic pressure, its broader political and economic effects could undermine U.S. strategic interests. The authors situate blockades in a broader typology of economic coercion and develop a theory centered on “arbitrage”: blockades create price differences that encourage neutral states and private firms to reroute, reflag, transship, or smuggle goods through or around the blockade. The more economically significant the neutral community, the more costly and difficult enforcement becomes for the blockader. Historical studies of British blockades against France during the revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars and against Germany in the two world wars support this argument. Britain repeatedly had to compromise with neutral powers because aggressive enforcement threatened diplomatic coalitions and sometimes provoked conflict with important states. A Malacca blockade would confront an even larger and more economically integrated neutral community than Britain faced. China could also rely on stockpiles, domestic production, overland routes, substitution, and food reserves to withstand the blockade. The authors conclude that Washington should favor economic measures that encourage cooperation with neutral actors rather than coercive blockade enforcement, which could fracture the global economy and strengthen China diplomatically.

title: Terror across borders, politics at home: Political influencers navigating diasporic threat and political identity on social media
abstract: Terror attacks occurring in one jurisdiction can shape the perceived political attitudes of populations in a separate jurisdiction—through diasporic ties or the mediation of political discourses via social media. This study examines how left‐ and center‐leaning Jewish influencers addressing American audiences perceived and expressed the impact of the Hamas terrorist attack on October 7, 2023, on their political attitudes and messaging in the context of the 2024 US Presidential election. This study implemented a three‐pronged digital ethnographic approach: digital observation on Instagram, 15 in‐depth interviews, and digital fieldwork analyzing interviewees' political posts in the lead‐up and aftermath of the election. Findings reveal heterogeneity of political attitude and orientation in the face of transnational terror and perceived threat to Jewish life—from preference falsification to single‐issue voting and calls for bipartisanship. Rather than describing a political transformation away from liberal or progressive thought, interviewees described a refocusing of political energy around Jewish safety. This study argues that the transnational threat of October 7, compounded by feelings of political abandonment domestically, was accompanied by a process of attitudinal navigation—complicating expectations of in‐group solidarity, threat‐to‐conservatism pathways, and the strategic communication of political influencers as emergent opinion leaders on social media.

title: Affective dynamics of welfare chauvinism under different policy funding structures
abstract: This research investigates how distinct emotional responses to immigrants—namely, compassion, anger, and anxiety—are connected to welfare chauvinist attitudes within varying welfare policy funding contexts. Leveraging Turkey's experience with large‐scale immigration and the exogenous nature of EU funding, a population‐representative survey experiment was conducted, manipulating claimant identity (native vs. immigrant) and the funding source of welfare assistance (state vs. EU‐funded). Results show that a “care deficit” operates as a key mechanism linking immigrant identity and lower support for immigrant welfare access, but only within the nation‐bound welfare system. Once compassion is evoked, however, it operates similarly for natives and immigrants. Furthermore, moderation analyses reveal divergent patterns of compassion, anger, and anxiety in shaping welfare chauvinist attitudes across different policy funding structures. Highlighting the crucial interplay between emotions and the policy funding schemes in which welfare assistance is delivered, this research contributes to the debate on what drives welfare chauvinism. Drawing on the political psychology literature, this study offers a perspective on the emotional dynamics associated with the persistent native‐immigrant welfare support gap and discusses potential factors that may contribute to narrowing this disparity.

title: When More Is More: Committee Overlap and the Diversity of Information in Problem Definition
abstract: Congress relies on a fragmented bureaucracy to monitor complex problems, raising concerns over whether it can aggregate the diverse information needed for effective policy‐making. I argue that competition among committees with different institutional ties to agencies should produce informational diversity without any coordinating body. Analyzing 92,375 instances of agency testimony across 131 agencies from 1973 to 2021, I find that a greater number of committees examining a problem is consistently associated with a broader and less concentrated set of agencies supplying information. I find little evidence that this association is systematically moderated by public salience.

title: Volatility in Evidence Use: A Computational Analysis of Punctuated Equilibrium Theory
abstract: How does the use of evidence in policy documents change over time, and what explains differences between stable, incremental, and abrupt shifts in its use? This study introduces a computational framework to evaluate change in evidence use across Congressional Research Service (CRS) reports. Using a combination of large language models and supervised machine learning, each document is scored on its alignment with evidence‐based policymaking principles and aggregated to the policy‐topic level. The results show that most policy areas exhibit gradual change, while punctuated shifts are less common and highly variable. Public salience is associated with punctuated evidence‐use trajectories, while media and executive attention are associated primarily with gradual change; partisan control plays a limited role once attention and institutional demand are taken into account. Substantial variation remains across policy topics, with areas such as Macroeconomics and Government Operations exhibiting relatively high dispersion in evidence‐use scores. These findings demonstrate that evidence use in policymaking is dynamic and attention‐sensitive over time.

title: Delayed Date and Motivated Vote: How Election Postponement Shapes Turnout
abstract: Autocracies postpone elections for political control, but we lack an understanding of how voters respond to election postponement in autocracies. This paper argues that election postponement motivates voter turnout across partisan groups, because voters see the postponement as a sign of regime weakness and increased electoral competitiveness. Evidence from a survey experiment in Hong Kong demonstrates that reminder messages about election postponement motivate various partisan groups to turn out, an effect robust to whether and how the message is framed. While the turnout effect is larger when the message’s narrative aligns with the subject’s partisanship—such as the propaganda and intimidation frames for government supporters and the electioneering frame for opposition supporters—all postponement reminder messages have an average turnout effect, with no significant differences across partisan groups. These findings suggest that election postponement is consequential in shaping citizens’ political behavior, with crucial implications for election turnout and authoritarian stability.

title: Democracy matters twice: How democracy relates to winner-loser gaps in political trust across countries and over time
authors: Marta Kołczyńska, Mariano Torcal, Matías A. Bargsted
abstract: This study explores how non-democratic experiences shape gaps in political trust between electoral winners and losers in contemporary democracies, complementing existing theories that focus solely on citizens’ limited democratic experience within democratic contexts. We argue that democracy matters twice: first through historical legacies of authoritarian rule, and second through contemporary democratic improvements. Using harmonized data from the European Social Survey and Americas Barometer across 40 countries in Europe and Latin America (2002–2018), we demonstrate that individuals with greater personal exposure to autocratic rule display stronger reactions to electoral outcomes, resulting in winner-loser gaps twice as large among those who spent their entire adult lives under autocracy compared to those with no autocratic experience. Our findings also reveal that political trust is not culturally fixed but responds to democratic quality. Short-term improvements in liberal democracy significantly narrow winner-loser gaps, primarily by increasing trust among electoral losers who benefit from enhanced checks on power, free speech, and minority rights. Conversely, democratic backsliding widens these gaps. These results enhance understanding of how historical legacies and current democratic conditions together shape political trust and provide crucial insights for understanding its political polarization (politicization) and democratic challenges in post-authoritarian societies.

title: Policy feedback and media framing of crime victims
authors: Holly L. Peterson, Ryan J. Williams, Sarah Koon-Magnin, Logan Berthelot
abstract: Drawing on framing theory and the social construction of target populations, this study examines whether and how landmark legislation is associated with shifts in media framing of the populations it targets. We examine this question through the Crime Victims’ Rights Act of 2004 (CVRA), landmark legislation that significantly changed the way the legal process understood victims. By expanding victims’ participatory rights in the prosecution of those who harmed them, it designated victims as deserving a voice in the process and institutionalised the fact that the victim’s experience mattered for the fair provision of justice. Treating the CVRA as a chronological anchor, we conduct a theory-driven framing analysis of 315 articles from four major US newspapers across the four years surrounding the CVRA’s passage to examine how media frames of crime victims shifted across this threshold. We document an asymmetric pattern: frames of victim power and agency shifted measurably in the direction a policy-feedback account would predict, while frames of victim complexity (indirect harm, secondary victimisation, and non-ideal representation), predicated by victimology, did not. We offer this pattern as one plausible instance of arena-refracted feedback effects , in which policy feedback is refracted by institutional carriers, such as the media, through which it travels to reach mass publics.

title: A Durkheimian Theory Against Empire: Central Australian Festivals and the Making of the Modern World
abstract: It has long been assumed that Durkheimian sociology helped create a sharp distinction between traditional and modern societies, rooted in a Eurocentric bias that treats the latter as a break with the former. However, a close examination of Durkheim’s work may challenge this assumption. Through an in-depth analysis of Durkheim’s posthumously published lectures alongside Les Formes Élémentaires de la Vie Religieuse , this article shows how Durkheim applied the model he developed for studying Aboriginal Australians to a counter-imperial reevaluation of European history. In examining Durkheim’s writings on the genesis of private property in Ancient Rome, the Crusades in the Middle Ages, the French Revolution, and the role of mythological truths in the Modern Era, the article advances a Durkheimian theory against empire, an approach that examines modern society through a theoretical lens drawn from studying Indigenous societies.

title: Palestinian Sumud: Toward a Southern Theory of Unsettled Times
abstract: Prominent sociological theories of action treat stability as the default and disruption as episodic. Yet for many marginalized communities, unsettledness is endemic. I intervene by “making strange,” a two-pronged strategy that shifts theory’s vantage point to destabilize what the center has naturalized. The first move examines the temporal occlusions that give extant theories of action their appearance of universality. The second centers Palestinian sumud (steadfastness) and Southern and postcolonial approaches to remake theories of action and time. Where extant accounts anticipate hysteresis, sumud reveals an ongoing effort to contest a temporal order designed to fragment and deplete. Because time is not a neutral medium for experience, habitus emerges as a vehicle for temporal intervention rather than merely a repository of accumulated dispositions. The result is a decolonial theory of action in which colonial power structures time without fully determining it.

title: The Why and How of Foreign Aid
abstract: Foreign aid has become a melting pot of motivations and policies, where differently motivated actors often converge on recommended policies while the similarly motivated diverge. Breaking down the “why” and the “how” can illuminate real tensions and reveal false ones. The “why” asks which problems to tackle and who benefits: the recipient, the donor through economic, political, or soft-power returns, or everyone through global public goods. The “how” asks which strategy most cost-effectively addresses a chosen problem. Evidence is central to the “how”: Use it where it exists, produce it where it does not. In particular, approaches that improve state capacity to use and generate evidence can satisfy multiple objectives: strengthen recipient countries, benefit donors, and provide a global public good of knowledge. Ultimately, the “how” is not a linear process, but rather an iterative one of learning, adopting, adapting, repeating, and then sharing so others can learn as well.

title: The Role of Private Debt in the Financial Ecosystem
abstract: This paper provides an introduction to the modern private debt market and examines its rapid expansion following the 2007–2009 global financial crisis. Traditionally, economists distinguished between public debt markets and private debt in the form of bank lending. In contemporary markets, however, “private debt” refers to credit originated and held by nonbank financial intermediaries, including private credit funds and business development companies. The paper reviews the key drivers of the sector’s growth; analyzes the distinctive features of private lending arrangements and funding structures; and discusses the implications for traditional banking, financial intermediation, and financial stability. While the sector’s rapid growth and increasing complexity warrant careful monitoring, the paper argues that private debt represents an important and likely durable component of modern financial markets.

title: Trust Violations in Research Universities
abstract: By nearly twice as much as in any other institution that Gallup tracks, public trust in research universities has fallen over the past decade. The causes are not only external. This essay examines two violations of trust that originate within the academy: research that is driven by political advocacy, and a professoriate whose range of ideological viewpoints has narrowed, especially in the humanities and social sciences. The first subordinates the pursuit of truth to political aims; the second erodes the diversity of perspectives that checks individual biases and lets research correct itself. Both break faith with the arguments originally advanced for tenure and academic freedom. Restoring trust demands a renewed commitment to disinterested inquiry and the cultivation of intellectual pluralism—objectives, both, that are best adopted voluntarily, without state censor or interference, and promptly.

title: The Meritocratic Consensus and Stratification in Higher Education
abstract: American colleges and universities are highly stratified by pre-college academic achievement, family background, and institutional resources. We study the meritocratic consensus in American higher education: Colleges that high-testing students (who are generally also from high-income families) attend spend dramatically more on instruction than do those that enroll lower-testing students. Stratification by test scores has been largely stable since the 1960s, but the stratification of instructional resources has risen sharply since 1970 at both private and public institutions. Nonacademic admissions criteria like athletics, legacy, and affirmative action are second-order in determining the allocation of students to universities. Potential economic justifications for the positive association of instructional expenditures with student prior achievement—q-complementarity between achievement and resources, convex social returns to high human capital, and incentives to invest in learning prior to college—have little empirical support. Resource stratification across universities has not increased in the past decade, largely due to increased public funding of universities that enroll lower-testing students through financial aid programs like California's CalGrant, but stratification within institutions is now rising swiftly.

title: Can Government Support for Innovation Create the Next Silicon Valley?
authors: E. Jason Baron, Shawn Kantor, Alexander Whalley
abstract: Can government support for innovation create the next Silicon Valley? We examine what public research and development can and cannot do to foster regional knowledge hubs. The historical record suggests that many successful hubs owe their origins partly to serendipity and favorable initial conditions. We then review causal evidence from universities, changes in intellectual property rules, new research institutions, wartime R&D, and the space race. Public R&D can raise local innovation, employment, and income, but the effects are heterogeneous, often modest relative to cost, and may partly reflect the relocation of firms and skilled workers from elsewhere. The evidence suggests a central role for complementary local inputs, including entrepreneurs, risk capital, skilled labor, firms, and institutions. Public R&D can help build a hub, but is unlikely to create one on its own.

title: Private Credit, Balance Sheets, and Financial Stability
authors: Gregor Matvos, Tomasz Piskorski, Amit Seru
abstract: Private credit has become an important source of business financing, raising questions about financial stability. We examine these questions using comprehensive fund- and asset-level data on private credit funds, the dominant form of private credit. Four facts emerge. First, private credit funds are primarily equity financed, with equity accounting for 65–80 percent of assets, compared with about 10 percent for US banks. Second, they engage in little maturity transformation: Fund lives span eight to twelve years, while underlying loans typically mature within two to four years. Third, portfolios are diversified across industries, geographies, and credit strategies. Fourth, equity investors have earned average net annualized returns of about 10 percent after fees, with equity cushions historically absorbing losses before creditors. These findings suggest that private credit funds do not currently replicate balance-sheet structures associated with banking fragility. We conclude by discussing potential vulnerabilities related to liquidity provision, valuation contagion, and loss transmission through investor balance sheets.

title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
authors: David J. Deming, Raffaella Sadun, Christopher Stanton
abstract: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers’ skills. We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training. The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development. We argue that organizational differences provide incentives for firms to train beyond traditional explanations that focus on labor market frictions. We illustrate how organizational heterogeneity can generate training investments through a knowledge hierarchy framework where top managers with different skills build bespoke organizations tailored to their unique needs. This, in turn, makes general skill firm specific, allowing firms to capture returns on training investment.

title: Systemic Cyber Risk: Linking Measurement, Market Incentives, and Policy
authors: Susan Athey, Neil Gandal, Tyler Moore
abstract: Many firms and sectors within the global economy heavily depend on a common set of critical technology products and software services, thereby consolidating risk across a small number of potential failure points. The widespread reliance on a limited set of products and services has given rise to many single points of system vulnerability. Such concentration of risk amplifies the potential fallout from security breaches, especially since attackers have strong incentives to attack such products and services. Despite the abundance of tools available to organizations and consumers for safeguarding their data against loss or compromise, advancements in individual defense measures have been more than counterbalanced by an increased susceptibility to systemic events. In this paper, we apply economic principles to the rising danger of systemic cyber risks. The paper is organized around four central economic lessons and uses case studies, new data, and policy discussion to develop and support them.

title: In Praise of the Bayesian Bootstrap
authors: Isaiah Andrews, Sarah Moon, Jesse M. Shapiro
abstract: The key takeaways from this article will be the following: (i) Anytime you can bootstrap, you should! (ii) Use the Bayesian bootstrap instead of the nonparametric bootstrap. (iii) If the bootstrap distribution looks different from the “theoretical” (usually, normal) distribution, don’t (only) report a point estimate and standard error. (iv) Instead (or in addition), report the bootstrap distribution with a plot if you have space for it or an interval if you don’t. (v) Give the Bayesian bootstrap a Bayesian interpretation. (vi) You can use a bootstrap even with (multiway) clustering.

title: The Shadow of 1776: Imperial Republicanism, Technocracy, and the New Gaza
abstract: This article situates the current governance of Gaza within the contrast between imperial rule and trusteeship and argues that the proposed US-led paradigm is a reimagining of the “Imperial Republic.” The technocratic trusteeship is introduced as a governing trope that promises self-determination yet defers it forever through expert administration. Through critical discourse analysis and legal–historical comparison between policy documents and mandate-era precedents, this study shows that sovereignty is displaced by managerial oversight, capacity building, and security conditionality. The most important discovery is that technocratic trusteeship transforms administrative performance into political freedom, efficiency, and neutrality, thereby annihilating any perception of disempowerment. This model has broader implications for international governance, indeed, unwrought by the legacy of 1776.

title: Tackling the Lack of Territorial Diversity: Lessons from a Two-Year Supply-Side Intervention in Brazil
authors: Victor Araújo, Malu A. C. Gatto, Magna Inácio
abstract: Political science increasingly acknowledges the importance of diversifying the discipline, yet authors based in the Global South remain underrepresented in top international journals. Addressing this imbalance requires tackling both demand- and supply-side factors. Focusing on supply-side factors, we piloted the Writing Academy, a training and mentorship program for Brazilian political science doctoral students. Drawing on survey data from applicants, we examine the main barriers to internationalizing their research. We find that a lack of knowledge of the rules for international publications—not language—is the primary barrier to submissions to international journals. Pre- and post-intervention survey data indicate that the Writing Academy reduced unfamiliarity with academic journals and increased participants’ confidence in publishing their research in international journals. These findings suggest that targeted training and mentorship can reduce supply-side inequalities in global scholarly participation.

The Election Monitoring Trilemma: Measuring Rare Elite Threats on Social Media With Large Language Models
authors: Sean T. Norton, Kevin T. Greene, Olivia Leu, Anthony J. DeMattee, Jacob N. Shapiro
abstract: In 2024, elections across more than 70 countries raised fears that social media would incite violence and erode democratic norms. We collected public posts from candidates, parties, journalists, and influencers in South Africa, India, and Germany, coding a random sample for five outcomes using human and LLM annotation. All five are rare on the public platforms we study: incitement to violence appeared in just 0.2% of posts, attacks on democratic norms in 1.9%, and civic duty appeals in 2.3%. While LLMs accurately identified true positives, their precision on rare categories was poor and for the two rarest and highest-stakes categories—incitement and ethnic appeals—the LLMs’ ability to catch true positives rests on a deliberately enriched sample. In addition to the limitations low precision poses to researchers, we further show that this precision shortfall confronts election monitors with a three-way tradeoff among coverage, throughput, and credibility that no single off-the-shelf configuration resolves.

title: Selective doors: The role of party ideology, candidate selection rules, and Muslim population in the selection of Muslim minority candidates in European countries
abstract: Candidate selection is an integral part of the political process in European democracies as political parties decide who will be on candidate lists. The candidates’ selection process can sometimes disadvantage potential candidates, especially minority candidates, including Muslims. This article has examined the selection of Muslim candidates in Belgium, France, the Netherlands, and the UK in 16 elections (2007-2022) and the factors that affect this. The results show that while Muslims are generally underrepresented in terms of candidates, there is significant variation between countries. A number of party-level and constituency-level factors, such as party ideology, the size of the Muslim population, and candidate selection rules, influence the selection of Muslim candidates.

title: Reframing moderation: Frame moderation as a radical-right party strategy
abstract: Many radical-right parties across Western Europe have normalized electorally while holding stable, hardline positions on immigration. This paper argues that these parties have moderated the perception of their core policies not through positional moderation, but through frame moderation: they change how they justify a policy without necessarily changing the policy itself, altering the considerations through which voters perceive their position. Conceptually, the paper distinguishes the range of frames a party invokes from the frequency with which it invokes these frames. Empirically, it develops a scalable measure of framing width and of change within frame categories using a novel method of sentence embeddings. Its usefulness is illustrated with the case of the French National Rally’s framing of immigration across manifestos from 1997 to 2022. As the party normalized, it widened its range of frames, increased its framing of immigration in terms of economic considerations, and moved from a cultural frame that emphasized ethnic homogeneity toward one that focuses on the defense of secularism and gender equality. Frame moderation enables stigmatized parties to appear more mainstream without moderating their positions. This suggests that positional measures alone may understate how radical-right parties have changed.

The second Trump administration and the Anglo-American special relationship: A test of alliance persistence
abstract: The Anglo-American ‘Special Relationship’ has entered a new and uncertain era under the second Trump administration. Drawing on the theoretical framework of alliance persistence, this article analyses how President Trump’s ‘America First’ policies have reshaped the foundations and functions of the UK–US partnership. It argues that the revival of ‘America First’ nationalism has intensified the structural tension between bilateral cooperation and the multilateral commitments that both states share within organisations such as NATO. While the enduring institutionalisation of intelligence sharing, nuclear collaboration and military interoperability continues to anchor the alliance, these aspects have increasingly been conditioned by Washington’s transactional approach to burden-sharing and its scepticism towards multilateral frameworks. The article demonstrates that the second Trump administration’s foreign policy has eroded confidence in the partnership’s multilateral dimension, compelling the United Kingdom to assume greater responsibility for sustaining the special relationship.
