title: Regime penalty and capability dividend: European public support for security cooperation
abstract: How does a potential partner’s regime type affect European public support for security cooperation and does military technology moderate this effect? We investigate how the European public navigates the conflict between political reliability and strategic utility. Using a pre-registered survey experiment with 15,400 participants across seven European countries, we manipulate the potential partner’s political regime and technological capacity in the context of a missile development project between the European Union and a non-member partner country. Ordinary least squares models show that democratic partners enjoy higher public support than both authoritarian and backsliding regimes, while technological sophistication independently increases support. Backsliding democracies receive more support than autocracies. High technology does not erase the regime penalty. The democracy advantage remains larger than the capability dividend. Structural equation model results suggest that regime effects operate through perceived reliability and perceived reputational cost with the larger indirect path running through trust. We contribute by empirically examining the tension between capacity and regime type in shaping public support.

title: ‘The party of workers’? The class politics of Reform UK candidates
abstract: Far-right populist parties’ claim to be on the side of ‘the people’ sits at the core of their appeal. Yet, this claim has seen surprisingly little empirical scrutiny. This paper examines Reform UK’s claim to be ‘the party of workers’ by unpacking the classed self-presentations, actual class locations and economic orientations of Reform candidates in the 2024 general election. Based on quantitative and qualitative text analysis, the paper finds a discrepancy across all three levels. First , to position themselves as credible alternatives to established elites, candidates emphasise their upward mobility rather than working-classness. Second , their actual class profiles reveal a high share of people from professional-managerial and petty bourgeois backgrounds. Third , their economic positions are more consistently pro-business than pro-worker. Together, these findings cast doubt on Reform’s claim to represent workers and highlight the need for scholars of far-right populism to focus more on the class politics of party elites.

title: The science of beauty: Looksmaxxing, self-help, and genetic fatalism in women’s online spaces
abstract: This paper examines the emergence of “looksmaxxing” in women’s online spaces. As a specific and underexamined element within what Jilly Boyce Kay analyzes as “reactionary feminism,” essentialist logics about gender and race are operationalized through the aesthetics of science and self-optimization rather than explicitly political rhetoric. Users construct the “science of beauty” through decentralized forms of expertise, from plastic surgery influencers to scientific racism to community-generated aesthetic taxonomies. We identify a thread of individualized and intimate genetic fatalism shaping both aesthetic frameworks and the tactics used to achieve them, mutating the postfeminist promise of self-transformation toward distinctly reactionary goals. This tension between the essentialism and malleability of the body makes the paradigm generative and self-sustaining, absorbing failure and keeping users invested. This case is a call to examine “fringe” and aesthetics-focused cultural formations for insight on how bioessentialist ideas about race and gender circulate today.

title: Big Tech’s power resources: four eras of corporate influence in the EU
abstract: The political clout of Big Tech firms has gained growing attention, as the tech industry has emerged as the largest lobbying force in Brussels. Drawing on a case study based on an extensive round of interviews in Brussels and other research, we argue that Big Tech’s penetration of European politics has proceeded in four overlapping yet distinct phases: harnessing an economic style of reasoning (1990s–2000s), leveraging platform power (2000s–2010s), championing European values (2010s–2020s), and exploiting dependence on American digital infrastructures (late 2020s). Advancing recent theoretical and empirical literature on this front, we show how each period relies on a distinct bundle of power resources. At one end are conventional lobbying techniques and a push for a deregulatory hegemony, while at the other are lobbying and hegemony-building strategies that utilize digital power resources. The findings invite a reassessment of established theories in this field. Policy implications also abound.

title: Income inequality, individual income, trust in government, and long-term individual concerns
authors: Juan J Fernández, Tobias Wiß, Hayley James
abstract: Humans frequently worry about their future, yet most research focuses on only one area of concern, limiting our understanding of general long-term worry. This manuscript addresses this gap through a cross-national analysis of 27 high-income societies. Using representative surveys conducted in 2022 and 2024 and multilevel models, we examine seven domains of worry spanning financial security, housing, and health. We identify two underlying forms of concern—financial and health-related—and argue that their prevalence is linked to country conditions. In countries with higher inequality and lower trust in government, citizens report higher levels of long-term concern overall. We attribute the role of income inequality in relation to worry to the influence of perceived instability and status-maintenance anxiety, and the role of trust in government to the presence of credible institutions. Policies that reduce inequality and enhance trust in government may mitigate material insecurity and psychological burden about the future.

title: Review of Archival Research for International Relations
Dead Men’s Shoes: Diversity, Distributive Justice, and Job Security
abstract: In this article, we make a normative argument for weakening the job security of those in senior positions in the workforce. This would increase turnover in these roles, which would facilitate diversifying those who occupy them in a way that distributes the burdens of doing so fairly. We draw particular attention to the fact that current measures to enhance diversity do not fare so favorably in distributive terms, because they decrease the opportunities of some of those applying to these roles while asking very little of those who currently hold them. Concerns relating to historical injustice, cohort inequality, and diachronic inequality all support distributing the burdens differently, and weakening the job security of those in senior positions is a plausible way to do so.

title: Sedimenting Migration Choices: Political Interpretation, Future Imaginaries and the Decision to Stay or Go Among Syrians Displaced to Turkey
abstract: The article promotes a focus on the processes through which potential migrants come to imagine the future in certain ways as a central element of migratory decision‐making. Drawing on empirical material from long‐term fieldwork with Syrians displaced to Turkey, it discusses the dynamics through which future imaginaries emerged in a context marked by profound historical ruptures. To do this, it unfolds how people's contemplations about migration entailed ongoing but uncertain interpretation of politics to foresee what might come to pass in various places. Over time, uncertainty gave way to more confidence as individuals continuously reaffirmed previous interpretations leading to a sedimentation of particular assumptions about politics. Through this process, some futures came to appear more likely than others and this impacted migratory decisions because these decisions were based on potential migrants' perceptions of future possibilities ‘here’ and ‘there’. Accordingly, the article suggests that the question of why some people migrate while others stay put should be answered not only with reference to potential migrants' divergent weighing of possibilities ‘here’ against possibilities ‘there’ but also with reference to the processes through which people come to perceive possibilities ‘here’ or ‘there’ in specific ways.

title: Migrant Network Opportunities and the Pathways to Social Integration: Evidence From Urban China
authors: Xueying Mu, Junru Cui, Yuanyuan Li, Wenping Xu
abstract: The integration of migrants into urban society has become a critical challenge in China's transition from land‐based to people‐oriented urbanization. Although migrant networks have been widely discussed as a source of migration‐related social capital, less is known about how the local concentration of co‐origin migrants creates opportunities for network formation and shapes migrants' social integration. Using data from the 2017 Chinese Migrants Dynamic Survey (CMDS) and generalized structural equation modeling (GSEM), this study measures co‐origin migrant concentration as the proportion of migrants from the same place of origin in each destination city, and examines its relationship with social integration. The findings show that co‐origin migrant concentration significantly promotes social integration, although the effects vary across birth cohorts: migrants born in the 1960s exhibit a stronger association than those born in the 1970s and 1980s. Housing outcomes and social interactions emerge as key mediating pathways. Migrants living in cities with higher co‐origin migrant concentrations are more likely to achieve homeownership, which in turn enhances integration. The findings also reveal contrasting patterns of social interaction. Greater co‐origin migrant concentration is associated with fewer interactions with local residents, potentially constraining deeper integration, but with more interactions with fellow migrants who have obtained local hukou , which are positively associated with social integration. By distinguishing the contextual opportunities for network formation from migrants' realized social ties, this study advances understanding of how the spatial concentration of co‐origin migrants shapes social integration through housing and social interaction.

title: Keep or Leave? Income–Happiness Trade‐Offs and Settlement Intentions in Urban China
authors: Feilong Yang, Li Chen, Yunxiao Dang, Wenzhong Zhang
abstract: Population mobility research has long examined how economic opportunity shapes residential trajectories, while subjective well‐being research has often treated happiness as an outcome of income, place or life circumstances. Less attention has been paid to how income and happiness are jointly associated with settlement intentions. Drawing on survey data from 59 Chinese cities between 2020 and 2022, this article examines the conditional relationship between household income, happiness and settlement intentions. Both higher income and greater happiness are associated with stronger intentions to stay, while their interaction reveals a modest conditional pattern consistent with partial compensation. Ordered‐response analyses further identify attenuation in the probability of intending to leave across a substantial subset of income–happiness combinations, with different patterns for staying and uncertainty. Multilevel analyses indicate that the income–happiness interaction is more pronounced in wealthier and more populous cities. These findings advance a relational understanding of mobility and immobility by showing how economic resources and subjective well‐being jointly enter residential evaluations.

title: Learning in a complex world: how multidimensionality affects policymaking
authors: Federica Izzo, Giovanna Invernizzi, Jesse Crosson
abstract: Policymaking inherently involves uncertainty about policy consequences. This uncertainty leads voters to rely on their past experiences when forming beliefs about policies, which ultimately shapes their electoral decisions. Officeholders, in turn, strategically weigh how their policy choices between bold initiatives and incremental options will affect voter learning and thus their electoral prospects. While conventional wisdom suggests leading incumbents always prefer safe policies and trailing ones pursue risky gambles for resurrection, this paper develops a model of policy experimentation showing that this logic often breaks down in multidimensional policy contexts. This study’s central result identifies a strategic substitution effect, whereby trailing incumbents may moderate on certain issues, while leading ones might pursue riskier policies than they otherwise would. This finding yields novel empirical implications regarding issue salience, policy extremism, and the incumbent’s electoral prospects, which this study illustrates through a preliminary plausibility check using U.S. data.

title: Forum shopping by non-state actors in international organizations
abstract: Non-state actors filing human rights complaints can often choose between international organizations. How does institution design shape these choices? We consider strategic forum shopping, arguing that individuals and NGOs select venues based on two key institutional features: whether decisions are legally binding and how long decisions take. We test this argument using original data on over 3,400 petitions filed in the Inter-American Human Rights System (IAHRS) and the UN Human Rights Committee (CCPR) over a period of forty years (1980–2020). We find that when states recognize the jurisdiction of an international court, making legally binding decisions possible, petitions to the IAHRS increase and petitions to the CCPR decrease. The two features trade off differently across actor types: NGOs are willing to tolerate lengthy processes in exchange for the prospect of binding, precedent-setting decisions, while individual victims are more sensitive to decision time and prefer the faster UN system. These findings show that overlapping institutions produce systematic sorting with important implications for the design, resilience, and enforcement capacity of the international human rights regime.

title: The Unintended Cost of Care: How Family Policies Impact Intimate Partner Violence in the European Union
abstract: Despite being considered the de facto world leader in gender equality, the European Union has a significant problem — its extremely high rates of everyday violence against women (EVAW). Contrary to conventional wisdom about development and gender equality, recent survey research shows the most industrialized countries in Europe also report a higher prevalence of EVAW. In this article, I argue that family policies — particularly those associated with the universal breadwinning model and increased women’s labor market participation — are related to intimate partner violence. Utilizing a nationally representative and comparable dataset on EVAW in the European Union, I find state expenditure on in-kind childcare is associated with a higher likelihood of a woman experiencing intimate partner violence, while more generous parental leave schemes have the opposite relationship. This underscores that while family policies are often designed to rectify gender disparities in formal and caring work, they may also yield unintended yet profoundly negative consequences.

title: Effective, Credible, and Acceptable: How to Ensure the EU ETS Delivers on Climate Targets
authors: Simone Borghesi, Albert Ferrari, Kai Lessmann
abstract: The European Union opted to rely on an Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) as a cornerstone of climate policy to reach its emissions reduction targets. However, its future hinges on more than just effectiveness in reducing emissions. While the EU ETS is widely recognized as a cost‐effective tool for cutting emissions, recent geopolitical trends and economic concerns among national governments and industries have raised questions about its long‐term viability. Indeed, carbon pricing is often perceived as a barrier to industrial competitiveness, economic growth, and social justice. As a result, the EU ETS faces growing scrutiny, requiring a renewed focus on three essential conditions for its success: effectiveness, credibility, and public acceptability. The EU ETS has successfully reduced greenhouse gas emissions. Its credibility grew thanks to long‐term regulatory certainty, but it remains subject to possible speculative behaviors and market distortions. Moreover, as emissions trading expands to sectors such as road transport and building heating with a separate ETS (EU ETS 2), its direct impact on households risks triggering resistance, making public acceptability a crucial concern. Credibility can be strengthened through clear policy signals and better market oversight. Acceptability could be improved through revenue recycling and complementary measures. The latter could make the EU carbon price even more effective. Effectiveness, credibility, and acceptability are profoundly interconnected and mutually reinforcing. Future climate policies must prioritize credibility and acceptability alongside emissions reductions to succeed. If not, loss of confidence and public resistance may hinder EU ETS expansion and future ambition. This article is categorized under: Climate Economics > Economics of Mitigation The Carbon Economy and Climate Mitigation > Policies, Instruments, Lifestyles, Behavior Climate Economics > Economics and Climate Change

title: Worker‐side discrimination: Beliefs and preferences
authors: Md Moshi Ul Alam, Mehreen Mookerjee, Sanket Roy
abstract: When agents choose among options with unobserved attributes to maximize expected utility, their choices conflate preferences with beliefs about those attributes. We develop a novel theory‐driven identification strategy for such settings, showing that compensating differentials separately identify beliefs from preferences. Noting that workers' preferences and beliefs shape labor market outcomes, yet remain understudied, we apply our method to provide the first evidence on the distribution of workers' preferences over manager gender, and their beliefs about managers' mentoring ability. In the absence of information on manager mentoring ability, workers are indifferent to manager gender. However, upon receiving information on manager mentorship ability, workers prefer to work for female managers, willing to forgo 1.7% of average annual wages. Hence, absent additional information, workers believe female managers are worse mentors (1.6% wage equivalent). Nonparametric estimates of the distributions reveal that 76% prefer female managers with mentoring information, and 67% believe male managers are better mentors absent information. Machine learning algorithms show that individuals with higher education are less likely to hold such beliefs. These beliefs are primarily driven by perceptions that women are less competent. Evidence suggests these beliefs are biased, highlighting scope for information‐based policy interventions.

title: Finite‐state Markov chain approximations: A hidden Markov approach
abstract: This paper proposes a novel finite‐state Markov chain approximation method for Markov processes with continuous support, providing both an optimal grid and a transition probability matrix. The method can be used for multivariate processes and processes with time‐varying components. It is based on minimizing the information loss between a hidden Markov model and the true data‐generating process. We provide sufficient conditions under which this information loss can be made arbitrarily small, provided enough grid points are used. We compare our method to existing methods through the lens of an asset‐pricing model and a life‐cycle consumption‐savings model. We find that our method can lead to more parsimonious discretizations and more accurate solutions, and that the discretization matters for the welfare costs of risk, marginal propensities to consume, and the amount of wealth inequality a life‐cycle model can generate.

title: Intrahousehold inequality and savings in retirement
abstract: The distribution of resources between spouses and the extent to which household savings reflect each spouse's motives are fundamental to analyzing married retirees' welfare. We provide one of the first quantitative assessments of intrahousehold inequality in bargaining power and its implications for consumption allocation during marriage, savings, and welfare in old age. To do so, we estimate a dynamic collective model of retired couples with individual‐specific preferences and relative bargaining power, in which spouses jointly choose consumption, saving, care arrangements, and housing in the face of health and mortality shocks. We find that wives' mean consumption shares are close to parity in retirement, although there is substantial dispersion. We also find meaningful gender differences in saving motives and preferences: wives have stronger precautionary motives due to their longer life expectancy and higher long‐term care risk, while men exhibit greater bequest motives toward children. Consequently, our estimated collective model shows that reforms to old‐age social insurance have different welfare effects for wives and husbands, revealing distributional consequences that would be obscured under a unitary framework.

title: Fertility, child gender, and parental migration decision: Evidence from China
authors: Zibin Huang, Lin Lin, Junsen Zhang
abstract: We study how the number and gender of children affect rural‐to‐urban parental migration in China. Exploiting variation from the “1.5‐child policy,” which allowed a second birth only if the first‐born was a girl, we separately identify the causal effects of fertility and child gender based on a novel semiparametric method. Using the 2010 population census, we find that an additional child increases the likelihood of joint parental migration by 12.1%, while the presence of a son raises it by a further 11.6%. These comparable magnitudes show that gender matters as much as fertility in shaping migration decisions. The results suggest that the higher financial demands of larger families—especially those with boys—outweigh the emotional costs of separation, motivating parents to migrate. Traditional IV estimates would be severely downward biased if only the number of children were considered.

title: A nonparametric test for diurnal variation in spot correlation processes
authors: Kim Christensen, Ulrich Hounyo, Zhi Liu
abstract: The association between log‐price increments of exchange‐traded equities, as measured by their spot correlation estimated from high‐frequency data, exhibits a pronounced upward‐sloping and almost piecewise linear relationship at the intraday horizon. There is notably lower—on average less positive—correlation in the morning than in the afternoon. We develop a nonparametric testing procedure to detect such variation in a correlation process. The test statistic has a known distribution under the null hypothesis, whereas it diverges under the alternative. We run a Monte Carlo simulation to discover the finite sample properties of the test statistic, which are close to the large sample predictions, even for small sample sizes and realistic levels of diurnal variation. In an application, we implement the test on a high‐frequency dataset covering the stock market over an extended period. The test leads to rejection of the null most of the time. This suggests diurnal variation in the correlation process is a nontrivial effect in practice. We show how conditioning information about macroeconomic news and corporate earnings announcements affects the intraday correlation curve.

title: Finite‐sample auction inference using transaction prices
abstract: We first provide inference on the quantile function of the bid distribution in first‐price or descending auctions, and the quantile function of the value distribution in second‐price or ascending auctions, with a known number of bidders with symmetric independent private values. Specifically, we provide finite‐sample, nonparametric, tuning parameter‐free, uniform confidence bands for these quantile functions when observing only the transaction price. We also show how these bands can be used to construct confidence intervals for many counterfactuals and economic quantities that are functionals of the value distribution. Some confidence intervals inherit the same properties of our bands, besides having conservative instead of exact coverage, while others require asymptotic arguments and/or tuning parameters. Even if the observed number of bidders varies across auctions, our bands' finite‐sample coverage is exact, assuming exogenous participation. With a fixed number of bidders, we also derive uniform confidence bands robust to auction‐level unobserved heterogeneity. This includes new partial identification results that bound the bid or value quantile function in terms of the transaction price quantile function. Empirically, our new methodology is applied to timber auction data to examine heterogeneity across appraisal value and number of bidders, which helps assess the combination of symmetric independent private values and exogenous participation, and to provide confidence intervals for the optimal reserve price and the economic benefit of running the auction instead of a random lottery.

title: School choice, skill measures, and graduation
abstract: This paper studies the effects of combining skill measures to construct the priority order in a centralized education market. We use data from Mexico City, where seat rationing relies solely on a one‐shot exam score. We first show that admission to the most oversubscribed schools decreases graduation among marginally admitted students, but this effect is heterogeneous. It decreases with the one‐shot exam score among inframarginal students and is negative for marginal students with low GPAs but null for those with high GPAs. We then use a model of school choice and graduation to study the equity and efficiency of counterfactual priority orders that combine the one‐shot exam score and GPA. Greater weight on GPA increases access to the most oversubscribed schools for girls and low‐SES students. However, assigning roughly equal weight to both skill measures maximizes their graduation rates at these schools.

title: Decomposing the rise in markups
abstract: A recent literature argues that the rise in aggregate markups is due to economic activity reallocating toward high‐markup firms rather than an increase in firm‐level markups. I show that standard decomposition methods used to analyze this phenomenon can estimate a nonzero reallocation effect even when the joint distribution of markups and market shares is time‐invariant. This is due to churning in the firm‐level distribution of markups and market shares. Empirically, I find that a large and positive reallocation effect is found by standard decomposition methods when the distribution is time‐invariant. I propose a new decomposition, which gives that the rise in the aggregate markup mainly comes from changes in the markup distribution rather than changes in the market share distribution.

title: Standard errors when a regressor is randomly assigned
authors: Denis Chetverikov, Jinyong Hahn, Zhipeng Liao, Andres Santos
abstract: We show that the OLS variance formula simplifies when values of the regressor of interest are assigned randomly and independently of other regressors. When the regressor of interest is independent not only of other regressors but also of the error term, the homoscedastic variance formula is valid even if regression errors are correlated. When the error term is heteroscedastic with respect to the regressor of interest, the variance formula has to be adjusted not only for heteroscedasticity but also for correlation structure of the error term. However, even in the latter case, some simplifications are possible.

title: Identification of daily oil price shocks and their uncertainties via conditional heteroskedasticity
abstract: This paper develops a daily structural VAR for identifying oil price shocks from conditional heteroskedasticity and quantifies the transmission of their time‐varying uncertainty. Identification exploits volatility clustering and spillovers in a structural GARCH specification and the complete identified set is derived. We derive covariance impulse response functions and introduce a time‐varying forecast error variance decomposition (TV‐FEVD) that allows for a decomposition of short‐horizon forecast uncertainty across episodes. We study the asymptotic properties of a two‐step quasi‐maximum likelihood estimator and demonstrate via extensive simulations the robustness of the estimator across a wide range of data‐generating distributions. Empirically, the model identifies three daily shocks with distinct first‐ and second‐order transmission. TV‐FEVD shows that oil‐price forecast uncertainty in early 2020 shifted from aggregate business‐cycle uncertainty, as pandemic news affected expected economic conditions, to oil‐market tightness risk during the Saudi–Russia price war and production cuts.

title: Scripts of Escalation and Restraint: State Messaging and Public Opinion in International Crises
abstract: Public opinion can both enable and constrain foreign policy, motivating governments to manipulate media during international crises. This study identifies four recurring communication strategies, one mobilizing and three moderating, each organized around a dominant cue: mobilization relies primarily on emotional arousal to stoke nationalist sentiment and foster assertiveness; censorship centers on the informational restriction of politically sensitive content; delegitimization uses normative appeals to discredit hawkish responses as irresponsible or illegitimate; and posturing employs performative displays of toughness intended to make moderate policies politically acceptable. Using a large-scale survey experiment in China, Vietnam, and the Philippines, the study evaluates how these strategies affect the public’s foreign-policy preferences and tolerance for policy deviation in a simulated fishing dispute in the South China Sea. The results show that mobilization shifts preferences in a more hawkish direction and reduces tolerance for deviation, whereas delegitimization consistently steers the public toward more moderate foreign policy preferences across countries. Censorship tempers policy preferences in all three countries but is strongest in Vietnam; posturing has no significant effect in China or Vietnam and produces a more hawkish response in the Philippines. Although the sources of this cross-national heterogeneity cannot be definitively identified, the findings suggest that propaganda effectiveness may depend partly on how audiences interpret different messages. Explicitly prescriptive strategies, such as mobilization and delegitimization, appear more portable across contexts, whereas informational or performative strategies, such as censorship and posturing, may be more contingent on audience predispositions, including baseline hawkishness, and on broader political and informational environments.

title: Evidence and measures of the digital usage divide from 40 million Windows devices
authors: Mayana Pereira, Shane Greenstein, Raffaella Sadun, Prasanna Tambe, Lucia Ronchi Darre, Tammy Glazer, Allen Kim, Rahul Dodhia, Juan Lavista Ferres
abstract: Digital infrastructure is crucial for economic opportunities, social inclusion, and civic participation, but benefits remain unevenly distributed. Existing measures, such as computer ownership and broadband adoption, do not capture the depth and variety of digital use. We develop measures using Microsoft telemetry collected during operating system updates from 40 million Windows devices in U.S. households. These measures provide greater coverage and granularity than existing commercial or government surveys. Device representations at the ZIP-code level reveal substantial variation in usage, including an urban-rural divide and disparities within narrowly defined Metropolitan Statistical Areas. Income and education correlate with these differences. These effects are large and suggest that digital usage gaps extend beyond the local availability of essential IT infrastructure. The findings call for interventions that complement infrastructure access with support for technology use and skills development. The resulting indices are publicly available to support future research on digital inequality.

title: Temporal dynamics of premenstrual dysphoric disorder revealed through predictive symptom networks
authors: Ella Schleimann-Jensen, Inger Sundström-Poromaa, Johanna M. Hoppe, Sinha Engel, Jeff Kiesner, Erika Comasco
abstract: Temporal dynamics of psychiatric symptoms challenge researchers and clinicians due to their inherent unpredictability. The cyclical on–off nature of symptoms linked to physiological rhythms, such as the menstrual cycle, provides a unique window to apply temporal and dynamic modeling of psychiatric symptoms. This can be studied in premenstrual dysphoric disorder, a female hormone-triggered condition characterized by cyclical symptoms. Yet intra-individual temporal patterns and dynamics of these symptoms remain unknown. Here we show that individuals with premenstrual dysphoric disorder differ widely in symptom timing, severity, and persistence, clustering into distinct temporal symptom profiles. Dynamic modelling uncovers temporal order among core psychiatric symptoms, with anxiety emerging as a central symptom in the unfolding of affective dysregulation. Depression shows the strongest predictive associations with subsequent severity of the other core symptoms, while irritability predicts the severity of depression at the longest time-interval. These temporal symptom dynamics reveal mechanistic psychoneuroendocrine pathways and inform precision, time-sensitive interventions for the mental health of individuals with premenstrual dysphoric disorder.

title: Coalition differentiation at scale: measuring intra-coalition rhetorical distinctiveness with supervised classification
abstract: Coalition parties face a unity-differentiation dilemma: they must uphold compromise to govern effectively, while maintaining distinct identities to maximize electoral success. Existing measures of coalition differentiation almost exclusively rely on static proxies to infer behavior, and the few dynamic measures often only cover a limited sample of governments, limiting comparative analysis. This article introduces a comparative, dynamic measure of rhetorical differentiation based on supervised classification of legislative speeches. Higher classification accuracy indicates greater rhetorical distinctiveness between coalition partners, while misclassification indicates greater rhetorical overlap. The measure provides monthly party-level scores for close to 50 coalition governments, across six European democracies, and thereby enables the dynamic analysis of coalition party differentiation in a public-facing arena, for a sizable comparative sample.

title: Blame attribution in authoritarianism: the public’s response to three safety crises in China
abstract: Citizens rely on information to evaluate the government, but their sources are limited in authoritarian regimes. This study shows that citizens can learn from extraordinary events, such as public safety incidents, which are socially salient, highly visible, and clearly attributable. When the state bears causal responsibility for a safety failure, political trust declines under both a controversial and an uncontroversial response. Using survey data that cover three national crises in contemporary China, the analysis compares respondents in the weeks immediately before and after the incidents. Trust in government declined following the 2011 bullet train crash and the 2018 vaccine scandal, but not following the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake. Further analysis finds no increase in perceived corruption, while perceptions of free expression declined after the train crash but not after the earthquake, consistent with dissatisfaction over information control. The findings have implications for authoritarian accountability and regime stability.

title: Social intolerance as a product of political identities: evidence from a conjoint experiment in five countries
authors: Mariano Torcal, Josep Maria Comellas, Alina Vrânceanu
abstract: Do group identities rooted in salient social and political characteristics foster homophily and social distance? If so, which identities shape social preferences more strongly, and under what conditions? While existing literature on affective polarization and inter-group relations privileges particular social and political identities, we know less about the dynamics that unfold when multiple identities are considered simultaneously. Using conjoint experiments in five multiparty systems (Argentina, Chile, Italy, Portugal, and Spain), we find that political identities are generally more influential than social ones among individuals with partisan affinities. This is especially true among left-wing individuals, who display greater social distance to radical right supporters. Our findings suggest that social distance is rooted in political attachments, which may channel salient social divisions.

title: Trade liberalization and the welfare state: how subnational geographies shape compensation
abstract: How globalization reshapes the welfare state in developing democracies remains contested, and evidence on whether trade liberalization expands or contracts social spending is mixed. Using a quasi-natural experiment in Brazil, I first find support for the “compensation hypothesis:” trade integration generates welfare compensation. I then argue that trade’s differential impact across subnational regions helps explain the mixed evidence. Subnational political and economic geographies mediate trade’s effect on social policy. In particular, I argue that the geographic concentration of political identities facilitates collective action. I find that geographically concentrated constituencies exhibit higher voter turnout and more participatory councils advocating for labor rights and welfare. Trade’s positive welfare effect is magnified where political or economic identities are geographically concentrated. The findings spotlight how subnational geography shapes globalization’s redistributive consequences.

title: Comparing belief certainty formats in the measurement of political knowledge
abstract: Psychological certainty plays a role in how respondents retrieve and express their attitudes, beliefs, and opinions. This study compares two question formats that allow respondents to express certainty about their political knowledge. Using a YouGov sample ( N = 2,161), a single-item certainty-in-knowledge format, where political knowledge and belief certainty are measured jointly, and a branching format, where knowledge is measured first, followed by certainty in a separate question, are compared. The results show that the certainty-in-knowledge format significantly reduces the likelihood of respondents looking up answers online. Including a “Don’t Know” option does not increase gender differences. These findings demonstrate a question format that improves validity in online surveys by reducing measurement artifacts.

title: Democratic hypocrisy: support for undemocratic responses to protest in Germany
authors: Morgan Le Corre Juratic, Markus Wagner, Daniel Bischof
abstract: Political tolerance is a cornerstone of liberal democracy, yet citizens apply it selectively: intolerance is higher for disliked groups. However, does this extend to democratic hypocrisy, leading to support for undemocratic responses to protest? We address this important question through a vignette survey experiment ( N = 5,000) in Germany, comparing reactions to similar protest tactics used by farmers and climate activists in a realistic, externally valid setting. We show that respondents were not only less willing to grant climate activists key democratic rights but also significantly more likely to support undemocratic responses to climate protesters, including imprisonment without trial. Our findings underline that citizens engage in democratic hypocrisy: their political biases lead them to support undemocratic actions against disliked groups.

title: Optimal party strategies on niche issues: a computational approach to multiparty competition for position and salience
abstract: How should parties respond to competition from a new challenger on a niche issue? Meguid argues that accommodation is effective, but recent evidence shows it may cost votes. We identify vote-maximizing strategies of established parties facing an extreme challenger using an extended Downsian model with position and salience. Based on empirical data from Germany, our results show that accommodation works only for low-valence parties, and only while the challenger is new. Otherwise, adversarial strategies benefit small parties. Major established parties maximize votes by holding moderate positions and engaging weakly with the issue. Our findings offer a theoretical baseline for understanding optimal strategies in party competition.

title: Multimodal Czech online handwriting and cognitive data from children with and without handwriting disabilities
authors: K. Zvončáková, J. Mekyska, A. Klocek, J. Mucha, Z. Galáž
abstract: Handwriting is a fundamental skill that significantly influences academic achievement and cognitive development. Despite its importance, open-access datasets combining online handwriting data with comprehensive cognitive profiles are scarce, particularly for children with handwriting disabilities. We present a multimodal dataset consisting of online handwriting and cognitive assessment data from 276 Czech children (ages 8–12), including 161 individuals with handwriting disabilities. The data acquisition utilized a Wacom Cintiq 16 tablet and a digital pen to record 16 graphomotor and writing tasks, capturing high-resolution x-y coordinates, pressure, azimuth, and pen tilt at an average frequency of 167 Hz. Alongside these raw data, the dataset includes scores from standardized assessments of cognitive abilities, visuospatial skills, phonological awareness, and self-reported handwriting proficiency. We provide raw data in SVC format and integrated, preprocessed records in JSON and RDS formats, supported by specialized Python and R processing scripts. This resource is intended to facilitate research in graphonomics, machine learning, and educational psychology, providing a benchmark for the development and comparison of computational methods for analyzing children’s handwriting.

title: Congressional Oratory Research Archive: A Comprehensive Data Set for Analyzing the U.S. Congressional Record, 1873–2025
Fandom Rupture in the Movement Society: Reactive Collective Participation Through Affective Practices
abstract: When an external shock draws heterogeneous actors into a single platform arena before any collective aim emerges, participation persists at movement-like intensity. Existing theories have not specified the cohering mechanism through which this formation sustains. This study conceptualizes this mode as reactive collective participation and specifies how affective publics cohere and persist under reactive conditions at the practice level. A mixed-methods design integrates in-depth interviews with 13 heterogeneously positioned participants (fans, anti-fans, bystanders) and computational analysis of Weibo discourse surrounding the 2023 Cai Xukun scandal (139,795 posts; 205,001 comments). Four affective practices recur across the event: Positioning, Storying, Attunement, and Calibration. These practices shift in relative weight across the event’s life cycle and distribute unevenly across actor positions, producing a stratified ecology in which insulated defense and exposed antagonism sustain each other. The study advances affective publics theory by specifying how affective publics cohere and persist under reactive conditions at practice level, and collective participation theory by conceptualizing reactive collective participation as a mode that reconnects the movement society and fan activism frameworks through a reactive pathway.

title: Women Sustaining TikTok as Supplementary Information Infrastructure for Flexible Work Arrangements: Gendered Conditions, Community and Surveillance
authors: Xuefei Li, Kiran Ijaz, Marta E. Cecchinato, Naseem Ahmadpour
abstract: Flexible work arrangements (FWAs) create practical and interpretive questions that formal workplace information may not adequately address, particularly around how flexibility is experienced and negotiated in everyday working life. As workers share and encounter FWA-related posts on TikTok, the platform can provide supplementary access to experiential knowledge. However, circulation alone does not explain how such knowledge becomes a durable and usable resource for workers. Drawing on infrastructure theory, we conceptualise TikTok as a supplementary information infrastructure (SII) and use a feminist perspective to examine the gendered conditions under which women contribute to and sustain it. Based on semi-structured interviews with 14 women who post about FWAs on TikTok, we analyse their relational information practices. Participants responded to misleading information with situated knowledge and interpretive resources that made workplace norms more visible and contestable. Sustaining this infrastructure came at a cost: credibility and continued participation were shaped by gendered conditions of recognition and unequal access to time and energy, while trust was challenged by shifting audiences, limited contextualisation and technological risks. Participation also exposed women creators to workplace-facing surveillance. We contribute an infrastructural account of digital workplace knowledge exchange by showing how creators’ repair and maintenance labour helps sustain TikTok as an SII. This extends research on digital workplace knowledge exchange by showing that supplementary workplace knowledge can also matter for workers who remain connected to formal workplace information. The SII’s possibilities for information justice nevertheless remain uneven because they depend on creator labour undertaken under gendered and platformed conditions.

title: Issue Ownership, Immigration, and the Far-Rightness of Two Irish Political Party Websites
authors: Clara Schenk, James Windle, Kevin Sweeney
abstract: Ireland has largely avoided the escalation of far-right populism seen across Europe. There has, however, been an upsurge in far-right politics and activism, underpinned by anti-immigration sentiment. Within this context, this paper aims to determine how two Irish political parties commonly identified by media outlets as far-right present their websites, which issues they seek to own and whether these issues align with far-right ideology. Qualitative thematic analysis was conducted on transcribed screen recordings of every textual and visual component of these websites during a period of routine politics sandwiched between the 2024 European and local elections and the general election. The key finding was that, while the two parties diverged on some issues, both sought to own immigration and exhibited high degrees of nationalism, which often veered into nativism. Immigration was the core issue for both parties and interwoven with other policy positions (Euroscepticism) and issues (housing, COVID-19, the economy).

Regionalism and the categorization of migrants in Africa – comparing ECOWAS and the SADC
abstract: This article examines the relationship between regional free movement frameworks and the political categorization of migrants in Africa through a comparative analysis of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the Southern African Development Community (SADC). Drawing on comparative regionalism and constructivist approaches, it explores how regional frameworks both shape and are shaped by the construction of migrants as “wanted” or “unwanted.” Empirically, the study combines document analysis of legislation and policy with semi-structured interviews conducted with policy actors and experts in both regions, focusing on Ghana and Nigeria (ECOWAS) and South Africa (SADC) as illustrative cases. The findings reveal a paradox in ECOWAS: despite an advanced free movement regime and references to a shared West African and pan-African identity, intra-regional migrants are constructed as economic liability and security risks. By contrast, the SADC lacks a coherent free movement framework and a corresponding category of regional citizenship, with migrant categorization primarily structured along skill and racialized notions concerning “African” migration. The comparison shows that free movement frameworks and migrant categorization are intrinsically linked, as constructions of migrants’ desirability along the axes of identity, economic utility, and security both foster and constrain the regionalization of mobility regimes. The article thus underscores the importance of migrant categorization for understanding the possibilities and limits of regional free movement in Africa.

title: Pink noise in dyads’ semantic similarity trajectories predicts conversation enjoyment
authors: Kathryn C. O’Nell, Kiara L. Sanchez, Emily S. Finn
abstract: Conversation is a core component of human social life. Many influential theories treat conversation as a linear system, i.e., the sum of its parts. However, linear accounts of semantic entrainment lose explanatory power at their upper limits: Discussing perfectly aligned opinions becomes boring. We propose an alternate account that considers the multiscale organization of semantic similarity over the course of a conversation, as indexed by pink noise. Here, we test whether pink noise can be found in interlocutors’ conavigated trajectories through semantic space. Not only is pink noise present, but its strength predicts positive conversation outcomes like enjoyment and connection, increases with practice, and is reflected in a large language model’s representation of conversation quality. These results demonstrate an important role for scale-free dynamics in characterizing successful conversation.

title: A natural field experiment on the effectiveness of economic sanctions before and after the Russian invasion of Ukraine
authors: Michael G. Findley, Daniel L. Nielson, J. C. Sharman
abstract: Here, using two rounds of natural field experiments based on an audit-study approach, we investigated whether sanctioned Russian government officials retain access to the international financial system. Researchers sent 7,081 email solicitations to intermediary firms in 202 countries and jurisdictions to establish shell companies and set up corporate bank accounts. Responses to sanctioned names (middle initial modified) are compared with equivalent solicitations from non-sanctioned placebo names. Round 1 results in December 2020 reveal no statistically significant difference in financial access for the sanctioned names compared with placebo. Round 2 findings in May 2022, after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, indicate that sanctioned individuals’ access to international corporate services and banking was significantly reduced (drop in non-compliant response rates: 4.0 percentage points, 95% confidence interval 1.2–6.8, P = 0.006, Cohen’s d = 0.207). The results suggest that factors related to the war and not sanctions law proved decisive in constricting sanctioned individuals’ access to the global financial system.

title: Cost-effective climate change mitigation through land sector contributions
authors: Leon Merfort, Alexander Popp, Nico Bauer, Florian Humpenöder, Gabriel Abrahão, Benjamin Leon Bodirsky, David Meng-Chuen Chen, Laurin Köhler-Schindler, Gunnar Luderer, Rahel Mandaroux, Anne Merfort, Jessica Strefler, Elmar Kriegler
abstract: Climate change mitigation from Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) comes with severe sustainability risks and faces major implementation challenges. Yet, the consequences of missing out on AFOLU mitigation potential for the transition of the energy sector and the achievability of climate objectives are not well understood. Here, using the Integrated Assessment Modeling framework REMIND–MAgPIE, we derive future mitigation pathways under different AFOLU policy portfolios. We show that, without AFOLU contributions to mitigation, limiting warming to 1.5 °C is out of reach within the twenty-first century and for keeping peak warming below 1.7 °C consumption loss relative to a current-policy baseline increases from 1.3% to 3.5%. A portfolio of options alleviates the burden of energy sector decarbonization and substantially reduces energy price markups, but puts the AFOLU sector under stress. We show that prudent policy measures, such as limiting total bioenergy use to 100 EJ yr −1 and restricting CH 4 and N 2 O pricing to US$75 per tonne of CO 2 equivalent, can largely attenuate this pressure by reducing the need for yield increases and diminishing food price markups without severely compromising the achievability of climate targets. Our findings highlight both the need for effective climate action in the AFOLU sector and the importance of balanced and judicious sectorally aligned policies.

title: Beyond Initial Acceptance: Exploring Trust Development in an Evidence-Transparent Short-Form Video Interface
abstract: People increasingly encounter news, opinions and factual claims through short-form videos. Although these platforms make information easy to access, they do not always make it easy to examine. A video may present a claim confidently without showing where the information came from, what evidence supports it ...

title: Longitudinal impacts of family conflict and school environment on youth mental health: An ABCD study
authors: Kayleigh Esparza, Robin Aupperle, Dalia El-Shafie, Herry Patel, Wes Thompson, Martin Paulus
abstract: Background: Adolescence is a critical period for social and emotional development during which these dynamics start to shift, placing them at an increased risk for poor mental health outcomes. Bioecological theory posits that various levels of one’s environment, including family and school, can impact youth development and mental health outcomes. Therefore, the current study aimed to explore the longitudinal relationships between family and school environment and youth mental health. Methods: The study used data collected as part of the longitudinal and multisite Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development Study (ABCD® Study). Baseline sample included 11,868 youth aged 9-10. The study used data from follow up year 1-year 3, as these time points had data for all variables. We examined family conflict, school environment, and youth and caregiver reports of youth internalizing and externalizing symptoms in a three-wave random intercept cross-lagged panel model. Results: Results indicated that family conflict impacted youth externalizing symptoms from follow-up year 2 to year 3. Youth internalizing and externalizing symptoms impacted family conflict from follow-up year 1 to year 2 and from follow-up year 2 to year 3. Moreover, school environment impacted youth internalizing and externalizing symptoms from follow-up year 1 to year 2. Youth externalizing symptoms impacted the school environment from follow-up year 1 to year 2 and from follow-up year 2 to year 3, while youth internalizing symptoms impacted the school environment from follow-up year 2 to year 3. Conclusions: Results support bidirectional relationships between family and school environments and youth mental health during varying developmental periods. Early detection of internalizing and externalizing symptoms is important for interrupting mutually reinforcing cycles of symptom escalation and environmental strain.

title: Fake–Real gaps in observed spread and detectability differ between health misinformation datasets built in different ways: a comparison of CoAID and FakeHealth
abstract: Health misinformation datasets don't reach a common ground about what misinformation is. FakeHealth labels mainstream health news by expert-rated reporting quality, while CoAID compares fact-checked COVID-19 claims with material from health agencies and health information publishers. We compared model-standardized Fake/Real ratios of observed social media posts, including items with no observed posts, between the CoAID News and FakeHealth HealthStory subsets, and evaluated leakage-controlled text classifiers within, across and beyond the two datasets. Fake items drew fewer observed posts than Real items in both datasets, but the ratio was 0.253 in CoAID and 0.840 in FakeHealth (ratio-of-ratios 0.301; 95% interval 0.154–0.645). The CoAID gap lay entirely in whether an item was posted at all and was concentrated among Fake items with no identifiable publisher, which points to limited findability as well as limited spread. In two FakeNewsNet collections outside health, Fake items drew more observed posts in GossipCop (ratio 2.144), and PolitiFact's interval included parity. Text showed a parallel split: Fake and Real were highly separable within CoAID (macro F1 0.926) and modestly within FakeHealth (0.675), transfer was poor in both directions, and word–label associations were uncorrelated across datasets. Fake items were shorter in both datasets, and length alone ranked transferred items and independent COVID rumors better than the word-based models. The distance between Fake and Real items, in language and in observed engagement, differed between datasets that define and source misinformation differently; these are comparisons between dataset contexts, not estimates of a pandemic effect. Engagement studies and detection benchmarks should report how labels, sources and collection were defined, check for source–label entanglement, shared-post dependence and simple length baselines, and test beyond a single dataset.

title: The Dutch Labor Movement as a Slowly Sinking Ship
abstract: In the summer of 2025, I was asked by Sociologie Magazine to contribute a short essay on the political impact and role of labor unions in the Netherlands, with a particular focus on membership, legitimacy and future scenarios. Sociologie Magazine targets a general (Dutch) readership that is interested in staying up-to-date with developments in the social sciences, e.g., alumni of the social science programmes. This manuscript contains an English translation of my essay3, with some minor alterations to improve understandability for non-Dutch-speaking audiences. I wrote the essay in my capacity as a (social) scientist, with the two goals in mind: 1) to both provide an overview of some basic – but currently sometimes seemingly somewhat forgotten – understandings of what labor unions are and do, and what forms the basis of their legitimacy, and 2) to provide a scientifically-grounded, critical reflection on current trends and their implications, that does justice to the complexity of the issue and the limits of our knowledge.

title: Age differences in entry into parenthood among siblings and cousins in Dutch and Finnish kinship networks
authors: Vera de Bel, Alyona Artamonova, Takayuki Hiraoka, Eszter Bokányi, Mirkka Danielsbacka, Marijtje A.J. van Duijn, Antti O Tanskanen
abstract: With fewer siblings and cousins sharing longer lifespans, their relationships may become increasingly important sources of social influence and support in ageing societies. This study makes an empirical and methodological contribution by comparing and analyzing the association of horizontal kin’s timing of entry into parenthood in two European countries: the Netherlands and Finland. We investigate whether horizontal kin being closer in degree of relatedness, share maternal lineage and have the same gender, are more likely to have their first child at approximately the same age. Our results show that cousins are more similar to full siblings in their age at first birth than we expected, whereas half-siblings have the largest age difference. Moreover, same sex kin pairs, except half-siblings, are closest in age at first birth. Besides this substantive contribution, this study serves as a methodological blueprint. In a handful of Western European countries, a new data source has recently become available that allows empirical analysis of kinship networks across the entire population. To our knowledge, this study is the first to apply statistical methods to analyze and compare horizontal kinship networks across different European contexts.

title: Has the Motherhood Wage Penalty Declined? Changing Selection into Motherhood Across Cohorts in Japan
abstract: Whether the motherhood wage penalty has declined amid family policy expansion and shifting gender norms has attracted attention. However, a change in the penalty over time could reflect both changing effects of motherhood and changing selection into motherhood, in particular selection on wage growth, which can produce spurious trends. Using nationally representative panel data from Japan, this study examines the wage consequences of motherhood over the ten years following first birth in an earlier (1960–1974) and a later (1975–1989) cohort, using fixed effects (FE) models and fixed effects individual slopes (FEIS) models, which account for individual differences in wage growth. Averaged over the ten years following first birth, the penalty was 10.1% and 3.6% in the earlier and later cohorts under the FE model, but 8.4% and 11.9% with no significant cohort difference under the FEIS model. Mothers in the later cohort also had steeper underlying wage growth than non-mothers, which is consistent with changing selection into motherhood on wage growth accounting for the apparent decline under the FE model. These findings provide no evidence that the motherhood wage penalty in Japan declined across cohorts, despite decades of family policy expansion and shifting gender norms.

title: The Ottoman Shadow: Federal Bypass Capture, Emerging-Donor Concessions, and Contested Development in Turkey’s Horn of Africa Diplomacy
abstract: Turkey’s engagement with Somalia since 2011 is usually presented as the renewal of an Ottoman-era partnership and as an example of emerging-donor engagement free of the conditionality attached to Western aid. This article asks what that engagement does to authority and revenue inside a fragile federation. It argues that Turkish agreements over Somali state assets and natural resources have been concluded almost entirely with the federal government, including over resources that the Provisional Constitution assigns to negotiation between the federal government and the member states. It names this pattern federal bypass capture and specifies three observable implications against which it can be tested. Process tracing of Turkish port, airport, defence, fisheries and hydrocarbon arrangements from 2011 to 2026 finds the first and third implications supported and the second partly supported, and shows that the resulting opposition, centred on Puntland, has been framed in constitutional terms. The Ottoman connection invoked in official discourse is real but narrow and discontinuous. Plausibility probes of Emirati port concessions in Puntland and Somaliland, and of Kurdish oil exports from northern Iraq through Turkey, suggest that the mechanism belongs to a wider pattern of tier selection. The article closes with four hypotheses for comparative testing. For development scholarship, the case suggests that the effect of emerging-donor engagement on a fragile federation depends on which tier of the federation the donor negotiates with.

title: NISBO Elderly Advisory Services as a Bridge between Older Migrants and Welfare Institutions: Historical Lessons from the Dutch Experience
abstract: This article examines the historical development and institutional significance of elderly advisory services for older migrants in the Netherlands, focusing on the Netherlands Islamic Elderly Union (NISBO) and its predecessor, the Turkish Islamic Elderly Union (TISBO). Employing a qualitative historical case-study approach, the research analyses TISBO project and preparatory documents from the mid-1990s, a NISBO planning text from the 1996 transition period, and NISBO reports from 1999 and 2001, supplemented by governmental records and academic literature. The study traces the advisory initiative from its establishment within TISBO in 1994 through a gradual institutional transition completed by 1997. Historical records document 697 advisory requests between January and May 1998, addressing income, housing, healthcare and welfare-related concerns. The analysis develops an institutional bridge framework encompassing five interconnected functions: informational accessibility, communication and mediation, trust and individual support, institutional coordination, and representation and organisational learning. The findings illustrate how migrant-led advisory initiatives sought to connect individual needs with mainstream welfare institutions through accessible guidance, mediation and organisational cooperation. Although the available documentation does not establish long-term service effectiveness, the historical NISBO experience offers relevant insights into culturally responsive assistance, institutional accessibility and community-based support within increasingly diverse ageing societies.

title: Making ascriptions of harmfulness
abstract: Criminologists and zemiologists regularly ascribe harmfulness to a range of social phenomena, from beliefs and motifs to social structures and subjectivities. But what does it mean – and what do we need – to assert that such phenomena are harmful to someone or something? In this article, I argue that an account of harmfulness is equally important to an account of harm, and that arriving at the latter does not necessarily provide us with guidance on what is harmful to someone or something. Moreover, I address several recently expressed worries about relativism about harm and argue that through properly accounting for both harm and harmfulness we can – and should – accept a certain type of relativism about harm, given that discourses, practices, social structures, and other social objects are not harmful simpliciter but harmful to someone, usually under certain conditions. I argue that social harm scholars and criminologists concerned with particularly freewheeling forms of subjectivism or relativism about social harm can allay some of these concerns by distinguishing between what is conditionally and unconditionally harmful to someone.

title: The Conditional Relevance of Value Orientations in Intergenerational Care: Institutional Context, Gender and Direction of Care in SHARE
abstract: Population ageing has intensified Europe’s reliance on family care, while long-term processes of individualisation are widely assumed to weaken family obligations. This study examines the conditions under which individual value orientations predict participation in intergenerational care among older adults in 27 European countries. Using wave 8 of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE, 2019–2020), it tests whether four indicators of value orientations (interpersonal trust, religiosity, risk aversion and planning horizon) are associated with care provided to grandchildren and to ageing parents. Grandparental childcare is associated with religiosity and, non-monotonically, with risk aversion; care for parents is associated only with risk aversion, in the same non-monotonic form. Contrary to the expectation that values matter more where discretion is greater, the associations do not differ significantly between the two directions of care, and gender does not moderate them. Institutional context does: the association of trust with caregiving is negative within post-communist Central and Eastern Europe and not negative, or weakly positive, outside it, in both directions. A supplementary analysis of at least weekly care shows that this moderation concerns participation only, while religiosity predicts regular care in both directions. The behavioural relevance of value orientations thus varies less with the direction of care or the caregiver’s gender than with the institutional context in which family care is decided.

title: Thick and thin accounts of social harm
abstract: Social harm is a concept on the rise in criminology and zemiology, yet one that remains under-theorised. This article argues that existing accounts misclassify certain harms, are anthropocentric, and struggle to struggle to account for variance in what makes someone or something’s life go best. I argue that these issues can be addressed though distinguishing between ‘thin’ and ‘thick’ accounts of social harm. Thin accounts provide us with formal statements about what is affected when someone or something is harmed (harm’s medium), what the baseline is for assessing whether this thing has been impacted (harm’s structure), and what makes a harm social (harm’s social ontology). Thick accounts add a final, crucial, ingredient: a subject-dependent substantive theory of whatever we take to be harm’s medium (harm’s currency). I then offer a thin account of social harm that avoids the challenges faced by existing accounts by treating wellbeing as harm’s medium, events which negatively affect someone’s wellbeing as harm’s structure, and human actions as structuring causes as its social ontology.

title: Critical Theory of AI: The Alienation of the Human Intellect
abstract: In this article, I present some fundamentals of a critique of AI influenced by the Critical Theory of the Frankfurt School. From this perspective, artificial intelligence represents a kind of apotheosis of instrumental rationality, an alienation of the human intellect, framed by economic calculations, geopolitical strategies, the reduction of reason to cognition, perception to classification and knowledge to an inventory. The article begins by defining machine-learning-based forms of artificial intelligence, distinguishing between different types of foundation model (LLM-based and non-LLM-based), describing how LLM-based GenAI works and discussing the realistic prospects for the emergence of AGI in the near future, especially when this is anticipated from increases in compute scale of GenAI. Then, it outlines the fundamental critical position of Frankfurt School Critical Theory, which is that human knowledge cannot be reduced to an inventory of items any more than the human intellect can be reduced to instrumental rationality. Against this background, it critiques the application of AI as a business machine and a warfare technology, arguing that it is crucial, in opposing corporate and military applications, not to uncritically accept the reduction of the human intellect to mental labor. Nonetheless, the implications of AI for the automation of mental labor are critically important, and so the article turns next to the microeconomics of AI implementation, inferring from the discourse of liberal economics that the disruptive structural transformation of the middle class through polarization and casualization is a real possibility. In conclusion, the article discusses the implications of this dialectical critique, not just in terms of the potential for a political convulsion, but also in terms of the urgent need for AI research to acknowledge (and address) the problems and limitations of current foundation models.

title: Substance Over Label: Semantic Drift and Zionist Self-Identification among Canadian Jews
abstract: A 2024 survey found that 94 percent of Canadian Jews affirm Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state, yet only 51 percent call themselves Zionists. Brym attributed the gap to semantic drift: the word Zionism has acquired a pejorative connotation, so many Jews who hold Zionist commitments nevertheless decline the label. If so, substantive markers of Zionism should predict attitudes toward Canadian policies that impose costs on Israel, and the label should add little once those markers are accounted for. Using weighted data from the same survey (N = 550), we find that emotional attachment to Israel and belief in its right to exist as a Jewish state explain 23 percent of the variance in opposition to sanctions on violent settlers, an arms embargo, and recognition of a Palestinian state, beyond self-identification. Self-identification adds less than 1 percent beyond those markers, a nonsignificant increment. Among respondents very attached to Israel, non-Zionists and self-identified Zionists differ by only 0.02 points on a five-point scale. The results add converging evidence for the semantic drift hypothesis and show that, among Canadian Jews, calling oneself a Zionist does not mark a distinct position on Canadian policy toward Israel once attachment is considered.

title: Rebates on the Ballot: Exposure to the $500 ACA Checks and Voting Behavior in the 2026 Midterm Elections
abstract: How do targeted, one-time fiscal rebates distributed amidst a sharp contraction in social insurance generosity affect electoral participation and partisan vote shares? In 2026, the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act (ACA) premium tax credits restored the statutory 400% Federal Poverty Level (FPL) subsidy cliff, eliminated zero-dollar ($0) premium plans for millions of households, and raised required premium contributions across all subsidized income tiers. Ahead of the November 2026 midterm elections, the federal executive distributed $500 rebate checks to unsubsidized Marketplace enrollees in the 30 states using the federally facilitated exchange platform. Combining county-level Marketplace enrollment and plan-pricing records with household survey microdata, regional economic indicators, and county-by-contest election returns, I estimate the electoral impact of county exposure to the $500 checks. To address the endogeneity of unsubsidized enrollment, I construct simulated instrumental variables isolating exogenous variation in statutory tax-schedule changes, zero-premium plan termination, and leave-own-rating-area-out insurer pricing applied to a fixed national reference population. Two-stage least squares estimates, supported by leave-one-county-out jackknife, omitted variable bias, and randomization inference checks, demonstrate that check exposure substantially increased voter turnout and Republican two-party vote shares, with the largest effects concentrated in lower-income counties and districts with high minority electorate shares.

title: NYC’S Unsettled COVID-19 Era Labor Market: The Case for an Active Labor Market Policy
abstract: This report combines an analysis of the current state of New York City’s changing labor market with a survey and examination of the city’s workforce system – the vast array of agencies, training programs, and support services designed to help jobseekers find work and careers. Unlike many cities and the nation overall, New York City has yet to recover from pandemic-induced job loss, with a particularly severe impact on lower-income workers of color and working parents. What is needed is an active labor market policy that takes a comprehensive approach, plans and coordinates across the four branches to connect with workers and businesses, education institutions and training providers, and identifies and builds many more career pathways and the ladders and supports needed to help workers climb those ladders. And that needs to be coupled with public and private policies to raise wages and job quality and to encourage and support businesses in adapting to a regime of better wages and jobs.

title: Mexico’s Gender Violence Alert and Violence Against Women and Girls: Causal Evidence from a Difference-in-Differences Analysis
abstract: This paper evaluates the impact of Mexico’s Gender Violence Alert (AVGM) on violence against women and girls. AVGM constitutes a key institutional response to violence against women and girls (VAWG) in Mexico, yet causal evidence on its effects remains limited. I employ a staggered difference-in-differences analysis to estimate the effects of AVGM declarations across Mexican municipalities. The analysis draws on longitudinal mortality data as well as survey data. Beyond femicides and self-reported violence, I study two intermediate outcomes: reporting behaviour and attitudes towards abortion as an indicator of gender norms. Across all specifications, the estimates provide no clear evidence that AVGM reduces violence against women and girls. The policy also shows no detectable effects on gender attitudes or reporting to authorities. A supplementary Bayesian updating exercise places these null findings in context and implies a downward revision of prior beliefs about the current effectiveness of AVGM. I discuss possible explanations for the null findings and argue that they are most consistent with implementation weaknesses and limitations in the policy design. The findings contribute to a better understanding of the effectiveness of top-down initiatives, which aim to address gender-based violence.

title: A New Connection Calculus: Young People’s Journey In and Out of Emotional AI Use
abstract: Young people are coming of age with AI that can simulate aspects of human relationships. Building on a survey of 2,383 young people ages 13–24, we conducted 29 in-depth interviews in January 2026 with young people ages 16–24 who use AI for personal and emotional support or who talk to AI characters and personas. Interviewees described a journey into relational AI use that often began with a rupture in a human relationship; weighed AI as less risky than disclosing to people; and found that AI magnified the relationship habits they brought to it. Those who understood AI’s problematic behaviors, and saw them as a problem, built the strongest self-protections. The interviews are not representative and do not establish causal effects. We discuss implications for those who build, fund, research, and support young people’s use of AI.

title: Heat-constrained potential accessibility to outdoor sport facilities in France: A dynamic supply framework for spatial planning
abstract: Spatial accessibility indicators assume that facilities within reach are available whenever residents wish to use them. For outdoor sport facilities, heat breaks this assumption. We develop heat-constrained potential accessibility, in which the supply of each facility is scaled by its hourly thermal availability. Availability is derived from regional wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT; ERA5-Land, 1991–2020) modified by facility attributes: cover, tree canopy and surface type. We apply the model to 97,816 public outdoor facilities and 62.6 million residents of metropolitan France, at 200-m resolution, with a 15-min walking catchment and a 26 °C WBGT threshold. On July afternoons, heat removes on average 25% of potential accessibility, and at least 47% in Occitanie, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur and Corsica. Served residents spend 139 h per season without any heat-available facility within reach, and 156 h in 2006–2025. Magnitudes depend strongly on the threshold (11% peak loss at 28 °C), whereas spatial rankings are stable. A regional WBGT without facility attributes underestimates mean losses by 12–15%.
