After regional standardisation, peak losses differ little across income groups, but desert exposure increases with income, in association mainly with the number of facilities within reach and secondarily with their peak availability. Under idealised complete shading, shading 5% of facilities chosen to maximise coverage removes 68% of heat-attributable desert person-hours (50% with half shade), against 21% when the hottest facilities are shaded first. Heat-constrained accessibility turns climate exposure into a property of supply that planners can map, compare and target.

title: From Management Practices to Customer Return in AI-Powered Service: A Scoping Review / من ممارسات الإدارة إلى عودة العميل في الخدمة المدعومة بالذكاء الاصطناعي: مراجعة نطاقية
authors: Badwan Adnan Al Shebli بدوان عدنان الشبلي
abstract: This scoping review protocol outlines a framework to map existing literature on the links between service-oriented management practices, frontline employee behavior, AI-driven service automation, and actual customer retention. Focused on premium sectors including luxury retail and real estate within the Saudi Arabian context, the protocol incorporates international frameworks (NIST, OECD) alongside local national regulations from the Saudi Data and AI Authority (SDAIA) to examine human-AI hybrid decisions and the mechanisms driving repeat customer behavior.

title: Relationship returns: traditional ecological relationship, and the direction of its yield Knowledge is what can be carried away from a home; relationship is what stays — and the family that stays is the unit that can voice it
abstract: 1. Indigenous scholars hold that all knowledge is relational. I agree, and ask what follows for a field whose product is knowledge, yet where relationship and knowledge move in opposite directions? For knowledge accumulates like a ratchet, each increment locked behind the last, and is carried from the place that produced it to wherever it is used next. Relationship runs as a loop, each participant and pass altered by the last, and is never carried off, because it exists only between the parties who keep and continue it. 2. I name the loop traditional ecological relationship (TER) and set it beside traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) — not to replace the term, but to name what TEK leaves behind when the interview is over: a family at home with the living beings of one place. Relationship, as I use the word, entails the valued currencies of regular recurring contact, caring connection, considerate contribution, and composition in community that includes return of the precious gifts of shared abundant health to their original source, rather than carried off as extracted wealth. 3. I call the primary place reality is lived, that relationship occurs, and where the currencies of value are applied in the transacting relations in that space - home - the primary place and time the body, heart, mind and soul of a person and family invests itself the most. 4. Over fifty years of residence on one home ground — a wood turtle nesting bank raised from fewer than fifty hatchlings a year to several hundred, and deer whose avoidance of people, the most uniform value in a statewide record of 7.8 million detections, has reversed on this home ground upon the basis of quiet stewardship with electric conveyance— are offered not as results but as what a relationship looks like in numbers when its own residents measure and read it. 5. Four proposals follow: treat lived and observed residence in a home with diverse co-inhabitants as a method with declared standards; read an animal’s response to people as one side of a two-way ledger; with respect make room for the voice of family-held record on its home ground; and design every partnership with a mechanism for return to its source. The positions that matter are not expert and informant, but family member, host, guest and visitor — and the home landscape is host to all four.

title: New York City’s Workforce Landscape Report
authors: Lena Bhise, Stephanie Birmingham, Justin Collins, Annie Garneva, Lina Karsten Moe, James A. Parrott, Sharon Sewell-Fairman, Andrea Vaghy
abstract: “New York City’s Workforce Landscape: A network of programs, providers, and organizations foundational for catalyzing a robust and equitable economic recovery,” is an extensive overview of NYC’s existing workforce development ecosystem developed in partnership with New York City Employment & Training Coalition (NYCETC) and the Center for New York City Affairs at The New School (CNYCA). As a culmination of an NYCETC survey to its members, the data generated details the size, scope, and budget of the organizations that make up New York City’s workforce ecosystem; outlines the areas of service, modes of program delivery, and range of certificates and trainings offered; and describes the current state of affairs for the sector in 2022, underscoring the top challenges, needs, and priorities of workforce providers. The report covers preliminary insight on patterns emerging from the survey data reported by providers, including: the impact of Covid-19 on providers, a stressful environment wrought by the pandemic coinciding with budget cuts and under capacity in training programs.

title: Open to Interpretation: How Frontier AI Developers Practice Openness through Licensing
abstract: Openness is a central but contested category in global artificial intelligence (AI) governance, yet policy debates often treat it as a binary property of developers, or even of states. This article asks how leading foundation model developers practice openness through release and licensing decisions, and what this implies for how openness is governed globally. We analyze an original longitudinal dataset of 1,313 model releases by twelve developers in the United States (US), China, France and Canada between January 2023 and October 2026. We find that openness is a property of model portfolios rather than of developers. We distinguish four configurations, defined by whether, and on what terms, a developer releases its most capable model: permissive, conditional, or non-commercial open flagship, or closed flagship with permissively licensed secondary models. Secondary models have converged on generic permissive licenses, while open flagships have moved towards bespoke conditions that target revenue rather than users. The sharpest division concerns whether third parties can inspect a developer’s most capable model without permission: all US developers now withhold this, while developers elsewhere, except Baidu, allow it. Drawing on the notion of a "polysemous compromise” and on practice-based accounts of norm formation, we argue that the meaning of openness is being settled not by states but in license files, largely outside the public eye.

title: Restraint and Silence: Customary Conflict Resolution and the Erosion of Public Voice in Somali Federalism
abstract: Abstract Somalia’s political crisis is usually explained through clan competition, external intervention, and the weakness of its institutions. This paper points to a factor that gets less attention but helps sustain these failures: a pattern of political silence among elites and officials, paired with a growing public disregard for the country’s future. The paper traces this silence through the colonial period, the Siad Barre era, the state collapse of 1991, and the federal settlement of the past two decades. It draws on Somali customary values and conflict-resolution practice, including xeer, diya-paying groups, the guurti and shir, and the tradition of oblique speech, to show that Somali society has long possessed effective means of naming wrongs and restraining violence. The paper argues that the decline of these mechanisms at the national level, and their replacement by a political culture in which naming a violation carries a high personal price, is a central cause of the federal breakdown now under way. It also addresses the counterargument that silence has often been a rational strategy for survival, and it distinguishes strategic silence from the civic silence that erodes the conditions for agreement. Scholarly contributions. This paper makes four contributions to the study of Somali politics and African federalism. First, it separates strategic silence, a temporary and purposive restraint tied to negotiation, from civic silence, a durable failure to name violations of the public good, and it offers a test for distinguishing the two. Second, it defines political silence as an observable phenomenon with three dimensions and extends Hirschman’s exit, voice, and loyalty framework to a setting in which exit runs through clan and diaspora channels. Third, it treats customary restraint as both a resource and a liability: the discretion that settles disputes between kin can conceal violations when the cost falls on those excluded from the negotiation. Fourth, it brings xeer, the diya-paying group, and the guurti into federal analysis as inputs to institutional design. It takes Puntland, which the paper treats as the first pillar of Somali federalism, as its central case for testing when customary legitimacy supports a durable federal settlement, and it uses the Borama process in Somaliland as a comparison.

title: You Talking to Me? The Diverging Effects of Organizational Communication on the Gender Ambition Gap
abstract: Women's underrepresentation in civic life is accompanied by a persistent ambition gap. Research attributes this gap partly to gendered socialization and unequal encouragement. How does organizational communication affect this gap, and can organizations narrow it by addressing women directly? We examine these questions through a pre-registered survey experiment with more than 7,000 members of a major Turkish public sector trade union confederation. Women and men were randomly assigned to a gender-neutral mobilization video, a video that addressed women directly and exclusively, or a placebo. The women-focused message increased women's willingness to participate in and lead union activities, while the gender-neutral message had no detectable effect among women. In contrast, the gender-neutral message appeared to speak primarily to men. Exploratory analyses link the success of the women-focused message to increases in self-efficacy and interest among women. These findings suggest that how organizations address their members can shape the ambition gap in participation, and that apparently gender-neutral appeals may not be neutral in their effects.

title: Counting Levels or Measuring Distance? Organizational Size and Hierarchy Across and Within Organizations
abstract: That larger organizations have more hierarchical levels is among the most replicated findings in organization theory. Yet Cullen, Anderson, and Baker (1986) found that the relationship did not hold within organizations as they changed size, and concluded that size–structure theory explains differences of scale rather than processes of change. We argue that this gap is partly a consequence of measurement. Because span limits force a new level only after a several-fold increase in size, and because the level count is set by the longest chain of command, the count registers growth only at widely spaced thresholds and moves for many reasons unrelated to size. Average geodesic distance, the mean number of reporting steps separating any two members, has neither limitation. Using published organograms of UK central government bodies (a cross-section of 70 organizations, 2011–2013, and a panel of 18 organizations observed 520 times, 2011–2025), we find that levels increase with size at a decreasing rate both across and within organizations. Within organizations, however, the count changes in only a third of periods and does not respond to period-to-period changes in size. Average distance is far more strongly associated with size in both designs and responds to growth and contraction. As predicted, distances also become more uniform as organizations grow, at similar rates across and within organizations, suggesting that differences of scale are the accumulated result of change. Distance-based measures thus give theories of organizational size and structure a more sensitive account of how hierarchies change.

title: Holding Options Open in the South: A Real Options and Institutional Theory of Entrepreneurship and Regional Economic Development in Southern China
abstract: Southern China has served for more than four decades as the country's principal laboratory for market reform, and its trajectory from export-processing zones to innovation-driven city-regions has made it one of the most consequential settings for entrepreneurship in the world economy. Yet theories of entrepreneurship in China have tended to treat the institutional environment as a static backdrop, and theories of regional development have tended to treat entrepreneurs as undifferentiated inputs. This paper develops an integrative theoretical framework that links the regional institutional context of Southern China to entrepreneurs' decision-making over time and, through venture-level outcomes, to regional economic development. Drawing on real options reasoning, institutional theory, the psychology of entrepreneurial persistence, research on organizational scope and the task environment, and work on legitimacy and media sentiment, the framework advances eight propositions. I argue that institutional experimentation in Southern China raised the value of holding entrepreneurial options; that entrepreneurs who staged reversible commitments and combined persistence with explicit exercise and abandonment criteria were best positioned to convert ambiguity into growth; that the performance consequences of venture scope and favorable media attention are contingent and, in the latter case, curvilinear; that artificial intelligence and cross-border institutional plurality expand the set of options available to entrepreneurs; and that regional development depends on whether institutions channel the exercise of these options toward productive ends. The paper concludes with implications for theory, for empirical designs that address analytic flexibility, and for policy in the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area and beyond.

title: Patriarchal blind spots of risk management under technogarchy? Gendered disinformation as a systemic risk under the DSA
authors: Martha Stolze, Philipp Darius, Rachel Griffin, Lukas Seiling
abstract: Large online platforms have become fora for political discourse, gaining substantial influence over communication, media infrastructure and public attention. Most of these platforms show a concerning presence of harmful content such as intentional false or misleading gender- and sexuality-based claims (gendered disinformation, GenDis). GenDis has served to reaffirm gender and sexuality norms, mute political adversaries, and delegitimize politicians and institutions, e.g. used by the Kremlin and radical right actors.. To address the spread of such harmful content in the EU, the Digital Services Act (DSA) requires very large online platforms (VLOPs) to manage “systemic risks”. However, platforms’ risk management of GenDis remains underexplored. Based on a systematic literature review of peer-reviewed journal articles, we conclude that GenDis-related risks fall under the systemic risk categories of the DSA. Conversely, our analysis of VLOPs risk reports indicates that X, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube inadequately address GenDis. We interpret the omission of GenDis in platform reports as a blind spot of patriarchal-technogarchic risk management, which facilitates misogynist and LGBTQI-phobic illiberal communication practices. We argue that risk management needs to acknowledge vulnerabilities resulting from social inequalities, avoid compartmentalisation, and allow for complex phenomena like GenDis to bridge several systemic risk categories.

title: Remittances and the Growth Nexus in Bangladesh: A VECM Based Study
authors: Asma Ul Hosna mim, Sufian Ahammed
abstract: Bangladesh is one of the world’s top remittance receiving nations. However, the macroeconomic channels through which remittance inflows affect long run economic growth have not been sufficiently explored. This study investigates the influence of remittances on the economic growth of Bangladesh from 1976 to 2021. We introduced foreign direct investment (FDI), official development assistance (ODA), exports and imports as control variables in our model. Annual data on each variable were collected from the World Development Indicators (WDI). The Augmented Dickey Fuller (ADF) test results identified that all variables are integrated of order one. Following that Johansen cointegration test confirmed a stable long run equilibrium relationship among the variables. Then, we employed Vector Error Correction Model (VECM) to estimate both short run and long run dynamics. The findings indicate the existence of a long run relationship among all the chosen variables. Specifically, remittances exert a positive significant effect on the growth of the Bangladesh economy. The error correction term (ECT) indicates that the system will eventually reach a long term equilibrium with a 26% annual adjustment rate in response to any short run disturbances. The Granger Causality test reveals unidirectional causality from remittance to economic growth. Overall, the findings suggest that remittances play a crucial role in promoting sustainable economic growth in Bangladesh, even after controlling for other external capital flows. Therefore, policymakers should strengthen formal remittance channels and encourage the proper utilization of remittance inflows.

title: From Revolutionary Warfare to Humanitarian Internationalism: Cuba, African Liberation, and the Evolution of Revolutionary Legitimacy in the Global South
abstract: Comparative scholarship on revolution has largely emphasized insurgency, political rupture, and the seizure of state power, whilst paying less attention to how revolutionary legitimacy is reconstructed internationally after armed struggle recedes. This article examines that problem through Cuba’s evolving engagement with African liberation and Global South humanitarian internationalism. It develops the concept of Humanitarian Revolutionary Legitimacy (HRL) to explain how revolutionary states reconstruct claims to moral authority by translating histories of anti-imperial struggle and sacrifice into humanitarian solidarity and South–South cooperation. Tracing Cuba’s trajectory from guerrilla revolution through military internationalism in Angola and the anti-apartheid struggle to post-Cold War medical diplomacy, the article argues that revolutionary legitimacy can endure through changing practices of solidarity. Yet this legitimacy remains contested: humanitarian commitment coexists with state interests, economic benefits, labour tensions, and domestic racial inequalities. The Cuban case therefore reveals revolutionary legitimacy not as inherited moral authority, but as an evolving and contested historical process.

title: Strategic Location and Survival Dynamics of Businesses in San Diego County: A Comparative Machine Learning and Geospatial Approach
abstract: Background: Municipal business registries provide valuable information for examining business conditions and characteristics associated with longevity. However, recorded business-status fields do not necessarily contain complete event histories required for formal survival analysis. This study therefore examines recorded active and closed/canceled business status rather than time-to-event survival probabilities. Purpose: This study compares logistic regression with four tree-based ensemble classifiers to distinguish recorded business status among San Diego County establishments. SHAP interpretation and unsupervised clustering are also used to examine structural and geographic patterns. Methods: The integrated dataset contained 158,330 initial records and 140,737 establishments after cleaning. The supervised modeling dataset included 137,814 observations after excluding 2,923 records without valid geographic coordinates. A stratified 80/20 split produced 110,251 training and 27,563 holdout test observations. SMOTE was applied exclusively to the training data, balancing both classes at 69,998 observations each. Five classifiers were evaluated on the same unaltered holdout set. SHAP was used to interpret LightGBM predictions, while K-Prototypes (k = 4) and spatial K-Means (k = 7) characterized business profiles and geographic patterns. Results: Logistic regression achieved an F1-score of 0.587087, accuracy of 0.661834, and ROC-AUC of 0.683970. LightGBM achieved the highest accuracy (0.835679), recall (0.760220), F1-score (0.792553), and ROC-AUC (0.911295). XGBoost achieved the highest precision (0.829190). SHAP identified business age as the strongest contributor to LightGBM predictions, followed by ownership, density, geographic, and industry features. Clustering identified distinct business profiles and spatial concentrations. Conclusions: Ensemble classifiers outperformed the logistic-regression baseline on the holdout dataset. Business age and ownership structure contributed substantially to model predictions. These findings represent associations with recorded business status, not causal effects or direct estimates of survival over time. Future research using longitudinal records and verified opening and closure dates could extend this framework to formal survival analysis. Keywords: Business Status Classification; Business Survival; Machine Learning; LightGBM; SHAP; Spatial Analysis; Business Clustering; San Diego County.

title: Viradas nas eleições majoritárias brasileiras: quando o segundo turno não repete o primeiro
abstract: In 2026, Lula lost the first round by 2.2 million votes and won the runoff. The article asks whether a comeback like this is unusual in Brazilian elections. In 106 of the 413 runoffs decided between 1998 and 2026, the winner had entered the second round at a disadvantage, a rate of 25.7%. In the 2026 presidential election the disadvantage was 2.0 points, and in the 51 races with a disadvantage of up to 2.5 points the comeback rate was 35.3%. The first-round lead is associated with lower risk and does not eliminate it, and the runoff narrowed the leader’s advantage in 67.8% of the races. In the model, the margin and the leader’s incumbency are the two variables most associated. Turnout falls between rounds and falls less when there is a comeback.

title: Operational versus Strategic Use of Analytics in Retail: A Comparative Case Study of Walmart and Zara
abstract: Retail firms collect detailed sales, logistics, and customer data, yet analytics may play different roles in routine operational decisions and in less structured strategic choices. This exploratory comparative case study examines publicly documented decision episodes at Walmart and Zara and asks whether organizational design, particularly commitment timing, helps explain the difference. A structured search yielded 27 documents published between 2003 and 2025. Using a codebook grounded in Simon’s (1960) programmed/non-programmed distinction and Galbraith’s (1974) information-processing perspective, the study classified 11 decision episodes: six operational, four strategic, and one ambiguous. In the documents reviewed, analytics is most visible in routine decisions made within short feedback cycles, and its role in documented strategic decisions is less clear. Zara’s reported in-season production commitments show how timing may make recent sales information actionable. This is a historical description rather than a claim about current practice, and the corpus does not document the timing of Walmart’s assortment commitments. The cases motivate a proposition that shorter commitment lead times may increase the share of comparable decisions materially informed by relevant current-period data. The corpus, however, neither measures that outcome nor tests the proposition. It is small, curated, and documentary; the firms differ in other ways, and one researcher conducted all coding. The study therefore makes no claim about causality, prevalence, or decision quality.

title: Too Much Support, Not Enough Ecosystem? Resource Munificence, Government Support, and New Venture Founding in Northeastern China
abstract: Northeastern China has received two decades of sustained state investment under successive revitalization programs, yet its rate of new venture founding continues to trail that of coastal regions. We integrate entrepreneurial ecosystem theory, real options reasoning, and the too-much-of-a-good-thing perspective to explain this puzzle. Using simulated survey data that mirror a two-wave design covering 1,000 firms in Liaoning, Jilin, Heilongjiang, and eastern Inner Mongolia, we find that ecosystem resource munificence is positively associated with the number of new ventures that firms found. Government support exhibits an inverted U-shaped relationship with founding, with a turning point slightly above the regional mean. Environmental dynamism strengthens the munificence and founding relationship, consistent with the view that rich ecosystems lower the cost of acquiring growth options under uncertainty. A complementary role for firm AI adoption appears in some specifications but not across a 144-specification multiverse. The results suggest that ecosystem depth, rather than support intensity, governs founding in transition regions.

title: Black Immigrant Women in the United States: Poverty, Income, Employment, and Health Insurance Coverage by Origin, Education, and Duration of Residence
abstract: This technical report describes poverty, income, employment, cash assistance receipt, and health insurance coverage among Black women in the United States, with comparisons by nativity, birthplace, educational attainment, duration of U.S. residence, and citizenship. The analysis uses the 2024 American Community Survey one-year Public Use Microdata Sample accessed through IPUMS USA: 128,151 women aged 18 or older who reported Black or African American race alone or in combination, including 16,877 immigrant women in six birthplace-based groups (Anglophone Caribbean, Haiti, Anglophone Africa, Francophone and Lusophone Sub-Saharan Africa, Horn of Africa, and Afro-Latino). Estimates use person weights with successive-difference replication over the 80 ACS replicate weights. Five logistic regression models of poverty, supplementary models of coverage and cash assistance among women below the poverty threshold, and a set of sensitivity specifications are reported in full, with 74 tables and three figures covering descriptive distributions, complete coefficient tables, design-based joint tests, predicted probabilities, pairwise contrasts, and variance comparisons.

title: Pivoting Enough, Not Too Much: Entrepreneurial Drive, Political Skill, and Post-Pandemic Venture Performance in South America
authors: Carlos Martínez, Kavin Alves Santos, Juan Giménez
abstract: How do ventures in emerging markets perform after a systemic shock? Drawing on upper echelons and dynamic capabilities perspectives, we examine how founder attributes and strategic pivoting shape post-pandemic venture performance in South America. Using survey data from 500 ventures in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Peru, we find that entrepreneurial drive is positively related to performance and that this relationship is stronger when founders are politically skilled. Strategic pivoting has an inverted U-shaped relationship with performance, and environmental dynamism shifts the performance-maximizing level of pivoting upward. Core results hold with an alternative outcome, without influential observations, and with country-clustered standard errors, although moderation effects weaken with the alternative outcome. We discuss implications for theories of entrepreneurial adaptation and for the “too much of a good thing” logic.

title: Dissecting Corpora Construction: The Case of Environmental Social Science
authors: Ryan Light, Xiaosu Tian, Hannah C. Waight, Nicholas Theis
abstract: The use of computational techniques to understand large text datasets has become commonplace. At the same time, the idea that the output generated from computational analyses is only as good as the data that was input into them has become ubiquitous. Yet the consequences of decision-making during the corpora construction process have not been adequately examined. In this paper, we dissect corpora construction using the case of environmental social science literature. Specifically, we ask about the consequences of including (or excluding) a massive publisher of megajournals on the overall structure of a carefully identified environmental social science database from 2008-2022 (n=166,804 articles). Results of a multi-pronged bibliometric analysis, including both topic models and structural topic models, indicate that the articles published by massive publishers exhibit some variation in subject matter as well as minor differences in content and style, including citation practices. Conclusions draw attention to the importance of dissecting corpora construction in an age of proliferating science.

title: Reciprocity, common pool resource management, and the social organization of labor in swidden agriculture
abstract: Agricultural labor exchange, in which farmers form cooperative groups to assist one another with seasonal tasks, is a well studied form of cooperation. However, its role in managing common pool resources (CPRs) has received less attention. We examine how land use decisions and group affiliations structure labor exchange in a swidden agricultural forest commons. Using a Bayesian latent network model, we estimate how kinship, shared church affiliation, village of residence, and the use of communal forest for cattle pasture shape reported labor ties among farmers. Our results show that while labor exchange networks are strongly organized around kin, church, and village affiliations, farmers who use communal forest for cattle pasture are named less frequently as preferred labor partners. We discuss whether this pattern reflects a process of social sanctioning and propose that labor exchange may act as a decentralized governance mechanism for managing CPRs in swidden landscapes.

title: Contribution of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Interventions to Reducing Mortality among People Living with HIV in Mozambique
abstract: The HIV response in Mozambique requires an approach that links clinical care with the social, economic and environmental determinants of health. INSIDA 2021 estimated a national HIV prevalence of 12.5% among adults aged 15 and over, corresponding to about 2.097 million people, and a viral load suppression rate of 64.1% among adults living with HIV. In this context, access to safe water, adequate sanitation and hygiene conditions, collectively known as WASH, may play a complementary role in preventing infections and clinical complications. This article analyses the extent to which WASH interventions can contribute to reducing mortality among people living with HIV (PLHIV), drawing on INSIDA 2021 data, the National Strategic Plan for the HIV and AIDS Response 2021–2025 (PEN V) and the available scientific evidence. The analysis shows that PEN V establishes the reduction of AIDS-related deaths and the strengthening of health and community systems as priorities, although it does not present WASH as a specific intervention within its response package. International literature indicates that water treatment and safe storage can reduce episodes of diarrhoea among PLHIV; however, data on the direct effect of WASH interventions on mortality remain inconclusive. It is concluded that WASH may contribute indirectly to preventing deaths associated with infectious complications, but this effect cannot be quantified for Mozambique with the evidence identified. Keywords: WASH; HIV; mortality; opportunistic infections; safe water; sanitation; hygiene; Mozambique.

title: CLIMATE CHANGE AND POVERTY DYNAMICS IN MOZAMBIQUE
abstract: 1 CLIMATE CHANGE AND POVERTY DYNAMICS IN MOZAMBIQUE Márcio Danilo Joaquim de Morais¹ Abstract This paper examines the relationship between climate change and poverty dynamics in Mozambique, focusing on the mechanisms through which climate shocks affect household livelihoods, consumption, health and access to essential services. It is a documentary study with an analytical and interpretative approach, supported by secondary quantitative data, scientific literature, institutional reports and empirical studies on poverty, climate variability and household welfare. The evidence reviewed indicates that Mozambique faces a combination of rising temperatures, rainfall variability and recurrent extreme events, while a significant share of households remains dependent on climate-sensitive livelihoods and has limited access to productive assets, irrigation, basic services and social protection. Studies on rural vulnerability and household consumption show that drought and extreme rainfall can undermine essential expenditure and deepen pre-existing inequalities. Research in Quelimane also identifies associations between temperature, precipitation and malaria seasonality, highlighting a relevant public-health pathway. The article argues that climate change does not independently explain poverty trends; rather, it interacts with structural inequalities, economic shocks, institutional constraints and unequal adaptive capacity. Sustainable poverty reduction therefore requires climate adaptation to be integrated into agricultural policy, social protection, public health, resilient infrastructure and territorial planning. Keywords: Climate change; poverty; climate variability; socio-economic vulnerability; Mozambique; sustainable development.

title: What sales-tax receipts can (and cannot) tell us about tourism: evidence from Tennessee's counties
abstract: County local-option sales-tax collections are available monthly, whereas official visitor-spending estimates arrive annually with a long lag. We test whether the collections indicate county tourism activity, emphasizing tests that could show them uninformative. Using a balanced panel of Tennessee's 95 counties over 80 months (January 2020–August 2026), validated against published county visitor spending for 2024 and 2025, we find that annual collections correlate with visitor spending at r = 0.91 in logs, but state sales tax does so equally (r = 0.915) and local collections add nothing once it is held constant. Year-over-year growth correlates at r = 0.37, falling to 0.16–0.20 after trimming outliers. Collections are spatially dependent (Moran's I = 0.18), yet few clusters survive false-discovery-rate correction, and neither a fixed-effects model nor a seasonal naive forecast dominates. The series suits the level, ranking, and seasonality of taxable activity, not visitor spending.

title: Beyond Parental Leave: Childcare Access and Research Participation in Higher Education
abstract: Childcare and caring responsibilities can shape researchers’ ability to participate in higher education beyond periods of parental leave, yet policy support often concentrates on career interruptions or additional costs associated with specific activities. This structured narrative review synthesises evidence from academic career research, wider labour-market studies and UK research policy to examine how caregiving demands and access to childcare may relate to research participation, progression and retention. The evidence suggests that parental status alone is an inadequate indicator of constraint: caregiving intensity, predictability and access to affordable, reliable replacement care are relevant to protected research time and mobility. Drawing on these findings, the review proposes an evidence-informed participation framework linking time and mobility constraints with access to career-building opportunities, research continuity and potential longer-term career outcomes. A mapping of UK policy distinguishes support for defined interruptions and activity-specific caring costs from provision for routine childcare. Direct evidence on the long-term effects of childcare affordability and the effectiveness of interventions in research careers remains limited. The framework therefore identifies testable mechanisms and priorities for evaluating how higher education institutions and research funders support sustained research participation.

title: Can crowds map war? Crowdsourcing wartime territorial control maps from Wikipedia
authors: Joe Hoskisson, Claudia Loomis, Juan Tellez
abstract: Who controls territory during an armed conflict, and how does that control shape the course of the war? Wartime territorial control is central to theories of armed conflict, yet cross-national data on control are coarse, static, or limited to single cases. We introduce a new dataset of overt territorial control---which armed group openly holds each town and military site---built from crowd-sourced Wikipedia conflict maps. These maps mark towns, villages, and military sites with icons colored by the faction that controls them. We scrape the full revision history of 20 such maps, roughly 35,000 revisions tracking some 25,000 locations across 45 state-based armed conflicts since 2014, and reconstruct which group held each point on each day and whether it was contested. Our data agree with expert-coded Carter Center maps of Syria in 90 percent of settlement-months, and the Wikipedia map of Ukraine agrees with two professional trackers of the war in 98.5 percent of place-days. Our validation effort also allows us to report which features of the data are most and least reliable. An accompanying R package provides helpful tools for aggregating and standardizing control into panel data.

title: Cedar Valley of Iowa Living Lab 2026: 10 Capacity-Building Briefs
abstract: This research report presents ten capacity-building briefs developed through the 2026 Cedar Valley of Iowa Living Lab. The study used a voice-centered, community-based design informed by the M³ Decision Architecture to examine how entrepreneurs’ experiences of institutional constraint reveal recurring gaps in regional innovation systems. Ten anchor entrepreneurs participated in structured dialogue with 67 civic, nonprofit, business, and public-sector participants, followed by distributed review involving approximately 100 community and academic stakeholders. The resulting briefs outline co-created regenerative and testable initiatives for housing redevelopment, youth mental health, grassroots nonprofit operations, newcomer navigation, food entrepreneurship, wholesale financing, civic advocacy, childcare infrastructure, workforce opportunity networks, and community wellbeing. Each brief preserves contributor interpretation, identifies a system-level tension, and specifies a collaborative experiment suitable for testing within nine months. The report contributes an applied method for converting situated entrepreneurial knowledge into testable regional capacity-building interventions. The findings are based on structured observations from a purposively assembled, mission-aligned group and support analytic rather than statistical generalization.

title: Transforming urban food systems: could food democracy and food citizenship be advanced by the personal and community impacts of co-production processes?
authors: Bramble Gardiner, Clare Pettinger, Amanda Haslam-Lucas, Barbara Diouri, Joanna Ruminska, Laura Dunn, Yve Ashton, Louise Hunt, Mary Hickson1
abstract: For complex challenges like food systems transformation, some scholars suggest co-production involving multiple actors including citizens is essential. Additionally, some argue the desirability of moving towards ‘food democracy’, aligning with participatory approaches gaining popularity more broadly. Urban food policy initiatives are examples of innovation in food democracy and food citizenship, but questions around delivery of participation and engagement remain. For example, delivering authentic participation is an ongoing challenge and the impacts on those engaged have rarely been studied. Furthermore, personal transformations are essential for collective action on urban food system transformation and similarly receive minimal focus. The need for development in these areas is reflected in the Milan Urban Food Policy Pact (MUFPP) goals including enhancing stakeholder participation (action 2) and enhancing food knowledge and action through participatory education, training and research (action 19). We report the experiences of 12 individuals engaged as community food researchers (CFRs) within transdisciplinary food system research in UK urban settings (FoodSEqual). Creative methods were used, including participatory mapping, collage, and poetic inquiry; alongside utilising assemblage theory concepts. We found CFRs developed relationships within and beyond their communities, expanded their food system knowledge and hope for change, and gained advocacy-related skills and beliefs. Our unique contribution demonstrates how personal outcomes from engagement in participatory research could support urban food systems transformation by creating conditions and capacities for active food citizenship and food democracy alongside personal transformations. This also suggests the CFR model could contribute to delivery of MUFPP goals, particularly actions 2 and 19 (described above).

title: Delivering participatory food systems research in our own communities: reflections about co-production by community food researchers and community partners
authors: Bramble Gardiner, Maria Roughton, Lisa Howard, Louise Hunt, Unis Nisa, Clare Pettinger
abstract: This article offers insights into delivering community-engaged research (co-production), from the perspectives of engaged citizens and community partners. It adds to scholarship addressing epistemic justice issues that the experiences of engaged citizens are rarely explored. The engaged citizens are community collaborators in FoodSEqual (a UKRI funded project aiming to co-produce solutions to food system inequality in four UK locations). During FoodSEqual’s delivery, it became clear contextual factors and practical delivery varied. To support shared learning, an in-person reflective session was held using the ‘open space method’ (Involve, n.d) (participants: Community Food Researchers (CFRs) (n=14), community coordinators (n=6)). Four key themes were defined during the session. A content analysis of observational notes was undertaken by a PhD Student (HG) and CFR (MR). Resulting outputs were checked with most of the original participants. Four areas identified as instrumental to successful community co-production were: 1. Engagement and building trust; 2. Co-designing practical research activities; 3. Balancing structure and flexibility; 4. Community engagement outside activities. Implications for practice include mitigating tensions between different ways of working, the need for better understanding and acknowledgement of community roles, and proposals for how the engagement model itself can contribute to food system transformation.

title: Thin Markets, Thick Ties, and Thinking Machines: Institutional Environments, IPO Markets, Technological Disruption, and New Venture Performance in Central Europe
abstract: New ventures in Central Europe grow up inside institutional environments that are neither fully mature nor fully void. Formal rules have converged on European Union standards, yet capital markets remain thin, informal ties remain consequential, and successful technology ventures frequently exit to foreign exchanges. At the same time, artificial intelligence and related digital technologies are altering what a new venture is, who acts on its behalf, and how investors evaluate it. This conceptual paper integrates institutional theory, signaling and legitimacy perspectives on initial public offerings, and research on technological disruption to explain how these forces jointly shape new venture performance in the region. We develop seven propositions. We argue that the IPO operates as a legitimacy substitute whose value rises where market-supporting intermediaries are weak, that positive media sentiment exhibits a too-much-of-a-good-thing effect that is sharper in thin markets, and that founder drive pays off most when paired with political skill in particularistic settings. We further propose that category-breaking ventures face an initial valuation discount but superior long-run performance, that artificial intelligence acting as an entrepreneurial actor weakens the dependence of performance on local institutions, and that organizational scope and supranational harmonization condition these relationships. We conclude with a research agenda and implications for founders, investors, exchanges, and policymakers.

title: Towards an Age of Transdisciplinary Research: An Inaugural Statement for the International Journal of Disciplinary Studies
abstract: The International Journal of Disciplinary Studies is launched with an enduring task: to support rigorous inquiry into questions that cross the boundaries through which knowledge is commonly organized. Its transdisciplinary orientation does not promise a universal method or a final synthesis of different ways of knowing. It asks for deliberate engagement, honest accounting of difference, and careful explanation of how a study’s parts contribute to its whole. These standards are demanding because the problems at stake are demanding, and because the authority of scholarship depends on the quality of the work rather than the breadth of its claims.

title: A Lacanian Interpretation of the Authoritarian Personality
abstract: In this chapter, I present a Zizekian interpretation of the authoritarian personality that I think provides an intellectually satisfying, sociologically plausible and politically effective alternative to the classical theory. Although Zizek is in general highly critical of Adorno, in his critique of the category of “totalitarianism,” he develops a theory of perverse political subjectivity that is effectively coextensive with the concept of the sado-masochistic character. However, Zizek’s concept of totalitarian subjectivity foregrounds the role of transgressive fantasy in supporting identification with the leader figure in a way that the classical theory does not. Because the Zizekian concept of perversion reframes it in terms of the disavowal of transgressive desires constructed in fantasy scenarios, rather than the denial of castration, it is alert to the political implications of rightwing authoritarian conspiracy theories and dystopian speculations. Furthermore, by reframing the basis for the authoritarian personality, not as the violently erotic expression of a sado-masochistic character, but as the eroticised violence resulting from a perverse form of subjective structuration, Zizek develops a psychodynamic model of contemporary authoritarianism. Central to this mechanism is the Lacanian understanding that the return of the repressed causes anxiety because of the transgressive nature of the political desire. It is this which leads to the characteristic “deterioration” of ego identity seen in cases of authoritarian meltdown. Finally, Zizek’s insight that the root of totalitarian subjectivity is a kind of self-instrumentalisation, designed to force absolute authority to become manifest, clarifies the logic of pre-emptive violence motivating authoritarian personalities.

title: Reading the City: Urban Sentiment, Technological Disruption, and the Exporting and Performance of High-Growth Firms in China
abstract: High-growth firms are disproportionately responsible for job creation and productivity gains in emerging economies, yet little is known about how the urban environments in which they operate shape their decisions to sell abroad and the returns they earn from doing so. Integrating real options reasoning with an institution-based view of urban task environments, we argue that city-level sentiment about economic development and technological disruption functions as a collective signal that shapes how high-growth firms value and exploit international opportunities. We combine a simulated firm-level survey dataset calibrated to the World Bank Enterprise Survey design for 25 Chinese cities (N = 2,700 firms; 540 high-growth firms) with city-industry sentiment scores produced through large language model text classification. Economic development sentiment is positively associated with export intensity, whereas technological disruption sentiment displays an inverted U-shaped relationship with export intensity. Exporting is associated with higher productivity and growth, but these returns are amplified by favorable development sentiment and attenuated by intense disruption sentiment. A multiverse analysis of 72 specifications supports the robustness of the core moderation result. The study advances research on emerging-market internationalization, high-growth entrepreneurship, and text-based measurement in international business.

title: Separating Campaign-Level Threat from Incident-Level Attribution: A Bayesian Framework for Assessing Russian Hybrid Operations in Europe
abstract: European debate about Russian “hybrid war” tends to collapse three different questions into one: whether Russia is conducting hostile activity below the threshold of armed conflict, whether that activity forms a centrally coordinated campaign, and whether a given incident was directed by the Russian state. This article develops and applies a Bayesian framework that keeps these questions apart. At the incident level, six exhaustive hypotheses distinguish Russian state operations, state-sponsored proxies, autonomous pro-Russian actors, other states, non-hostile causes, and non-incidents; evidence enters through explicit likelihoods with dependence weights, and uncertainty in those likelihoods is propagated by simulation. At the campaign level, eight evidence blocks are weighed against three hypotheses: coordinated campaign, fragmented activity, and over-attribution. Applied to five cases spanning the evidentiary spectrum—the Wagner-tasked Leyton arson, Nord Stream, the Eagle S cable damage, the December 2025 Polish grid attack, and the November 2025 Dutch drone sightings—the model yields posterior probabilities of state direction ranging from below 0.05 to above 0.99. At the campaign level, the probability of sustained Russian activity exceeds 0.97 under every prior and dependence assumption tested, whereas the probability of central coordination ranges from 0.56 to 0.87 and is driven chiefly by assumptions about source dependence. The framework shows which conclusions are robust, which are assumption-dependent, and which evidence would most reduce uncertainty. A census of all 255 incidents in a recent open-source dataset, coded against a tiered evidentiary standard, shows that a Russian link is established for 41% of covert incidents and state direction for 24%, that none of 28 drone sightings is established, and that roughly one in five recorded incidents is overt or lawful state activity. The findings support graduated public attribution and investment in forensic and financial evidence over the accumulation of incident counts.

title: Coastal Flooding Resilience in Sitio Kagang and Sitio Tapusok of Barangay Utod: Integrating Local Worldviews and Futures Thinking for Adaptive Management
authors: Marloudiza McMillan, Jedess Miladel Salomon, Ma. Kresna Mansueto, Anna Rossini Parcero, Mohaliden Mohammad, Ulysses Nolan Paredes, Erick Glenn Juanich
abstract: This study examines how sustainability worldviews shape residents' understanding of coastal flooding and their preferred management responses in Sitio Kagang and Sitio Tapusok, Barangay Utod, Baybay City, Philippines. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, we surveyed 99 coastal residents (87.6% of households), conducted 8 focus group discussions with residents using causal mapping, and consulted 9 expert key informants through individual interviews and a focus group discussion with environmental scientists. Survey responses classified 90 residents (90.9%) into three worldview orientations: hybrid (n = 50), primary ecocentric (n = 27), and primary anthropocentric (n = 13). Residents across all groups agreed that poor waste management (M = 4.60), upland deforestation (M = 4.58), and climate change (M = 4.51) drive flooding, with no significant group differences. Groups differed, however, on whether inadequate drainage (p = .014) or mangrove destruction (p = .042) is the primary cause. Support for stronger seawalls (M = 4.58), upstream reforestation (M = 4.41), mangrove restoration (M = 4.37), and combined engineered and ecosystem solutions (M = 4.10) did not differ by worldview. The sharpest divide concerned knowledge: anthropocentric residents rejected the idea that local knowledge is as valuable as scientific knowledge (M = 1.85), while hybrid and ecocentric residents endorsed it (M = 4.06 and 4.30; p < .001). Of three management scenarios, residents rated integrated adaptive management highest (M = 4.56; 89.9% agreeing), consistent with scenario discussions and expert interviews favoring a combination of structural protection, ecosystem restoration, and participatory governance. The findings suggest that worldview diversity need not block agreement on flood measures, but that resilience planning in these communities must also address whose knowledge counts in decision-making.

title: Occupational mobility and developments of inequality along the life course: The German case
abstract: On the basis of inter-cohort comparisons, this paper describes patterns of intra-generational occupational mobility in Germany and their long-term trends since World War II. It also presents conceptual links between individual mobility and developments of inequality along the life course, with a special focus on the question to what extent employment careers are characterised by specific forms of cumulative advantage and disadvantage. Finally, it is asked how intra-generational developments are related to inter-generational social mobility. The paper also discusses how mobility patterns can be linked to specific institutions which – together with labour market conditions – are crucial determinants of the development of inequality within a cohort. In its empirical part, the paper presents evidence from cohort-specific analyses based on life-course data from a broad range of West German birth cohorts.

title: From Catastrophe to Legislation: The Payatas Dumpsite and the Transition to Ecological Solid Waste Management
authors: Marloudiza McMillan, Erick Glenn Juanich, Ma. Kresna Mansueto, Anna Rossini Parcero, Maria Theresa Valderama
abstract: The 2000 Payatas landfill collapse in Quezon City, Philippines in which hundreds of people were crushed by an avalanche of trash after a landslide at a landfill created by illegal trash disposal was a critical destabilizing event that changed the solid waste governance regime for the Philippines. It led to the passing of Republic Act 9003 (Ecological Solid Waste Management Act). Twenty plus years have passed since this event and while there has been progress towards ecological solid waste management it is still incomplete. Progress occurred at the National Level through legislation, however, local governments continue to struggle implementing the law due to ongoing practices of open dumping, and continued marginalization of community based actors. This study examines the Payatas transition as a case of sustainability in the Philippines utilizing four theories from transition management literature: (1) governance principles of diversity, dynamics & complexity; (2) The Transition Management Cycle that includes arena-building, visioning, experimentation & monitoring; (3) The X-Curve Framework developed by Hebinck et al. (2022), analyzing the case along the paths of Breakdown/Buildup and evaluating the composite regime strength score for each pathway; and (4) Evaluating government, market & community coordinating mechanisms. Results indicate persistent deficits in co-production among stakeholders, long-standing capacity shortfalls in funding and technical capabilities on the part of LGUs, low utilization of the knowledge and skills provided by informal waste sector workers, and lack of formally established multi-stakeholder transition arenas. Based upon a SWOT Analysis of the Payatas Community, four transitional action plans are suggested: Formalize community enterprises; Establish a community health, housing & human capital program; Develop community-led Zero-Waste Hubs with a digital monitoring system and integrated digital markets platform; create a community political voice/governance platform.

title: Beyond Bürgergeld: Who Can Afford to Say No? Guaranteed Minimum Income, the Refusal of Work, and Control over One's Time
abstract: Germany’s July 2026 welfare reform strengthened the priority of job placement and the use of benefit sanctions, reinforcing the disciplinary role of means-tested income support. This paper examines whether a guaranteed min-imum income (GMI), independent of work-availability requirements, could weaken these pressures and strengthen workers’ capacity to resist unfavorable employment conditions. Drawing on Italian operaismo, the paper approaches wage labor and social protection as contested relations of power. Its central premise is that economic dependence and workplace domination can generate resistance and that collective countervailing power can emerge even under adverse conditions. The analysis distinguishes individual autonomy, bargaining power, and collective organization as related but dis-tinct dimensions of economic security. Evidence from recent cash-transfer experiments is examined alongside the institutional alternative of an adequate, accessible minimum-income scheme with limited work requirements. The findings suggest that material security can expand individual choices, but neither improved working conditions nor collective power follows automatically. A guaranteed minimum income cannot replace collective struggle. It may, however, change the material conditions under which workers resist, organize, and challenge existing power relations.

title: Pakistan Is Not Poor, It Is Poorly Managed: An Empirical Investigation of Energy, Water, and Demographics in Pakistan
abstract: Context: Developing economies frequently attribute macroeconomic instability and infrastructure deficits to natural resource scarcity. This study evaluates that claim in Pakistan by comparing physical resource endowments with actual developmental outcomes across three core sectors: energy, water, and human capital. Interdisciplinary Approach: We combine political economy frameworks—specifically institutional quality, contractual lock-in, and common-pool resources—with practical software and data engineering perspectives, including automated metering, telemetry, and open digital infrastructure. This allows us to pinpoint the governance bottlenecks that prevent effective resource utilization. Empirical Findings: In the energy sector, although the Thar coalfield holds 175.5 billion tonnes of in-situ lignite, commercially proven measured deposits stand at only 2.70 billion tonnes (with 1.57 billion tonnes mineable in Block II). Meanwhile, rigid take-or-pay sovereign contracts have pushed annual capacity payments past Rs 2.18 trillion, driving total energy circular debt to Rs 5.286 trillion (including Rs 1.835 trillion in power liabilities that breached IMF targets by Rs 221 billion). In the water sector, the 16.2 million hectare Indus Basin Irrigation System delivers over 90% of national food production but maintains live reservoir storage of merely 13.168 million acre-feet (MAF). This represents only a 30-day carryover buffer—compared to 120–220 days in India and 1,000 days in Egypt—worsened by 64% canal conveyance losses and widespread groundwater overdraft (affecting 50.2% of irrigated land). Demographically, the 2023 Digital Census records 241.49 million citizens with 67% under age 30 (160.11 million youth). However, sovereign debt servicing absorbs 81% of net federal tax revenues, heavily crowding out education and public health. Simultaneously, promising IT exports ($4.60 billion in FY2026) face serious infrastructure hurdles, including internet throttling, payment gateway barriers, and unstable power grids. Policy Model: We formulate a practical, quad-pillar governance model: (1) centralized public project execution dashboards, (2) independent forensic audits of sovereign power generation contracts, (3) real-time smart-meter telemetry for power feeders and canal headworks, and (4) regulatory facilitation for digital service exporters. We conclude that institutional transparency and verifiable data accountability are the essential preconditions for sustainable economic stability in Pakistan.

title: Meaning through Relations: Lévi-Strauss and Large Language Models
abstract: Claude Lévi-Strauss’s structuralism offers a useful perspective on large language models (LLMs) through its emphasis on relationships within systems of meaning. This paper recalls relational meaning, oppositions and mediation, transformations, and bricolage, illustrating these ideas through Lévi-Strauss’s analysis of myth and an everyday example of gift-giving. It then examines their connections with contextual representations and generative processes in LLMs. These connections support a productive comparison, although similarities do not establish that language models implement or validate structuralist theory. Practical implications include assessing whether models preserve relevant relationships across reformulations, examining the cultural categories expressed in their responses, and distinguishing coherent explanations from empirically justified claims. Structuralism can inform the interpretation and evaluation of LLM behaviour, while LLMs offer opportunities to investigate how relationships are learned, represented and transformed. The comparison therefore provides a basis for exploring meaning and creativity, with attention to the differences between linguistic competence, cultural understanding and knowledge of the world.

title: Scientists held their ground, science did not: public trust in 95 countries before and after the Covid-19 pandemic
abstract: Trust in science, an institution, and trust in scientists, its practitioners, are usually read as one. In Wellcome Global Monitor microdata for 95 countries surveyed in the same mode in 2018 and 2025, with nearly four billion adults, I compared the two questions each respondent answered. Strong trust in scientists rose slightly, tracking trust in doctors, nurses and journalists. Strong trust in science fell from 34% to 30% in the average country, losing ground relative to every other group asked about. Science led scientists in 2018; by 2025 the order had reversed, a 5.5-point swing (95% CI 4.1 to 6.9), about 150 million adults; 112 alternative analyses pointed the same way. Telephone interviewing was associated with about 6 points higher strong trust in science, a caution for mixed-mode trends. Scientists were judged like other institutions; science lost standing on its own. Surveys asking only about scientists would miss it.

title: Seeds of Change: Black women’s organising, Rosa Parks and the gendered memory of the Montgomery Bus Boycott, 1946–1956
abstract: The Montgomery Bus Boycott of 1955 to 1956 is remembered as a protest that a single woman’s refusal set in motion. This article argues that the boycott is better understood as the culmination of a decade of organised political work by Black women in Montgomery, and that the compression of that work into the story of one seated woman was itself a gendered process with identifiable causes. Drawing on the memoir of Jo Ann Gibson Robinson, the testimony of boycott participants, the litigation record of Browder v. Gayle and the scholarship on Black women’s activism, the article reconstructs three arenas in which women made the protest possible. The first is the Women’s Political Council, founded in 1946, which proposed a bus boycott eighteen months before Rosa Parks was arrested. The second is the fundraising, catering, driving and walking that sustained a 381-day withdrawal of custom. The third is the federal suit brought by four Black women whose testimony, rather than Parks’s arrest, ended bus segregation in Alabama. The article then asks why the ministerial leadership of the Montgomery Improvement Association and later commemorative practice preserved Parks as a symbol while displacing the organisation around her.

title: The NGO-ization of Women’s Empowerment in Pakistan: Impacts, Challenges, and the Politics of Inclusion
abstract: Women’s empowerment has been a key development priority for decades, but Pakistan, which ranks last out of the 148 countries included in the Global Gender Gap Report 2025, remains among the world’s most gender unequal societies. This paper argues that the NGO-ization of women’s empowerment, the shifting of rights-based work from the state to donor-funded NGOs have depoliticized the struggle for gender equality. By building upon Kabeer’s discussion of agency in addition to Sen’s capabilities approach and Moser’s distinction between practical and strategic gender needs, it seeks to demonstrate that the NGO approach of microfinance, skills training and awareness campaigns address pragmatic needs while leaving the structural causes of women’s subordination untouched. It then goes on to examine the ways in which donor-driven design excludes rural and religious-minority women, with a particular reference to the Benazir Income Support Programme and how the depoliticized logic of charity has made its way into state policy. This paper concludes by arguing that women’s empowerment is a political responsibility of the state that cannot be delegated to NGOs

title: Urban–Rural Gaps in Household Living Conditions in Nepal: Evidence from the 2022 Nepal Demographic and Health Survey
abstract: In 2022, 94 percent of rural Nepali households had electricity, while 21 percent used a clean main cooking fuel. Using 13,786 households from the 2022 Nepal Demographic and Health Survey, I compare nine living conditions across urban and rural municipalities. The largest urban advantages are in clean cooking fuel, finished floors, and finished walls. After adjusting for geography, household assets, and household-head characteristics, the gaps are 18, 15, and 13 percentage points. For housing materials and crowding, the estimated urban gap is 0.357 index points with an asset measure that excludes the outcomes. Adding the three building-material indicators to that measure lowers the estimate to 0.122. Nearly half of the households lacking clean cooking fuel, a finished floor, and finished walls live in urban municipalities. A rural-only rule would reach 51 percent of these households, while a rule based on missing at least one basic service would reach 41 percent.

title: Measuring Couples' Gender Composition: Evaluating Partner Proxy Reporting on a Two-Step Gender Identity Measure
authors: Christopher Julian, Wendy Manning, Alexandra VanBergen, Claire Kamp Dush
abstract: Many household surveys rely on proxy reports, in which one respondent answers for other household members. Two-step gender identity measures are well-tested for self-identification. Far less research has tested these measures for partner-proxy reports of couples' gender composition. Using dyadic data from the National Couples' Health and Time Study (NCHAT), we evaluated proxy reporting among partnered adults aged 20–60. Nonresponse to proxy reports of sex assigned at birth and current gender identity was comparable to self-reports, and similar to or lower than proxy nonresponse for other demographic characteristics. Proxy and self-reports on these measures showed high agreement, meeting or exceeding levels observed for other demographic measures. Within the two-step measure, congruence was lower for self-identified transgender or gender-diverse partners than for self-identified cisgender partners. Among discordant reports, proxies were also more likely to report a self-identified transgender or gender-diverse partner as cisgender than to report a self-identified cisgender partner as transgender or gender-diverse. Overall, our findings provide new insights into partner-proxy reporting of gender identity and reveal a directional pattern of discordance that warrants further attention. This study is one step toward better measuring gender diversity within couples and underscores the need to intentionally include couples with an LGBTQ+ partner in data collection.

title: Capital Market Depth, Technological Advancement, and Entrepreneurial Activity in Europe: A Calibrated Simulation Study of Curvilinear and Contingent Effects
abstract: European policymakers have paired the Capital Markets Union agenda with large public investments in technological advancement, yet the joint consequences of these two levers for entrepreneurship remain poorly understood. This study develops and tests a framework in which capital market depth shapes how technology development translates into entrepreneurial activity. Drawing on finance-and-growth theory, the knowledge spillover theory of entrepreneurship, and the too-much-of-a-good-thing perspective, we argue that technology development has an inverted U-shaped relationship with new venture entry and that deep capital markets shift the turning point outward and flatten the downturn. At the venture level, we argue that capital market depth amplifies the growth returns to venture-level technological advancement, particularly in munificent task environments. We evaluate these predictions using a calibrated two-level simulation of 4,500 country-industry-years across 30 European economies and 14,000 new ventures, combining two-way fixed effects, instrumental variables, formal turning-point tests, and a 216-specification multiverse analysis. The inverted U holds where capital markets are shallow or average but disappears where they are deep, and the venture-level interaction is robust for growth but not for survival. The study offers a transparent, replicable design for future work with administrative European data.

title: Place-Based Identity and the Demand for Local Candidates
abstract: Voters are known to reward candidates with local roots. Research offers two explanations: an instrumental account, in which local ties signal that a candidate will understand, prioritize, and deliver for the area, and an expres- sive account, in which voters respond to markers of localness themselves. In- creasingly, this expressive preference is understood as an expression of voters’ place-based identity: the local cue signals that a candidate shares the voter’s social group. Whether identity drives the local vote has rarely been tested di- rectly. I combine a nationally representative British survey with a preregistered US experiment (n = 4,803) that pairs a vignette prime of place-based identity with a candidate-choice conjoint. Identity is associated with greater impor- tance placed on candidates’ local traits, and the prime—though containing no candidate information—increases the weight placed on local attributes, with no effect on non-local attributes.

title: Finnish Court-Ordered Foster Care Placement Data (LASTU)
authors: INVEST Flagship, Mikko Hertzig, Mika Pihlajamäki, Henri Salokangas
abstract: This paper describes the construction of LASTU, a new individual-level dataset covering all Finnish court-ordered out-of-home placement decisions from 2000 to 2025 (n ≈ 14000). The dataset was built by digitising, pre-processing, and structuring the free-text content of administrative court records, and linking the resulting case-level variables to the INVEST Full Population administrative regis ters. We document the data structure, the text-partitioning and variable-extraction pipeline, and the multi-stage validation protocol. The pipeline follows a rules based approach exploiting the highly consistent structure of Finnish court deci sions to partition text into thematically defined segments before conducting ex traction of variables . The resulting dataset enables causal analysis of placement effects on children’s long-term educational, health, and labour market outcomes as well descriptive evidence, and supports research on the determinants of court decisions and regional variation in child welfare practice.

title: Response to matters raised on the MEECC
authors: Lavanyaa V P, Tejal Kanitkar, T Jayaraman
abstract: This reply responds to the notes by Schaeffer et al. (2026) and George and McJeon (2026) on the Model for Energy Equity and Climate Compatibility (MEECC), introduced in Kanitkar et al. (2026). It addresses the main conceptual issues; a more detailed response to methods- and coding-related questions is provided in the Supplementary Material (SM).

title: Does Inflation Shape the Phillips Curve? Panel Evidence from the Next-11 Economies
authors: Asma Ul Hosna mim, Zakia Sultana, Sumiya Akter Sua, Sabiqun Nahar Mily
abstract: This study re-examines the Phillips Curve in the Next-11 (N-11) economies using annual panel data for 1991–2024. Because unemployment rate is non-stationary while inflation is stationary, the trade-off is specified in terms of the change in unemployment within an expectations-augmented framework. The model also includes lagged inflation, output growth, foreign direct investment, broad money growth and exchange rate depreciation. Panel diagnostics reveal strong cross-sectional dependence, heteroskedasticity and serial correlation, so we estimate dynamic fixed-effects models with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors. For the panel as a whole, a one percentage point rise in unemployment lowers inflation by about 2 percentage points in the same year and inflation is highly persistent. The trade off, however, differs sharply by inflation regime. In high inflation economies (Egypt, Iran, Nigeria and Turkey), the short run slope is −2.72 and inflation is driven by money growth. In low inflation economies the slope is only −0.75 and not robust. But inflation responds mainly to exchange rate movements in these countries. An interaction model confirms that the difference between the two groups is statistically significant at the 1% level. The result holds with year effects with unemployment in levels and the exclusion of the COVID-19 years. The findings suggest that the inflation–unemployment trade off is high where inflation is high and monetary discipline is weak. Policymakers in the two groups should therefore set different priorities.

title: Mostly schooling and rurality: why older adults' internet access tracks fixed broadband across Chilean municipalities, 2013 to 2024
abstract: Older people's internet access varies between places. These gaps between places can be read in two ways: as reflecting features of the places, such as their infrastructure, or characteristics of the people who live there, such as their schooling and income. In Chile, the share of people aged 60 and over with internet at home rose from 41% to 92% between 2013 and 2024, mostly through phones. The share is higher in municipalities with more fixed broadband subscriptions per household. We ask how much of the gap in access between municipalities with more and fewer subscriptions reflects the older people who live in them. For 331 municipalities, we link five waves of the national household survey to the regulator's subscription counts, comparing municipalities with each other and over time. Once the older population's schooling, income, age, sex and rural residence are held constant, 62% to 85% of this gap disappears, mostly through schooling and rural residence. Measured infrastructure (antenna density and download speeds) accounts for 8% to 17% of the gap. Much of that 8% to 17% overlaps with rural residence. Over time, access rose little or no faster in municipalities where subscriptions grew faster. Most of the gap therefore reflects the older people who live in each municipality. Rural residence describes the place as well, since rural areas cost more to connect. Chile's national policy puts infrastructure first, and the findings fit pairing networks with skills and support that let older adults use them when they choose to.

title: She Is Anyway: The Chatbot as Compliant Auxiliary in a New Psychodramaturgy for Voice-Hearers
abstract: This paper proposes a new therapeutic modality I am calling psychodramaturgy, and a new role for the large language model within it which I am calling the compliant auxiliary. The method extends narrative therapy (White & Epston, 1990) into dramatic writing, with the chatbot held in the role Moreno (1946) called the auxiliary ego, and the voice-hearer held in the role of playwright. The modality is proposed as homework between group meetings, for clients already in the stabilization phase of the Maastricht approach (Romme & Escher, 2000), with the group's embodied performance of the client's chatbot-authored script as the necessary completion of the work. Drawing on Boal's Forum Theatre and Levinas's ethics of the face as a strained but useful rung, the paper argues that the voice-hearing community is uniquely placed to develop the phenomenology of address that this kind of instrument will require. Risks are named candidly: sycophancy, session closure, surveillance, and externalization without integration. A protocol sketch and a brief illustrative session transcript are offered. The paper is written from a Lived Experience Expert standpoint and engages directly with Read (2019) on the inversion of the diagnostic question.

title: Energetic Affordances: Climate Change and Industrial Transformation
abstract: Climate change is reorganizing the material foundations of economic life. Why do some countries coordinate low-carbon industrial change while others stall? This article argues that the answer lies in “energetic affordances,” defined as what inherited energy infrastructures make politically possible. Drawing on interviews with 116 informants (including automotive executives, union officials, and policymakers), factory visits, and documentary analysis, I compare efforts to shift from manufacturing internal combustion to electric vehicles in Brazil and South Africa. Despite similar levels of development, democratic institutions, and integration into global automotive value chains, the cases diverged because their energy infrastructures made different responses politically viable. Brazil’s renewable grid and ethanol infrastructure afford multiple technologies that can credibly meet its emissions goals, enabling coalitional alignment among automakers, labor, and agricultural producers; institutional coordination across administrations; and sovereign partnerships with Chinese manufacturers. South Africa’s coal dependency forecloses those options: zero-sum conflicts fragment coalitions, paralyze institutions, and channel the country toward restrictive climate finance. Energetic affordances thus specify a cross-sectoral form of path dependence, in which the energy base shapes downstream industrial change, working through markets, coalitions, institutions, and geopolitics.
