The concept reorients the sociology of climate change toward classic questions of industrial transformation.

title: Measuring Rohingya children’s happiness through fathers’ eyes: Revisiting validity with a culturally responsive lens
abstract: Accurately assessing happiness among displaced Rohingya children is essential for designing effective psychosocial and educational interventions. This study reports the cross-cultural adaptation and Rasch validation of an existing children’s happiness instrument — originally developed in Western contexts — using father-report proxy methodology for use in Rohingya camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. A total of 14 dichotomous parent-report items were translated, back-translated, expert-reviewed, and pilot-tested through cognitive interviews to ensure linguistic and cultural appropriateness. Following administration of the instrument to 392 fathers of children aged 2 to 6 years, we analyzed the data using the Rasch one-parameter logistic model to examine item fit, person–item targeting, dimensionality, and differential item functioning (DIF) by fathers’ education and employment status. Eleven of 14 items fit within a priori criteria (0.79–1.20 MNSQ), yielding a person reliability of 0.68. Dimensionality analyses supported a primarily unidimensional structure with closely related social–emotional components. Three items showed a small uniform DIF by education and one by employment. A 9-item short form, refined through item-fit and DIF review, achieved improved person reliability (0.71) and retained conceptual coverage. Overall, the adapted instrument demonstrates promising internal structure and fairness evidence, supporting its use as a culturally grounded tool for humanitarian research and policy evaluation.

title: The Quality of Resources Used in Google AI Overviews for Health Topics
abstract: Background: The growing number of consumers seeking health information online are increasingly offered Google AI Overviews atop their searches. Recent research has identified pitfalls of using large language models for health information generation. Objectives: To examine sources employed in generating AI overviews for minority-language queries and evaluate their quality. Methods: Query topics were derived from the Czech National Medical Library's patient information portal, entered in Google, and information about sources linked to AI overviews was collected and statistically analysed. Results: Of 145 distinct queries, 40 (27.6%) did not yield AI overviews. The remaining 105 queries produced 1,231 unique URLs (mean=11.7). General web pages were most frequent (68.9%, n=848), followed by Wikipedia (5.4%, n=66) and peer-reviewed articles (2.9%, n=35). Private-sector entities owned 55.7% of sources, public sector 29.5%, and non-profits 14.8%. Quality scores ranged from −1.5 to 7.0 (mean=1.85). Poor-quality sources comprised 28.4%, while 10.6% were excellent. Discussion: Quality variability strongly correlates with sector ownership. Public sources and structured initiatives demonstrate best practices, while private entities often introduce commercial bias and non-evidence-based content. Conclusion: Source quality for Czech health AI overviews is highly variable and sector-dependent. Rigorous quality control measures are essential for consumer safety.

title: Media Framing of the Rohingya Crisis and Its Implications for Regional Diplomacy in South Asia, 2017-2026
authors: Mohammad Mohtasim Rahman, Jannatul Ferdous Lamia, Junayed Hosen, Md Shahnoor Mridul
abstract: Nearly nine years after the 2017 mass displacement of Rohingya from Myanmar, the crisis remains one of the world's largest and most protracted refugee situations. This article examines how media framing of the Rohingya crisis in Bangladesh, Myanmar, and selected international outlets evolved from 2017 to 2026, and how these frames have shaped regional diplomatic responses. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combines quantitative analysis of UNHCR, IOM, and UN OCHA data on refugee populations, humanitarian funding, and maritime movements with qualitative framing analysis of a comparative corpus of 1,071 English-language reports from nine outlets, as coded by Islam and Shuchy (2026), and of later 2025-2026 coverage. Results show a clear shift from atrocity-centred reporting in 2017 toward humanitarian-managerial and securitised frames by 2026, even as the registered Rohingya population in Bangladesh grew to 1,204,492 and funding shortfalls deepened. The framing patterns sit beside diplomatic stagnation: Myanmar's repeated symbolic repatriation pledges without implementation, Bangladesh's rising security and fiscal costs, and a 96 percent increase in embarked refugees in early 2026. The article argues that humanitarian visibility without sustained genocide recognition depoliticises state responsibility and weakens pressure for durable solutions. It concludes with recommendations for newsrooms, donors, and regional bodies.

title: Climate Change as a Securitizing Factor in the Kashmir Water Dispute
abstract: Climate change as a securitizing factor in the Kashmir water dispute is examined here through the lens of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) of 1960 has been characterised as one of the world's longest water-sharing treaties, as it has endured the wars in 1965, 1971 and 1999 between the two nations. The recent glacial melting in the Karakoram and western Himalaya that has intensified over the years and the decision by India to keep the treaty in abeyance after the attacks at Pahalgam on 23 April 2025 has added another underexamined dimension into the Kashmir water dispute: the securitization of climate change. This paper argues that glacial melt and hydrological uncertainty are strategically framed not as a technical or territorial problem or even as a socio-economic one, but as a 'securitization' of water as an 'existential security threat' according to the framework developed by the Copenhagen School (Buzan, Wæver, and de Wilde, 1998), and the hydro-hegemony approach developed by Zeitoun and Warner (2006). While the Kashmir issue was viewed as simply a territorial and/or ideological dispute, the paper examines how glacial retreat, glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), and variability in monsoon patterns become incorporated in political and strategic discourse, providing justification for extraordinary measures including the suspension of the treaty and the unilateral release of water. Based on official documents, treaties, arbitration records, glaciological information from ICIMOD and peer-reviewed hydrological modelling, the paper provides a climate-integrated assessment of the post-2025 suspension and highlights that the scholarly discourse has been primarily centred on the episode as a political-strategic development, rather than one of environmental securitization involving ongoing processes. It concludes that integrating glacial and hydrological variability into the IWT's dispute-resolution framework would otherwise enhance the scope for renegotiation, arbitration and regional water diplomacy in a basin that is becoming more climate volatile in a manner that is likely to be articulated in terms of security as well as technicalities.

title: The Geometry and Dynamics of Power II : Interacting Political Path Integrals: Collective Dynamics and Probabilistic Futures
abstract: This study develops a mathematical framework for interactions among alternative political trajectories represented as an evolving ensemble of weighted stochastic paths. The model combines pairwise attractive–repulsive forces, replicator-type weight dynamics driven by a mean-field effective action, absorption, and statistical elimination. The effective action approximates the Onsager–Machlup path measure; it is not the exact likelihood of the coupled system. Simulations of Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, South Sudan, Tanzania, and Uganda over ten years show strong concentration of path weights: effective path counts approach one and path entropy approaches zero. Jamming diagnostics show a strong but transient early signal. Its decline is driven primarily by loss of path density through absorption and elimination, not by demonstrated recovery of collective mobility. At the reference interaction parameters, the leading terminal-state share shifts by at most about 0.06. The pooled difference is detectable at 1,500 replications per country (p = 2 × 10⁻⁵), but not reliably in blocks of 300. Interactions nevertheless alter path-loss mechanisms, while substantially stronger coupling or longer interaction ranges can change terminal distributions. A 2016-calibrated historical hindcast matches the pre-registered outcome classification for five of six countries, missing Tanzania. The interacting and non-interacting models obtain comparable hindcast scores, so this result does not establish an advantage from path interaction.

title: La comprensión del mundo desde una modernidad incierta: Sociología de la Incertidumbre y el Riesgo existencial
abstract: This research paper analyzes, from the perspective of contemporary sociology, the causes and consequences of the rise in risk and existential uncertainty in advanced modern societies. Through a literature review based on key theorists such as Ulrich Beck, Anthony Giddens, Zygmunt Bauman, and Richard Sennett, existential uncertainty is conceptualized as a loss of control and a lack of certainty regarding one's own biographical trajectory and traditional support institutions. The study argues that the shift from external to manufactured risk, the processes of individualization and reflexivity, the social acceleration driven by consumerism, and global interdependence have created a paradox: the relentless pursuit of technoscientific safety and control ultimately exacerbates subjective insecurity and "liquid fear". Furthermore, it examines the impact of this phenomenon across four critical dimensions of everyday life: the fragilization of romantic bonds, the corrosion of character within flexible work environments, vulnerability in personal identity formation, and the progressive erosion of institutional trust. The paper concludes that late modernity places individuals in a state of continuous negotiation with instability, highlighting the need for interdisciplinary approaches combining sociology and psychology to mitigate the disruptive effects of existential risk.

title: Identifying numbers in the archaeological record
abstract: Numbers are one of the longest-lived cultural systems the world has ever known, but we still do not know how old numbers might be, or where and why they might have first emerged or in what form. Contemporary number systems have implications for examining and interpreting the archaeological record for signs of pre-Historic numeracy. To define what we should be looking for in the archaeological record and how we might recognise numbers in markings on pre-Historic artefacts, current assumptions, evidence, methods, and issues are reviewed, and recommendations are offered for incorporating interdisciplinary data and insights into archaeological investigations and interpretations.

title: Multi-Cohort Behavioral Telemetry and Longitudinal Attrition Metrics Across Gated LMS and Open-Access Streaming Environments (2014–2025)
abstract: This data descriptor documents a unified collection of four longitudinal datasets capturing user interaction telemetry, retention dynamics, and attrition boundaries across self-paced digital mind-body interventions (relaxation, mindfulness, physical yoga, and yoga philosophy) recorded between May 2014 and December 2025. Telemetry was extracted from two parallel technological architectures: a gated, structured Learning Management System (LMS, Udemy) and an ungated, algorithmically driven video streaming environment (YouTube). Collectively, the repository comprises 1,787 anonymized individual student progression logs in the LMS environment, aggregated country-level demographic distributions across up to 52 territories, granular video-level retention and sequential playlist drop-off metrics across 107 instructional modules, and multi-year annual view timelines. The data architecture is specifically structured to support survival analysis (e.g., Kaplan-Meier estimation), activation gap modeling, gaming/speeder detection, and cross-platform attrition comparisons. All tabular files strictly enforce Tidy Data principles, include automated schema validation via Frictionless Data specifications (datapackage.json) alongside semantic manifests (ai-manifest.jsonld), and are publicly released at Zenodo under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license.

title: A Transdisciplinary Research Agenda for the Sharing Economy in BRICS: Co-producing platform knowledge with workers, users, communities, and public institutions
abstract: This paper develops a transdisciplinary agenda for BRICS sharing-economy scholarship. It asks how bibliometric mapping can be connected to knowledge co-produced with workers, users, communities, firms and public institutions. The evidence is a Web of Science corpus of 443 records, mapped with VOSviewer, together with the earlier bibliometric work of Duan and Sandhu (2023). Three observations shape the agenda. First, the maps show a field with economic, sustainability, tourism and digital concerns, and each BRICS country is tied to a different set of topics: environmental and business terms for China, consumer adoption for Brazil and India, and tourism and ride-hailing for South Africa. Second, formal co-authorship and keyword ties cannot stand in for community participation. Third, the five BRICS countries fall into five separate clusters in the country coupling map, so comparison cannot assume a shared body of knowledge. The paper therefore treats maps as prompts for choosing questions and stakeholders, and it proposes a staged process for validating constructs and outcomes with affected groups. A next phase should give local participants a defined role in research governance and interpretation. Keywords: sharing economy, BRICS, bibliometrics, interdisciplinary research, transdisciplinary research, sustainability

title: A Multidisciplinary Account of the Sharing Economy in BRICS Countries: Multiple disciplinary perspectives on platforms, markets, society, and sustainability
abstract: This study treats the BRICS sharing economy as a multidisciplinary research problem. Platform markets in Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa have to be understood through economics, management, information systems, public policy, labour research and sustainability science. The evidence is a Web of Science corpus of 443 records, mapped with VOSviewer. Three conclusions follow. First, the topic has several disciplinary homes: business and management, environmental sciences, sustainability, tourism and transport sources all carry weight in the co-citation and source-coupling maps. Second, closeness in a network shows shared references or shared terms and does not show integrated theory. Third, country comparison needs attention to institutional and sectoral settings, because the international co-authorship network is centred on China and the USA, with the other BRICS members in smaller roles. The paper proposes a multidisciplinary evidence matrix that links concepts, methods, settings and outcomes, and suggests testing it against country-level platform cases. Keywords: sharing economy, BRICS, bibliometrics, interdisciplinary research, transdisciplinary research, sustainability

title: The Degrees of Freedom Principle of Human Economic Behavior: From Dissipative Structures to State Spaces
abstract: For extended periods, the application of entropy theory in economics has been impeded by theoretical bottlenecks such as conceptual generalization, ill-defined states, and the scarcity of rigorous quantitative modeling, frequently casting doubt on its logical isomorphism with thermodynamics and statistical mechanics. To resolve these challenges, this paper formalizes the state space of economic systems from a statistical mechanical perspective and develops a series of entropy models—including Economic Entropy and Consumption Entropy—thereby furnishing mathematical tools for researching the Degrees of Freedom Principle (DFP). The DFP, proposed herein as a foundational postulate for social systems, posits that human agents possess an inherent propensity to expand their behavioral degrees of freedom. Building upon this foundation, this paper establishes a theoretical linkage between utility and negative entropy, investigates the generative mechanisms of human behavioral complexity, and uncovers the intrinsic link between micro-agent behavior and macro-social evolution. Thus, from the evolutionary perspective of open dissipative systems subject to thermodynamic constraints, we construct an entropy dynamics framework for economic behavior. This framework offers a unified analysis of individual actions, resource allocation, and economic state space dynamics, thereby mitigating economic theory's exclusive reliance on subjective psychological preference assumptions and providing a novel theoretical bridge connecting micro-agent agency with macro-system complexity.

title: Malachy Postlethwayt on slave trade and the prospects of the British Empire in Africa
abstract: Malachy Postlethwayt, former director and propagandist of the Royal African Company, was an authority on commercial matters among Anglo-American abolitionists. The author’s unique journey would be appealing to the antislavery cause. In less than a decade, Postlethwayt shifted from offering an apologetic defense of the transatlantic slave trade to arguing that it could hinder the development of a civilized, humane, and profitable commerce in African commodities and staple crops. Over the next decades, the author became the recognized source for an important argument for abolition: the commodity trade with African territories could be at least as profitable as the slave trade. This article reappraises the historical context of Postlethwayt’s publications in the 1740s and early 1750s to demonstrate how the argument for a legitimate commerce with Africa arose amid mid-eighteenth-century debates about the fate of the Royal African Company.

title: ‘The more the merrier?’ Do earnings trajectories following fathers’ parenting leave uptake vary by contextual support?
authors: INVEST Flagship, Anna Erika Hägglund, Satu Helske, Simon Chapman
abstract: Despite policy reforms extending fathers’ parenting leave rights, many fathers still refrain from taking longer leaves. While fear for career disadvantages provides a prominent explanation for men’s limited use, empirical evidence on earnings consequences remains mixed. The extent to which leave uptake shapes fathers’ post-birth earnings trajectories could differ depending on how normalized leave-taking is within a given context. In this study, we ask whether potential negative implications decrease if leave entitlements targeted towards fathers expand and uptake becomes more widespread. We examine this question both at the national policy level and in the local workplace context. Empirically, we draw on Finnish register-based data for the period 2000–2020, and analyse hourly earnings among first-time fathers using stacked regression estimators. Our findings suggest that interruptions beyond the period earmarked to the father may be associated with lower earnings, if the policy and workplace context are less supportive; yet selection is also crucial.

title: Meritocratic Ideals and Beliefs: Social Divides in Normative–Descriptive Alignment across Europe
abstract: The persistence of meritocratic beliefs despite enduring social inequalities raises a central question about the legitimation of inequality: why do people perceive social outcomes as deserved when opportunities are unequally distributed? One possible explanation is that individuals who endorse meritocratic principles are also more inclined to perceive existing outcomes as deserved, a form of normative--descriptive alignment consistent with just-world reasoning. Yet the strength, social distribution, and contextual variability of this association remain unclear. Using Round 9 of the European Social Survey, we analyse 33,811 respondents in 29 European countries through multilevel models distinguishing within- and between-country variation in normative support for meritocracy. We find a positive but modest average association, substantially smaller than differences linked to education, political orientation, and subjective economic circumstances. Crucially, alignment is socially and contextually differentiated. It is particularly strong among respondents experiencing comfortable economic circumstances, a pattern robust across alternative specifications and more consistent with position-justification interpretations than with stronger alignment among disadvantaged groups. Higher education is also associated with stronger alignment, despite lower overall levels of descriptive meritocratic belief. At the contextual level, alignment is stronger in countries with higher human development and GDP per capita, whereas income inequality shows no significant moderating association. Political orientation, meanwhile, strongly differentiates levels of descriptive belief but not the strength of alignment. These findings demonstrate that the social determinants of meritocratic beliefs cannot simply be inferred from those of normative--descriptive alignment. Understanding meritocratic legitimation therefore requires examining not only whether ideals correspond to perceived reality, but also the social positions and national contexts in which this correspondence is strongest.

title: Written as ‘he’: Colonial inheritance, constitutional language, and women’s representation in Anglophone Africa
abstract: Anglophone African constitutions retain masculine-default language inherited from British legal drafting, a register many of the region’s own languages cannot reproduce. Reform advocates and parts of the scholarship assume that gender-inclusive constitutional language supports women’s political representation. This article measures that assumption for the first time. A systematic census of gendered pronouns in the constitutions of Ghana, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, The Gambia, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, and Rwanda reveals three drafting regimes: masculine-default texts (Nigeria 524:0 masculine-to-feminine tokens; Tanzania 373:0; Sierra Leone 439:1; Ghana 427:8), paired-inclusive texts (The Gambia, Uganda, Rwanda), and Kenya’s pronoun-avoidant 2010 text. Set against representation data for 2000–2023, textual inclusivity does not track women’s parliamentary presence. The weak cross-national association rests on Rwanda alone, while states with enforceable gender quotas average 36.8 per cent women against 9.0 per cent without. The masculine default emerges as a removable colonial inheritance that half the sample has already discarded. Constitutional text marks who a republic imagines holding office; allocation rules decide who takes the seats. Language reform is a dignitary and decolonial measure that complements structural provision and never substitutes for it.

title: Tolerance for Inclusion: Scale Development, Psychometric Evaluation, and Initial Examination of Cross-Contextual Applicability
authors: Takazumi Ono, Hiroko Costantini, Misato Nihei
abstract: The inclusion of people with diverse circumstances and needs is an important goal of contemporary society and building such an inclusive society requires mutual tolerance among its members. This study aimed to develop a scale measuring individuals’ attitudes and behaviours based on the concept of tolerance for inclusion and to evaluate its psychometric properties. The study comprised three major steps involving four surveys. First, we developed the Individual-level Tolerance for Inclusion Scale (ITIS) based on a conceptualization in previous qualitative research. Second, we conducted three online surveys in Japan. Survey 1 (n = 165) was conducted to explore the factor structure of the newly developed scale. Survey 2 (n = 2,526) and Survey 3 (n = 428) were conducted to evaluate its construct validity, internal consistency, test–retest reliability, and standard error of measurement. Third, we conducted Survey 4 (n = 1,114) in Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States of America and examined the cross-cultural validity of the new scale and its concurrent validity with an existing measure of individual-level tolerance. The results of present study support the validity of the ITIS for assessing tolerance for inclusion and its reliabilities may also be acceptable. In addition, the findings provide initial support for the applicability of the concept of tolerance for inclusion in a combined sample from three English-speaking countries.

title: Corporate Governance, Audit Transparency, and Task Environment: An Integrative Framework for Understanding Financial Outcomes in Chinese Public Firms
abstract: This essay develops an integrative framework linking corporate governance, audit transparency, and the task environment to the financial outcomes of Chinese publicly listed firms. Drawing on agency theory, resource dependence, and real options reasoning, I argue that governance mechanisms and audit-related transparency are complements whose effectiveness is contingent on the munificence, dynamism, and complexity of the environment in which firms operate. Because China's listed firms combine concentrated and state-linked ownership, an evolving legal system, and politically shaped information incentives, the marginal value of governance and transparency differs systematically from that observed in Anglo-American settings. By synthesizing evidence from the accounting, finance, and management literatures, I advance seven propositions, including non-monotonic relations in which additional signals of quality or favorable external attention yield diminishing, and eventually negative, returns. Ultimately, the essay concludes with measurement guidance, identification challenges, and a concrete research agenda for scholars studying transparency and performance in transition economies.

title: Medical Mesocosms of Cohort Differences in Spousal Abuse Victim Decisions in Sub-Saharan Africa.
abstract: Background: Contradictory evidence exists on whether medicine explicates social disparities in health perceptions. This study evaluates healthcare systems as mesocosms to understand social differences in spousal violence perceptions in sub-Saharan Africa, concretely, cohort differences in victim decisions in spousal violence (VDSV). Conceptual framework: Medical dominance theory criticizes medical power asymmetry, while socio-ecological theory illuminates social disparities in human behavior. This study investigates socio-behavioral patterns in medicine as parallels to spousal violence behaviors, analyzing how power asymmetry influences VDSV in sub-Saharan Africa. Methods: A cross-sectional study analyzed data from the latest Demographic and Health Surveys (2001–2024) across 31 countries, focusing on 193,232 women aged 15–49 years and their VDSV patterns: none, Discordant, and Other types. Unadjusted odds ratios (ORs) examined associations between VDSV patterns and birth cohorts (BCs) while adjusting for confounders. Interaction terms assessed the impact of neighborhood ethnic diversity, relationship power differences, and healthcare access. A two-level hierarchical multinomial logistic regression model analyzed VDSV variation, considering individual, cluster, and household-level confounders with random country effects. Spatial interpolation addressed geographical clustering. Analyses were performed using the McLogit package in R (Version 4.4.0). Results: Across BCs, a greater percentage change in predicted marginal probabilities was observed for Other type VDSV compared to Discordant VDSV. Overall, women with recent healthcare access had smaller percentage changes; those with a large relationship power difference, especially, showed the opposite trend. Notably, observed healthcare access effects persisted beyond socioeconomic disparities. Discussion: Higher VDSV amongst younger birth cohorts suggests lower SV-accepting attitudes. VDSV differences across healthcare access intimate anti-violence intervention exposure effects; relationship power differences play moderating roles. Persistent adjusted healthcare access effects suggest roles for narrowing socio-health inequalities in SSA. Conclusion: The study results advocate for macro-societal policies within healthcare that address social issues, particularly through theory-based approaches. Future research may evaluate the potential influence of healthcare funding cuts.

title: A Forgotten Chapter of Migrant Democracy: TISBO's Pioneering Political Participation Project for Older Turkish Migrants, 1994
abstract: This article examines the pioneering political participation initiatives undertaken by the Turkish Islamic Elderly Union (Turks-Islamitische Ouderen Bond, TISBO) in the Netherlands in 1994. At a time when older migrants were frequently discussed in relation to welfare provision, social dependency and care needs, TISBO promoted a forward-looking approach that recognised older Turkish migrants as active participants in democratic and civic life. Employing a qualitative historical case-study design, the research draws on original organisational correspondence, meeting programmes, prepared political speeches, provincial government documents and contemporary administrative records. Particular attention is devoted to political information programmes organised in cooperation with provincial authorities in North Holland and South Holland in January 1994. The archival evidence documents TISBO's efforts to bring older Turkish migrants into direct contact with elected representatives and political parties, explain the Dutch political and electoral system, provide Turkish-language information and encourage participation in public affairs. The involvement of representatives from different political parties demonstrates the pluralistic orientation of these initiatives, while cooperation with provincial institutions illustrates the organisation's capacity to establish connections between migrant communities and formal democratic structures. The study distinguishes documented organisational activities from intended outcomes and avoids assuming measurable changes in electoral participation without supporting evidence. It argues that TISBO's initiatives represented an early migrant-led approach to civic inclusion that extended beyond conventional welfare-oriented perspectives on older migrants. The findings contribute to the historical understanding of migrant ageing, political participation and civil society representation in the Netherlands.

title: Parental occupational configurations and changing occupational expectations: Evidence from PISA, 2000–2022
abstract: Research on occupational expectations has largely examined mothers' and fathers' occupations separately, paying less attention to how they combine within families. Using six PISA waves (2000–2022) across 20 countries, this study examines changes in parental occupational configurations and adolescents' expectations of entering Technical STEM, Health, and Education. Four configurations are distinguished: Both-parent, Mother-only, Father-only, and Neither-parent. Descriptive analyses, a symmetric Kitagawa decomposition, and survey-weighted logistic regressions examine changes in configuration prevalence, expectations within configurations, and their associations over time. Results show declining Technical STEM expectations, increasing Health expectations, and modest changes in Education. Within-configuration changes accounted for most historical change in Technical STEM and Health, whereas compositional changes contributed more substantially in Education. Parental configurations remained associated with occupational expectations after socioeconomic and achievement adjustments, with limited evidence of systematic changes in these associations over time. The findings show that changing occupational expectations can coexist with continuing differences associated with parental occupational backgrounds.

title: Now, That’s What I Effing Call Music: Singing, Rapping, and Cussing on the Billboard Hot 100, 1958–2025
abstract: Swearing has moved from the margins of the music industry to the mainstream. Male artists have historically cursed more than female artists, but over time women have closed the gap and, in some cases, surpassed the level of male profanity. I measured swearing in the lyrics of 27,614 Billboard Hot 100 songs that first charted between 1958 and 2025, from 6,059 lead artists, using a tiered word list checked line by line and against second lyric sources. In raw terms, men swear more across eras, but women have gained quickly in relative terms. Women’s songs were 38% as likely as men’s to contain a strong or moderate swear in the 1990s; that jumped to 73% as likely in 2020–25. What remains of the gap largely reflects genre composition. By 2020–25, 65% of men’s hits came from rap artists (the most frequently swearing genre), against 17% of women’s. Holding the genre mix fixed tells a different story. By the 2020s, women’s songs were about 22% more likely than men’s to contain a swear, and they used nearly twice as many swears per word. Inside rap, women’s songs carried swears about as often as men’s in the 1990s and more frequently since 2010. Outside rap, women also passed men in the 2010s and reached about twice men’s rate in the 2020s. From 1958 to 1989, using a measure built on milder words (“damn” and expletive “hell”), men led women by about 2 to 1. Earlier studies of lyrics disagree about which gender swears more in music; differences in genre mix offer a plausible reason.

title: Data Center Urbanism in Silicon Valley: Load-Based Accumulation and Ecological Accommodation
abstract: Data centers increasingly restructure urban infrastructure and environmental governance. This analysis compares how two municipalities in Silicon Valley absorb computational expansion into planning and utility regimes. Drawing on official records and reviews, it identifies two mechanisms: load-based accumulation and ecological accommodation. Santa Clara exemplifies load-based accumulation by converting electricity sales into municipal revenue via its municipal utility. Lacking its own utility, San José extracts value through property taxation and conditional land use agreements while coordinating grid access with PG&E. Across both places, current mitigation addresses site-specific impacts but may not account for resource consumption and impacts across administrative domains.

title: Fractured Trust: The Spillover Effects of Police Violence on Satisfaction with Democracy and Political Trust
abstract: Does police violence affect satisfaction with democracy? We answer this question with three studies in Latin America. In a vignette experiment with a Brazilian sample, exposure to violent policing reduced police trust and democratic satisfaction. Using a triple differences-in-differences design with a Chilean panel around the 2019 protests, residents of zones with documented police abuse reported lower political trust and democratic satisfaction than residents of unexposed zones in municipalities without a protest surge. In a cross-national survey of fifteen Latin American countries, respondents who reported police abuse also reported lower police trust, political trust, and democratic satisfaction. In descriptive decompositions, political trust accounts for more of the abuse-satisfaction association than police trust alone. Together, the studies connect violent policing to weaker institutional trust and democratic satisfaction.

title: Expanding Mortality Research: The Demography of Bereavement
abstract: The study of mortality is the oldest enterprise in demography. Despite centuries of advancements, mortality research has long expanded within a monolithic framework of death as an individual demographic outcome. Yet, in recent decades, social demographic research emphasizing family relationships and linked lives, matched with the development of computational and formal demographic kinship methods, has set the stage for new perspectives on mortality, which are coalescing into a new demography of bereavement. In this review, we argue this new subfield has expanded mortality research, and demography more generally, in notable ways. Specifically, the demography of bereavement has recalibrated our sense of the significance and scope of mortality conditions; aided the development of the concept of demographic memory; produced experiential perspectives of mortality regimes; facilitated understanding of the cumulative inequality in mortality conditions; and centered mortality as a cause, not merely consequence, of inequality. We identify future directions that could advance these conceptualizations further.

title: Diverse Paths After First Birth: Maternal Employment Trajectories in Hungary, East Germany, and West Germany, 1991–2012
authors: Lili Vargha, Antonino Polizzi, Anette Eva Fasang
abstract: East Germany shares a socialist legacy of full-time maternal employment with Hungary and, since 1990, a family-policy framework with West Germany. Did these shared conditions lead to similar maternal employment pathways after first birth? Comparing these contexts requires following mothers longitudinally, capturing the diversity of their pathways, their employment intensity and stability, and separating them by subsequent childbearing, which can prolong interruptions and differs across contexts. Using panel data on first births in 1991–2012, we apply group-based multi-trajectory models and bias-adjusted regressions to six years of monthly employment, separately for mothers with one child and mothers with additional children. In both groups, Hungarian mothers were concentrated in one dominant pathway, whereas German mothers spread across several. Among one-child mothers, no or very late return became similarly uncommon across contexts by 2007–2012, but mothers returned through different pathways: late full-time in Hungary, part-time in West Germany, and mixed pathways in East Germany. Among mothers with additional children, no return within six years remained at two thirds in Hungary but fell to about one fifth in both German contexts, first in the East and then in the West. East-West differences in employment intensity persisted and were larger among mothers with additional children.

title: Complete-Association Factorizations of Discrete Copulas: Existence, Tree Characterization, and Log-Linear Representations
authors: Melissa Bora, Pablo A. Mitnik, Junchao Tang
abstract: For multivariate categorical variables, the discrete-copula and log-linear approaches provide two different representations of dependence: the former uses probability distributions with discrete-uniform one-way margins, and the latter uses interaction parameters computed from full-table or marginal distributions. This article studies the exact division of the dependence represented by a positive discrete copula into factors that are themselves complete associations among disjoint groups of variables treated as composites. Although no nesting, tree, ordering, or binary structure is imposed in defining admissible factors, every rooted tree on the component variables generates a regular complete-association factorization: the map from the positive discrete-copula space to the product of the individual factor ranges is a smooth bijection with a smooth inverse, and the node factors are globally variation independent. Conversely, every regular complete-association factorization necessarily has this rooted-tree structure. The article also establishes several connections with log-linear analysis. Saturated full-table interactions and discrete copulas encode the same margin-free dependence information, while tree-induced marginal log-linear blocks provide complete, smooth, variation-independent coordinates for individual association factors. Such a factorwise representation cannot be obtained by directly partitioning saturated full-table interactions for a nontrivial tree. The tree factorization guarantees that complete-association factors can be manipulated independently, through recursive application of iterative proportional fitting. A regular parameterization permits direct implementation of such manipulations by substituting parameter blocks if and only if each block is a smooth, invertible transformation of the corresponding tree-induced marginal log-linear block. The article also shows that every multifurcating node admits an exact binary refinement without loss of dependence information, and that refinement, local rotation, and collapse provide smooth transformations between the factor values associated with different rooted trees. The article’s results support structured dependence models, sensitivity analysis, simulation, and counterfactual-based decompositions, including Shapley decompositions.

title: Diffusion Maps and Sparse Reconstruction: A Two-Tier Approach to Ideal-Type Measurement
authors: Paula Pirker-Díaz, Radost Waszkiewicz, Matthew C. Wilson, Karoline Wiesner
abstract: Composite indices such as V-Dem’s Electoral Democracy Index (EDI) impose a priori weights on their component indicators; potentially obscuring how political regimes vary, particularly among non-democracies. We propose a data-driven alternative that uses regime similarity, rather than deductive aggregation, to characterize variation across the EDI’s disaggregated indicators. Applying Diffusion Maps, we derive a low-dimensional embedding without imposing a priori weighting. To render this embedding interpretable, we use LASSO regression to build a sparse reconstruction: the Spectrum of Regime Similarity (SRS) that recovers most of its structure from a handful of indicators, principally opposition autonomy and election quality. Validating the SRS against intrastate conflict onset and infant mortality, we find an inverted U-shaped relationship with both outcomes that the EDI obscures, and lower predictive error than the EDI for infant mortality, with comparable performance for conflict onset. Results demonstrate that regime similarity better discriminates among non-democracies and complements concept-driven democracy measurement.

title: Parenting education through an adult learning lens: A qualitative content analysis of a parenting education workbook
abstract: This study examined the curricular features of an online parenting course through the lens of adult learning theories. The purpose was to identify curricular features that may contribute to meaningful learning experiences for adult learners. Using Krippendorff's (2019) approach to qualitative content analysis, the course materials were analyzed through a deductive, a priori coding process. The coding framework drew on key principles of Knowles's adult learning theory and Kolb's experiential learning theory. The study applied themes and subthemes from these frameworks to the curriculum in MAXQDA and examined recurring patterns to identify the course's instructional characteristics. The findings revealed four prominent features: cycles of experience, reframing existing understandings, attention to emotional and embodied learning, and active learner participation. The curriculum positioned learners' prior experiences as background knowledge as well as resources for meaning-making, reflection, analysis, and continued learning. The course reflected a learner-centered and experience-based approach to parenting education. The findings suggest that parenting curricula may become more meaningful and influential when they actively engage adults' experiences, emotions, reflection, and participation in the learning process. Keywords: Parenting, content analysis, adult education

title: Evaluating the reach of an online video advertising campaign to counter cybercrime tutorials on YouTube
authors: Asier Moneva, Joeri Loggen, Eric Rutger Leukfeldt, Maurice van der Stoel
abstract: Individuals interested in learning about cybercrime often begin by searching for guidance on popular social media platforms. Many of these platforms host a wide range of harmful content, including video tutorials that explain how to launch cyberattacks or use cybercrime tools. On YouTube, such tutorials are often uploaded by creators with thousands of followers and attract even larger audiences. Because many of these videos can be followed with only basic technical skills, they make cybercrime accessible to a broad audience and may serve as a pathway into cybercrime, particularly among youth. As part of a broader effort to prevent cybercrime through awareness and influence campaigns, law enforcement agencies and researchers have collaborated to counter the potential impact of these tutorials. In this study, we partnered with the Cyber Offender Prevention Squad (COPS) of the Netherlands Police to deploy a series of YouTube video advertising campaigns targeting tutorials related to two forms of entry-level cybercrime: distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks and remote access trojans (RATs). We examine the engagement generated by these campaigns among the target audience, focusing on when and where engagement occurred, who was exposed to the ads, what exposed users were searching for, and which ads performed best. The results indicate that DDoS-related ads generated higher levels of engagement than RAT-related ads, while socialization-based messages achieved greater audience retention than deterrence-based messages. Analysis of the target audience (18-24 years old) further showed that the vast majority of users who viewed and engaged with the ads were estimated to be non-parents, with males comprising most of this group. These findings provide valuable insights for law enforcement agencies considering the use of online advertising campaigns as a cybercrime prevention strategy.

title: Shared Answers, Different Paths: Gender and University Plans among Japanese Adolescents
abstract: Educational expectations are often compared by gender as if shared responses denoted shared goals. Using Japan’s Longitudinal Survey of Newborns in the 21st Century, I examine 10,227 adolescents who selected a university plan in grade 9, when the questionnaire offered no separate junior college option. I classify their grade 10–12 reports by whether a four-year university plan was maintained or which alternative was first named, and decompose the gender gap in four-year university entry at ages 19–20. Boys’ entry exceeded girls’ by 3.01 percentage points. The composition component rises from 0.88 points under a binary classification to 2.77 under three categories and 3.09 under five. Girls more often named junior college or college of technology; a majority of them later entered junior colleges. Without identifying when intentions formed, the results show how aggregating response categories can make gendered postsecondary pathways look like unequal realization of shared plans.

title: Willing or not: how older adults in Chile respond to the obligation to go online
abstract: Forced digitalisation, the withdrawal or downgrading of offline channels, makes going online an obligation that many older adults do not experience as a choice. During the lockdowns, family contact also required going online. Research on proxy internet use and non-use shows that many older adults meet this obligation through others, but says little about how their stance towards it relates to their use, or how that relation varies across situations. We classify how older adults respond to that obligation. We draw on 44 interviews with older adults at day centres in Chile's Metropolitan Region, analysed thematically and coded by episode: one response to the obligation in one situation. Responses vary along two analytically independent dimensions: endorsement, the stance a person takes towards the obligation, and engagement, whether they use technology alone, through others or not at all, and how far beyond the required task. Delegation was the commonest response. Two further results stand out. First, stance and use come apart: several participants who are resigned to the obligation use technology extensively, while a few who accept it go no further than the required task. Second, the same person takes different stances depending on what the technology is for: most participants express more than one, pursuing the channel that reaches their family while leaving the state procedure to a relative or declining it. A simpler grouping by overall stated stance gives three profiles, Proactive users, Resigned users and Resisters, which match how participants describe themselves but hide this variation. Whereas social gerontology explains digital inequality and non-use through skill, use and help, the study adds the stance a person takes towards the obligation. Reluctant use and non-use can be reasoned positions, and treating them as skill deficits misrecognises them. Skills provision should therefore be paired with offline channels of equivalent quality.

title: Forecasting Cohort Fertility with a Simple Neural Network
abstract: Forecasting completed cohort fertility (CCF) helps resolve ambiguities in total fertility rate (TFR) trends, yet conventional cohort forecasting methods perform little better than a freeze-rate baseline (Bohk-Ewald et al., 2018). Inspired by deep learning advances in mortality forecasting, this paper tests whether an untuned ensemble of Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), named CCF-Net, can improve cohort fertility forecasts. Using data from the Human Fertility Database and the models and evaluation criteria of Bohk-Ewald et al. (2018), CCF-Net ranks first among established methods. On average across jump-off years 1985–2013, CCF-Net forecasts higher CCF than other methods; it appears to better capture rises in fertility among some cohorts born in the late 1970s and early 1980s. However, its accuracy varies considerably across jump-off years, and it falls behind other methods in 2006–2011. When trained on data through 2019, CCF-Net forecasts substantially and perhaps unrealistically lower CCF than all benchmarks, which raises doubts about whether its historical performance will continue.

title: Building climate resilience in Australian homes and households
authors: Michaela Lang, Subhadarsini Parida, Priya Rajagopalan, Ralph Horne, Lyrian Daniel, Megan Robinson
abstract: This project defines climate-resilient housing in Australia, develops climate-ready housing guidelines (CRHG) outlining adaptation measures for a range of environmental threats, and establishes a framework for government and industry action to future-proof the nation’s homes. It is part one of an AHURI Inquiry into making Australia’s housing climate-resilient by 2050. Climate change is making heatwaves, bushfires, floods and storms more frequent and severe, and risks are expected to increase as global temperatures rise. Such events can damage or destroy homes and make them uncomfortable or unsafe. Many Australian homes are not designed for current and future climate conditions, and regulations to improve resilience are inadequate. This research provides guidelines for policy and practice to strengthen climate resilience in all homes and improve the community assets that help residents cope with climate change.

title: Immigrants and their descendants as supporters of the populist right: Finding a coherent narrative
authors: Gianni D'Amato, Camilla Bilò, Simon Mastrangelo, Leonie Mugglin, Didier Ruedin
abstract: Observers are often surprised to find immigrants and their descendants who support the populist right with their exclusionary conception of the demos. This article explores the internal contestation of the demos and how immigrants and their descendants cope with boundaries and exclusion. We show how immigrants and their descendants construct coherent narratives through which they reconcile their political engagement with exclusionary conceptions of the demos. Drawing on interviews with party representatives and activists in the Swiss People’s Party (SVP/UDC), we outline their experience and reasoning. We compare these experiences to other representatives of the populist right and party representatives in the left-wing Social Democrats (SP/PS). This comparison shows that the left offers a readily accessible and widely shared narrative where immigrants and their descendants can feel at home. However, there are different internally coherent narratives through which immigrants and their descendants present their support for the populist right as coherent and non-contradictory. We conclude that narratives offer opportunities to better understand political participation in a world of changing cleavages, and that narratives are a central symbolic mechanism in the contestation over the demos.

title: Incidental Perceptions Shape Strategies for Responding to Violence: Evidence from a Lab-in-the-field Experiment in Kenya
abstract: What shapes people's behavior during violence? Choices made in dangerous environments accumulate into a range of political outcomes, from refugee crises and mass riots to civilian resilience during conflict. I argue that decision-makers' perceptions of control and certainty influence preferences for dealing with violence, and that those perceptions can carry over from unrelated sources. Using a large lab-in-the-field experiment in Kenya where participants' perceptions of control and certainty were manipulated through a financially incentivized video game and non-violence-related information treatments, I show that participants primed to feel more ``in control'' are 4 percentage points per choice more likely to respond to locally-relevant violence scenarios by engaging threats (rather than avoiding them). Participants encouraged to feel more certainty are 12.6 percentage points per choice more likely to select conservative, less disruptive strategies (rather than drastic strategies like fighting or fleeing). This study contributes to research on civilian agency and strategic decision-making during violence by showing that manipulating perceptions changes strategy preferences even when people face identically-presented threats, and that perceptions formed in other domains can ``intrude'' on high-stakes decisions

title: Electoral Systems and Resistance to Democratic Backsliding
authors: Sean Gailmard, Andrew T. Little, Carlo Prato
abstract: We study how electoral institutions affect incentives for elected elites to resist democratic backsliding by a chief executive or party leader. Conventional wisdom suggests that party-centered systems, such as list PR with centralized candidate selection, should weaken co-partisan resistance by making legislators more vulnerable to the leader’s retaliation. Using a formal model, we show that this logic is incomplete: legislators do not solely respond to the electoral cost of resisting but also to the leader’s capacity to retaliate after successful resistance. In candidate-centered systems such as single-member districts with primaries, leaders may still be able to punish dissenters after removal. In party-centered systems, punishment is more severe if the leader survives but weaker if resistance succeeds, in which case the leader loses control over the party. So, party-centered systems produce stronger complementarities in the incentive to resist. We show that equilibrium resistance decreases with the effectiveness of punishment (highest under closed-list PR), but increases with its contingency on the leader’s own survival (highest under centralized candidate selection). As a result, party-centered institutions can generate more co-partisan resistance and offer stronger protection against backsliding.

title: Who Speaks in the News? Measuring Voice through Automated Quote Extraction.
authors: Emma Bonutti D'Agostini, Etienne Ollion, Guilhem Sicard
abstract: Quotes are central to journalism and a valuable resource for media analysis. Yet, they remain underexplored in large-scale empirical research, due to challenges in automatic extraction. We argue that quotes offer valuable opportunities to revisit core questions on the mediated public sphere – provided an extraction strategy exists that measures up to concrete social science research problems. To this end, we introduce QED (Quote Erat Detectendum), a lightweight, open-source, multilingual tool that comprehensively identifies direct, mixed and indirect reported speech triplets – composed of a source, a statement, and a cue – and attributes them to speakers. QED vastly improves on classic techniques and outperforms generative LLMs in flexibility, granularity, and scalability. Applying QED to French political news, we demonstrate its analytical value for contemporary social scientists via three illustrations in political sociology, analyzing the voice of political actors in news content.

title: Mapping the Digital Public Organisation: Adapting Kevin Lynch’s Methods to Digital Tool Imageability in a Local Authority
abstract: Digital transformation is altering the socio-technical experience of working within organisations. Software, platforms, and artificial intelligence systems have become the legible features of the workplace geography in which individuals operate. This technical note details a novel research methodology that translates methods from Kevin Lynch’s seminal work The Image of the City into an organisational context. It aims to illuminate a methodology for investigating how individuals perceive their socio-technical workplace. It engages public-sector development management planners and digital transformation officers in forming the methodology. The technical note presents the methodology, example research artefacts, and a discussion on its approach and expansion.
